title: A Record of Modern Rebirths in the Pure Land, As Heard on Occasion
excerpt: Note: To make these accounts easier for modern readers, the wording has been slightly altered.

blocks.text: 1. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Bhikshu Qingju Knew the Time in Advance and Passed Away in Peace)

Bhikshu Qingju, whose native place is not known, was tonsured under Elder Monk Lianqing at Fahua Hermitage, and afterward made his home at Mixin Hermitage at the east end of Dayi Town (commonly called Tuozi Hermitage). As the place had no incense income, he made his living by selling medicinal herbs, wooden combs, and the like.

, one winter evening as he sat in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name, he saw two youths come and say to him: “Hurry back to your master’s hermitage and prepare for rebirth.” Master Qingju paid them no heed.

The next evening the two youths came again to urge him, saying: “If you do not go back now it will be too late.” The following morning he hired a one-wheeled pushcart and carried his luggage and belongings to Fahua Hermitage, telling his master what had happened. At that time a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat was under way at Fahua Hermitage. He gave his master a silver pocket watch, offered the little money that remained to the resident community, and bought cakes, fruit, and other food to share with the reciters at the hermitage.

Toward nine in the evening his master sent someone to look in on him, and found him sitting cross-legged on his bedding, looking most peaceful, eyes lowered, quietly reciting the Buddha’s name. His master then asked some of those in the retreat to go and assist him with recitation, and they recited until about eleven o’clock. When Bhikshuni Guoyuan of Tianzhu Hermitage came with a lamp to see how he was doing, Master Qingju had already passed away. The ten-year-old novice nun Zhenhui stood beside him assisting with recitation, and with her own eyes she saw that Bhikshu Qingju showed no trace of pain or distress when he passed, but was naturally released amid the sound of Buddha-recitation. She knew him well and knew that after reciting the Diamond Sutra each day he would recite Amitabha Buddha’s name without cease. To know the time in advance and pass away in peace like this — this is truly the excellence of the Pure Land Dharma gate.
Recorded by Shih Zhenci at Linggu Monastery

blocks.text: 2. Taking Leave of the Assembly and Departing

inline.s: (Original title: Master Yicheng Calmly Took Leave of the Assembly and Departed Sitting Cross-Legged)
Master Yicheng was over sixty years of age and lived in the bell tower of Daxingshan Monastery at the south gate of Xi’an in Shaanxi. In A.D.
, on the
2nd
month,
the 28th

day, he announced his leave to the whole monastery: “On the first day of the third month I shall enter nirvana.” He also went to the homes of the laymen Fang Zhaoyang and Wen Qifan in Xi’an to take leave and tell them the date of his rebirth. When the first day of the third month came, his body was as usual. After breakfast Master Yicheng walked ahead and the others followed; when they reached the top of the drum tower he said to the assembly: “If I die up here you will still have to carry me down, which is inconvenient.” He went down of his own accord, refusing any hand, and when he reached the bottom he sat cross-legged and calmly passed away.
Recorded by Fayin of Lingyan Mountain Monastery
(Original title: Elder Monk Dingxian Knew the Time Himself and Sat Cross-Legged Reciting the Buddha’s Name; authenticated by Vinaya Master Hongyi)
[Vinaya Master Hongyi] — that is, Master Hongyi (

), an eminent monk who revived the Nanshan Vinaya school in the Republican era. A native of Pinghu in Zhejiang, his secular surname was Li, his given name Guanghou, his style Shutong. Before leaving home he was gifted in many arts; poetry, song, calligraphy, painting, seal carving — in none was he unskilled. After leaving home his Dharma name was Yanyin, his style Hongyi; he devoted himself to spreading the Nanshan Vinaya school, and the world called him Vinaya Master Hongyi.

The Master’s Dharma name was Weiquan, his style Dingxian, his posthumous name Lihe. He was a son of the Huang family of Tonglin in Jinjiang; his mother was of the Chen family. In the geng year of the Xianfeng reign,
on the 11th
month,
the 24th

day, his mother dreamed by day that a woman in white entered the room, and so the Master was born. At that time a rare fragrance filled the house, and it was known that the child born was no ordinary one. In childhood he disliked eating meat, so deep were his good roots. Before he came of age his strict father passed away, and he mourned beyond measure. To provide savory food for his kind mother, he went with his elder cousin to Taiwan to do business; before long he heard that his mother had taken to her bed, and he hurried home to prepare her broth and medicine, attending at her side

never undoing his clothes day or night. When his mother passed away he vowed to keep the Blood-Bowl fast; he built a thatched hut and kept vigil at her grave for three years. The villagers, moved by his sincerity, all called him a filial son. At that time the family held only one elder sister, and the Master made arrangements for her marriage (her leaving the family to wed).

When worldly toils were done, he reflected that this body and life are not lasting and that the pursuit of the Way is what matters. Thereupon he and Master Fohua and sixteen others withdrew together to Longchi Rock in Zhangzhou. Over many years they studied together the great Dharma that transcends the world, and all of them were then still laymen. In the eighth year of Guangxu, the gentry and patrons of Xuefeng Monastery in Nan’an, hearing of Master Fohua’s reputation for the Way, respectfully invited him to restore that monastery, and the Master went along. There he was able to meet and consult Elder Monk Can. Rejoicing that a bond from former lives existed there, he at once had his head shaved and took him as his teacher. In the winter of the eighteenth year of Guangxu he received the full precepts at Nanshan Monastery in Zhangzhou, under Master Focheng. Later, with the two elders Huiquan and Zhuandao, he went as a companion to Tiantong Monastery in Zhejiang to consult the Eight-Fingered Ascetic. Again and again he received instruction, and gradually attained lightness and ease. Then he saw a white light; remembering the sutra’s words, “Whatever has marks is illusory,” the white light vanished. He knew that what appeared was a good state in samādhi, and never lightly showed it to others.

Afterward he paid homage at all the sacred places — Putuo, Wutai, and Jiuhua — and then returned to Fujian to assist Master Yunguo in restoring Chengtian Monastery. In the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu, the patrons of Yipian Monastery in Nan’an, hearing of the Master’s virtue and repute, asked him to serve as abbot there. Having entered the mountain, he followed the legacy of Great Master Baizhang: “A day without work, a day without eating.” He cleared wasteland and planted tea with his own hands, and after three years of labor the monastery buildings were renewed and gleaming. The Master dwelt quietly in a single room, devoutly reciting the Lotus Sutra as his daily practice.

, hearing that war had broken out between China and Japan and grieving for living beings sunk in misery, he added daily to his recitation of the sacred texts and dedicated the merit universally, hoping to dissolve the sufferings of the many. On the twenty-sixth of each month he held a Buddha-recitation session at Kaiyuan; when the beggars lined the corridors he gave away all the alms he had stored in his bowl over the years. When people had strange illnesses and were cured by asking him to recite sutras on their behalf, the cases were too many to count.

, after hearing that war had broken out in the Pacific and that the nations were arming, he felt all the more compassion for heaven and pity for men. He said of himself that he had already passed his eightieth year, and that though he remained in the world he could bring no benefit to his country or to the teaching. He often thought of casting it aside, and constantly made vows, hoping to return by his vow, to restore Kaiyuan again and continue the unfinished work of the former worthies. Therefore, beginning on the eighth day of the eleventh month, he resolved to give up food. On the fifteenth, at the repeated urgings of the monastery’s assembly, he took rice broth twice more, and then would permit no further food. On the morning of the twenty-fourth he said that this day was the day of his coming and also the day of his going. He told his senior disciple, Master Liaozhi: “After I enter quiescence, on no account give notice of my death to acquaintances. But you must take the personal funds I have set aside and give them to the resident community to prepare a good vegetarian feast, sharing it with the monastery’s assembly as my final offering — that is enough.” At the hour of shen (three in the afternoon), knowing his time had come, he sat cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name, and his breathing ceased. His mouth went on moving slightly in the manner of recitation for half an hour before it stopped. The assembly assisted with recitation until midnight, and saw his countenance as bright and alive as ever, as though in samādhi. The next day, when he was washed, his body was soft as cotton. When he was placed in the coffin his face was still as before, and all who saw him sighed at the rarity.
The Master was born in the gengshen year of the Xianfeng reign and entered quiescence in A.D.
. He lived eighty-two years, with sixty rains-retreats as a monk and fifty as a precept-holder. The Master’s secret practice and hidden virtues throughout his life are too many to recount.
Recorded with reverence by Fengde
(Original title: Master Wuxin Gave His Instructions for What Was to Follow and Passed Peacefully to the West)

Haiyun Chan Monastery stands outside the west gate of Wujiang in Jiangsu. At the end of the Qing the place was desolate, with only one or two broken rooms left to keep off the wind and rain. In the center was enshrined an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, most magnificent, much like the Kṣitigarbha image at Qingliang Mountain in Nanjing. In the first year of the Republic Master Wuxin came to Wu, and the local people asked him to take charge. The monastery had no land of its own; the Master begged in all ten directions, and with his great power of vow he restored it step by step, rebuilding the mountain gate and constructing the Maitreya Pavilion. Last year he built the great hall — a vast undertaking — and it has already been completed. Three Buddha images were also installed, but before they could be consecrated the Master suddenly, on the
9th
month,
the 15th
day, entered quiescence.

Moreover, the Master’s lifelong austerities and many years of heart’s labor went wholly into adorning the Way-place. He separately begged for provisions to meet his daily needs, while keeping himself exceedingly frugal. His countenance was gentle, and people loved to draw near him. A few days before his end, knowing his time had come, he sent a letter summoning Master Shicheng, who happened to arrive from Suzhou just then. They spoke a few words, he gave his instructions for what was to follow, and then he passed peacefully to the West. When he was placed in the jar, his body was soft and the crown of his head warm — a rare sign of rebirth in the West. All agreed that for so eminent a monk, after cremation, his sacred relics should be enshrined in a stupa beside the monastery, there to remain forever for the local people to venerate and make offerings to, as a field of merit. And they prayed all the more earnestly that the Master would return by his vow to deliver all living beings.

The Master was a native of Hengzhou in Hunan, and lived seventy-six years. In recent years, living at home, I knew that the Master upheld Haiyun with great toil and merit. That he should have been granted this auspicious response at the end may be called seeking benevolence and obtaining it, his merit not cast away in vain. I have therefore made this record, hoping that monastics and laity far and near may hear of it and rouse themselves.
— recorded by Yang Dianchen.

blocks.text: 5. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Nengxiu Bowed Toward the West at the End and Departed Sitting Cross-Legged)

The Master’s style name was Shounian; he was a man of Haizhou, of the Jin family by birth. His family had honored the Buddha for three generations. When the Master was six his father died, and from childhood he ate vegetarian food with his widowed mother. At nineteen his mother passed away; the family was poor, and none of the kinsmen took pity on him. He wept bitterly over his mother’s coffin and buried her in haste, and thereafter did no more than weep at her grave each day.

Long admiring the virtue of Elder Monk Longchao of Haitian Cave on Mount Yuntai, he went and sought to leave home. The elder asked: “Leave home from what?” The Master could not answer, and knelt in entreaty from morning until noon. The elder, pitying his sincerity, shaved his head and made him a novice. The Master attended the elder, living in the cave for nine years without ever showing the least trace of resentment, and the elder thought him remarkable.

, when he was thirty-four, the elder sent him to Mount Baohua to receive the full precepts. As he was leaving, the elder charged him: “The single phrase Amitabha — never let it slip from mind; to benefit self and others, this is what matters most.” When the precept period was complete he made pilgrimage to Mount Jiuhua and paid homage to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. The following spring (at thirty-five) he went to Zhejiang and stayed at Yuwang Monastery, bowing to the relic for three years, until he saw the relic’s golden light as large as a Buddha bead. That night he dreamed that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva gave him a scroll of the Great Compassion Heart Dharani. From then on he recited the Great Compassion Mantra eighty times a day and the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times as his fixed daily practice.
(at the age of thirty-eight)

he set his heart on pilgrimage to Putuo to pay homage to Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. He built a thatched hut and lived there two years, but was not at peace, so he left for Mount Jin. He stayed at Mount Jin for three years, and there was a certain Lu Xitang who was in deep accord with him. At that time the Master planned to go north, and Xitang asked him to wait until he himself had attained rebirth before going; the Master nodded. That autumn, in the eighth month (the twentieth year of the Republic), Lu Xitang, without illness, sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away. The Master alone was at his side assisting with recitation. In the ninth month the Master went north; passing through Yangzhou, he stayed at Gaomin Monastery to see in the new year.
In the spring of 1932

, after nine days of begging his way along the road, he arrived to stay at Huxin Monastery in Huai’an. He stayed three months, and the resident community, respecting his devotion to the Way, asked him to be hall master; the Master did not accept. He then asked for a room in the sutra library, and read the canon there for four years.
In the spring of 1937

(at the age of fifty-one), Layman Wang Hongju of Caodian and others founded a Buddha-recitation hall at Dingshan Monastery in Ta’ertou and asked the Master to be hall master. Layman Shao Hetian of Chejiao and others, also admiring the Master’s virtue, sought to take refuge; the Master would not permit it. He only exhorted them with such words as reciting the Buddha’s name, releasing living beings, and relieving the poor. Layman Shao and the rest revered him all the more, and gave thirty mu of paddy land to the Release-Life Hermitage of the town. To help run the Buddha-recitation hall they also asked the Master to be hall master, and he smiled and nodded. Dingshan Monastery was more than twenty li from the Release-Life Hermitage, and the Master went back and forth between them, leading monastics and laity at both places in reciting the Buddha’s name, never shrinking from the toil.

(at the age of fifty-three), the two prefectures of Baoying and Huai’an fell, and most of the people fled; the Buddha-recitation hall came to an end with them. He then accepted the invitation of the monastics and laity of western Caodian and Cuijiabao to serve as abbot of Ksitigarbha Monastery. He swept away entirely the unorthodox observances that had existed there — the Ten Kings Society, the Regeneration Society, the Immortal Father and Immortal Mother, and the like. He also laid down monastery rules: two assemblies morning and evening, six sticks of incense and recitation of the Buddha’s name as the daily practice, and he led the monastics and laity in the practice himself. The monastery had no fixed property, yet the provisions for a hundred and several tens of monastics and laity were all freely offered by donors, and for several years were never lacking — such was the response to the Master’s virtue, a truly flourishing state.
In the autumn of 1943

, the Buddha-recitation hall of Wanyuan Hermitage in Baoying devoutly and reverently invited him. There was a Master Changtian whom the Master held in closest regard. On leaving he told him: “I shall go west on the sixth day of the tenth month. Although Wanyuan Hermitage presses me to come, I shall soon return. You may have someone bring over that jar Layman Wang gave me, and keep it ready.” With that he left. Not two months later, on the second day of the tenth month, he did return from Baoying, and at once felt slightly unwell. Each day he took half a small bowl of thin gruel, lay on his side facing west, and recited the Buddha’s name without cease. So it went for three days; on the morning of the sixth, at nine o’clock, he rose of himself and bathed. Master Changtian, Layman Jin Huideng, and a young novice were attending him and moved to support him. The Master waved them off; when the bath was done he put on his robe, spread his mat, and bowed three times toward the West. Then he sat cross-legged upright and recited the Great Compassion Mantra seven times aloud, and passed away. Moreover, when the Master returned from Baoying, Master Changtian, seeing no sign of illness in him, asked how he knew he was about to return to the West. The Master said: “Once as I entered samādhi I saw Great Compassionate Guanyin setting out countless boats; among them a great boat came to welcome me. On every boat hung the Great Compassion Mantra in Sanskrit letters, all emitting light; so I knew the time of my rebirth had come.” He asked again when it would be, and in what grade he would be born. He answered: “According to what the Bodhisattva showed, it will be at the chen hour of the sixth day, in the lower grade of the upper birth.” Master Changtian showed grief and attachment. The Master said: “Even the Buddhas, when they appear in the world, still manifest nirvana; coming must be followed by going — such is the natural principle. Fellow cultivators who have the affinity, exhort all people to seek rebirth in the West — that is right view indeed,” and so on.
The Master was born in the thirteenth year of Guangxu and entered quiescence in
, at the age of fifty-seven.
Recorded by Shenglian

blocks.text: 6. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Shuijiao Abandoned Chan for the Pure Land at the End and Passed Away Reciting the Buddha’s Name)

The Master’s name was Shuijiao; he was a man of Shaoxing. He loved to talk of Chan and was skilled in boxing. He knew letters and was expert in chanting. So whenever he came to a monastery he was usually asked to serve as a leading officer. Later he stayed at Lingyin and Shaoqing monasteries by West Lake, and it was the same there. But by nature he was proud and looked down on everything. Being a man of many skills, honored everywhere as an eminent guest, he grew ever more arrogant and wild. If anyone crossed him even slightly he would curse without end, and even beat and kick them, so that the assembly feared him. Though he loved to talk of Chan, it was no more than having seen a few koans and picking up the spittle of others. Being so wild, he had of course never really practiced; how could he have understood the matter beneath his own feet? Yet he was quite fluent in the sharp exchanges and turning words, and he peddled them before others, so that many who heard him suspected he had already broken through the root of investigation, and none dared oppose him.

In the seventh and eighth years of the Republic he moved to Yuquan Monastery. As his illness grew grave he groaned on his sickbed in unbearable suffering, and the abbot, Master Yuanfa, instructed him: “Shui, you have always loved to talk of Chan, yet to this day you have no certainty at all. Why not abandon Chan and take up the Pure Land? Would that not be safer? Besides, now the matter hangs by a single thread; at this crucial pass, if one breath does not come, rising or sinking is decided at once — should you not be careful?” Hearing this, Master Shui was startled and said: “If so, quickly bring those who will assist with recitation. And bring four more masters to recite half of the Ksitigarbha Sutra.” The abbot said: “Why half? One recitation, or two?” He answered: “Half is enough; there is no need of more.” When the masters arrived they were divided into two groups: one recited the Buddha’s name inside the room, one recited the sutra outside. As they recited, the sound of the Buddha’s name became slightly hurried, and Master Shui said to those assisting him: “Please slow the bell and wooden fish a little; if it is too fast I cannot keep up.” When the Ksitigarbha Sutra was about to reach the halfway point, he indeed passed away peacefully amid the sound of the assembly’s recitation.

Master Hongchan of Shengshui Monastery knew the man and witnessed the affair, and told it to me. I record it here especially, as a respectful word to those who pride themselves on Chan. Yet it was also because Master Shui’s roots from former lives were deep: doubtless in a past life he had worshiped and recited with diligence, which brought him in this life a fine chanting voice and skills a cut above others. Although he practiced the Pure Land, unhappily he gave no attention to faith and vow for rebirth, and so did not attain liberation. Fortunately the seeds of old ripened in this life, so that Abbot Yuan’s instruction woke him at a single word, and he went straight to the West and won the great liberation. This is ample proof that the Buddha Dharma is inconceivable, and that reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the West is inconceivable beyond all else.
, in the
2nd
month — recorded by Xiulun.

blocks.text: 7. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Chizi Took Leave to Go West and Rare Fragrance Filled the Hall)

At Tianxian Hermitage in Chong’an County, Fujian, there was a master who was a man of Quzhou in Zhejiang. Because his speech was halting, so that even a single word had to be repeated several times before he could get it out, people all called him Chizi (pronounced “jiezi,” the stammerer). His faculties were dull and he knew nothing at all. He did no evil, but neither did he know how to cultivate good; he might be called a commonplace monk who kept to his own place.

Later, when he was vomiting blood severely, a newly ordained monk urged him to recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly. Having no learning at all and not even knowing what the Pure Land Dharma gate was, the Master asked how it should be recited. The man then briefly explained the gist of the Pure Land and taught him the way of recitation. Hearing it, the Master joyfully believed and followed. At first it did not come easily to his lips, but with long practice it gradually became fluent, and he recited day and night without break. Even while lying ill he never slackened in the least. Before long his illness cleared up completely, and he believed all the more that Buddha-recitation is inconceivable. So he came to regard the single phrase of the Buddha’s name as his very life, close and unbroken, never for an instant interrupted.

Thus, in less than three years, he could know his time in advance. One day he put on his robe and took up his seat cloth, went first to the various halls to pay homage to the Buddhas, and then took leave of the abbot. The abbot did not know why, paid it no mind, and did not ask what it was about. When the next morning came and the assembly passed through the hall for gruel, the Master alone was missing. The abbot asked after him and at once sent someone to call him, but he was nowhere to be found. When they came to the great hall, they suddenly saw a man sitting upright and majestic as if in samādhi. Looking closely, it was the Master. They felt at his nostrils: his breath had long ceased; they knew then that he had passed away sitting there some time before. At that moment a rare fragrance filled the hall and had not yet dispersed. The assembly then understood why he had taken leave the day before, and all sighed that it was most rare. This was a matter of twenty years ago. Now, having heard Master Hongchan of Shengshui Monastery tell of it, I wet my brush and set it down.

I reflect privately that the Pure Land Dharma gate is truly inconceivable. A man so dull and knowing nothing — had he been asked to cultivate other Dharma gates, he would not even have known where to begin, and how could any attainment have been hoped for? There was only the teaching of the single phrase Namo Amitabha Buddha, to be held in mind day and night; and so he was able to wipe away a grave illness in this life, pass away peacefully sitting up at the end, and go straight to the West. Thereby he transcended the ordinary and entered the sage, until he perfects unsurpassed bodhi. Compared with those who penetrate the Chan schools and the teachings but do not cultivate the Pure Land Dharma gate, the benefit he gained is higher by a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand times. May those who slight the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation ponder this deeply.
, in the
2nd
month — recorded by Xiulun.

blocks.text: 8. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Zhouming Sat Up at the End, Had His Head Shaved and Changed His Clothes, and Passed Peacefully to the West)

Master Zhouming was a man of Jingjiang County north of the river, of the Wang family by birth. At nine years of age he came to Eryan Pure Monastery on North Street in Nanqiao, Fengxian, to leave home, and was tonsured under Elder Monk Tihe; this was the yichou year, the fourteenth year of the Republic. His spiritual roots were planted deep in former lives, and his nature was kind and gentle. His countenance was mild, and people loved to draw near him. He promoted the Pure Land school and awakened the deluded many. The good men and believing women who received his grace cannot be numbered. I, Huirun, being heavy with former karma, had no opportunity to meet the Master early.
In the thirty-second year of the Republic, on the day of Shakyamuni’s enlightenment, within Eryan Monastery, I was favored with his face-to-face instruction. Last year
in the
4th month,
the 23rd
day, when at the Qian residence he spoke the Dharma to deliver the lotus friend Jinxiang, and
in the
7th month,
the 13th
day he gave an exhortation at the Huanhe Lotus Society — earnest instruction whose echo still rings in my ears.
In the
10th month,
the 13th

day, at Baiyun Hermitage a Buddha-recitation week was begun and the Master was earnestly invited to lead the assembly. His health had already begun to disagree with him, and he sometimes coughed blood; he ought to have rested. But the Master’s heart for saving living beings was urgent, and he looked on this body as illusory; so together with Master Xinliang he came and lectured on the Amitabha Sutra for seven days and nights. The strain was too great, and after returning to the monastery his coughing of blood grew worse. Then his large intestine became inflamed and his diarrhea was frequent, and he lingered on.
In the
12th month,
the 25th

day he passed into quiescence. Alas! That the Master should return to the Western Land of Lotuses is in itself matter for rejoicing; yet we afflicted beings grieve to have lost so good a guide, and the thought of it is hard to bear.
Three days before his rebirth (
in the
12th month,
the 22nd

day) he knew his time was near, and so he instructed beforehand that his head be shaved and all preparations made. Half an hour before the end he sat up and lay down freely on his own. After changing his clothes he lay down in the auspicious posture. Amid the sound of Buddha-recitation he passed away in peace. Though long afflicted by illness, at the very approach of death his mind was clear and his right mindfulness distinct. Such being the signs, judged by the sutras and treatises, his rebirth in the Pure Land is beyond doubt. This year
in the
2nd month,
the 14th
day is the Master’s seventh-week memorial; on the
15th
day the cremation was held, and that day fell exactly on the day of Shakyamuni’s parinirvana. Huirun also attended the ceremony. First, on the
14th

day, I arrived at the monastery and recited before the memorial tablet. At six in the afternoon we assembled before the coffin, recited sutras and made offerings; Master Xinfu spoke the Dharma, and the coffin was carried out to the open ground east of the monastery. At four in the morning on the
15th

day, Elder Monk Tihe spoke the Dharma and lit the fire. The fragrance was dense, with no smell of burning flesh; white smoke curled up in unbroken threads. The solemn sound of Buddha-recitation rolled like thunder. Could such a scene be anything but the response to the Master’s virtue?
, in the
3rd
month; the humble student Lu Huirun, faithfully setting down what he saw and heard, records it thus.
Lu Huirun
Original title: Master Kuanzong Passed Away After First Praising the Buddha)
Master Kuanzong was a native of Hangxian. He had served as a middle-school teacher; awakening to the impermanence of the world, he left home at Hupao.
he went to Guoqing Monastery on Mount Tiantai as monastery warden, and soon after was made assistant lecturer.
, in the
6th
month, he fell ill. By the
10th

month he saw that he would not recover, gave his mind wholly to the West, and asked others to assist him with recitation. Suddenly he opened his eyes and said: “The Buddha has come.” He passed away chanting the verse in praise of the Buddha.
Honghua Monthly
(Original title: Young Master Miaorui Departed on Smelling the Scent of Lotuses)

Master Miaorui was a native of Xiaoshan, of the Tang family by birth. At fifteen he was tonsured; at sixteen he received full ordination. He then entered Jiangtian Monastery on Mount Jin, studying under Master Renshan.
, in the
4th
month, he fell ill. The Master urged him to set his mind wholly on the West, and a Buddha image was brought and enshrined in his sickroom. By the
13th
day his breath was growing faint. As the Master assisted him with recitation he suddenly cried: “The scent of lotuses!” and passed away in peace.
Master Ren described it in a letter, and added: “Do not wait until old age to learn the Way; the lonely graves are mostly young men.” I record it as a warning to the world.
— Honghua Monthly

blocks.text: 11. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: West Hall Master Liangpu Held Fast to the Buddha’s Name and Passed Peacefully to the West)

Master Liangpu, whose Dharma name was Ruli, was a son of the Ma family of Hanchuan in Hubei. He had once served in the army, and, sensing the impermanence of worldly appearances, conceived the resolve to leave the dust. After being tonsured he received full ordination at Gude Monastery in Hankou.

This was in the third year of the Republic, when the Master was thirty-three. He soon went to Putuo for study, turning his heart to the Pure Land. Then, hearing of the Way-style of Lingyan, he entered that monastery in the fourth month of the twentieth year of the Republic to practice exclusively. Master Yinguang and Abbot Miaozhen held him in deep regard. The Master’s heart for birth and death was urgent, and he once lived in the Putong Stupa Court, keeping the thought of rebirth before him. Each day he sat in the rebirth niche, holding the hand-bell, reciting the Buddha’s name with one mind. Later he served as West Hall master. He promoted the One-Practice Altar for the exclusive cultivation of one-practice samādhi. The winter intensive retreat of this monastery was also arranged in careful detail and held on time at the request of the Master, Master Xingzhen, Master Lianyin, and others to Abbot Miaozhen. Ordinarily his vow for the West was keen; he thought only of the Buddha and sought only the Pure Land. In conversation with others he compared all things to the seven-jeweled adornments of the West. He felt deep revulsion for the Sahā world, and whatever offerings he received he gave away as circumstance allowed. His robe and bowl were bare; he kept no surplus goods. He constantly cultivated the contemplation of impurity, and urged others to cultivate it too.
The Master’s constitution had always been sound. This year
, in the
4th
month, he suddenly fell ill with a stomach ailment; he ate little and vomited whatever he took, yet he recited the Buddha’s name with extraordinary diligence. By the
6th
month,
the 23rd

day his illness had grown severe. He at once took his robe and bowl and sent them to the storeroom to be valued, to fund a vegetarian feast for the community. The Buddha-recitation hall specially chose several bhikshus to assist him with recitation. By the
7th
month he had quite recovered, and his spirits were strong. On the
12th
day the monastery held as usual the banquet for those completing their term of office, and the Master ate a little. Toward evening he chatted and laughed at ease with his fellow vow-makers. On the
13th

day, when he came back to the hall from the morning gruel, his fellow vow-makers went again to assist him with recitation. His tongue seemed stiff, yet his recitation remained close and steady. Suddenly he asked whether the Abbot was at the monastery. The one assisting replied: The Abbot is in Suzhou; your affairs after death will be handled according to the Dharma. The Master smiled and said: Good — his voice was very loud. When he had spoken he still followed the recitation. They gave him to drink the Great Compassion water that Master Yinguang had held; at once his tongue grew soft. Reciting the Buddha’s name, he became even more close and steady. At 8:50 the Master recited aloud, and by nine o’clock he had passed away in peace. That day fell exactly on the birthday of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva.

While ill, the Master once said to Master Xingzhen: “I shall attain rebirth on the Bodhisattva’s birthday.” This was surely the Bodhisattva’s descending compassion, and also the response to the Master’s utmost sincerity. Tracing his birth, he was born in the Qing dynasty, in the Guangxu reign, in
the 8th
year,
the 2nd
month,
the 21st

day — the birthday of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. With Samantabhadra’s great vows he cultivated Mahasthamaprapta’s wondrous practice; thus in the present and in the future he was certain to see the Buddha.

The day before the Master entered quiescence the lingering heat was fierce; on the day he entered quiescence it was especially cool. When the coffin was sealed the sun blazed like a fiery umbrella; but when the coffin was carried to the stupa court, thin clouds suddenly appeared and shaded the whole mountain. Was this brought about by the Master’s power of vow, or was it the Bodhisattva’s compassion, to encourage students to be diligent? For true practice and real effort are never wasted; the spiritual power of the Buddhas manifests according to conditions. The praise says: His countenance was lofty as the ancients. / His awesome bearing grave and ordered. / His faith and vow were earnest, / his Vinaya strict and pure. / His words were plain and straight, / his heart was truly compassionate. / He urged his fellow vow-makers on, / with the West as their appointed goal. / Therefore all who drew near him / honored his teaching and revered his noble model. / All conditions laid down, / right mindfulness never moved. / In a flash he left the five turbidities / and entered at once the lotus pool. / May he never leave the Land of Peace and Nourishment, / but bend down his great compassion, / return into the Sahā world, / and point out the practice, / that living beings may all end birth and death, / and students be spared from weeping at the forked road.
By a Lingyan attendant

blocks.text: 12. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: Original title: Master Hengzhi Adorned Buddha Images and Knew the Time in Advance)

The Master’s Dharma name was Yinchang; he was a man of Hefei in Anhui. Honest and faithful by nature, he bore hardship and toil. In the eighth year of the Republic he was tonsured at Sansheng Hall on Mount Putuo. In the thirteenth year he traveled on foot to Lingyan, where he practiced austerities, growing vegetables to supply the community. In the eighteenth year he went to Baoguo Monastery, where he managed the storeroom and also tended the garden, cultivating with great diligence.

So it went for eight years, until the abbot, because of his age, had him retire to rest and devote himself to reciting the Buddha’s name and vowing rebirth in the West. Yet he did not give up his austerities, and still helped look after the garden. From his arrival at Lingyan through his years at Baoguo, more than twenty years of ascetic practice, respectful to those above and loving to those below — truly hard to match. But all his life’s savings amounted to forty silver dollars, which he would handle and fondle every day. A few months before his rebirth, his fellow practitioner Master Xingzhen said to him: “All your life you have practiced austerities; I fear this money will be your undoing in the end. Why not give it away? The mountain is building the Maitreya Pavilion; give these silver dollars to gild the compassionate statue of Maitreya, and the merit will be inconceivable.” Hearing this, the Master resolutely gave it to adorn the Buddha image. Such courage in doing good came from the depth of his faith. Thus he was able to take a high place among the lotuses and cast off all the defilements of the Sahā world. The day of the Master’s rebirth happened to be Maitreya’s birthday. I, Changji, respectfully set down in order what I saw with my own eyes, to encourage those who come after.

1. He knew his time in advance. The Master was old and frail, and I looked after his food and daily needs. The day before he left he said to me: “I am going. Please make the preparations.” I answered him offhandedly, and urged him to set his mind at ease, recite the Buddha’s name, and seek rebirth in the West.

2. He was peaceful at the end. Normally the Master could not sit in meditation. Just before he was to go he suddenly rose and sat cross-legged. I straightened him and propped a small stool behind his back. The Master said to me: “This summer-cloth mosquito net will still serve you a few years.” I asked whether he had any other concerns. He answered: “None.” I asked Layman Tang Fuqing to go and inform the abbot. It happened that a great offering was being made in the hall and none of the masters had time. So Layman Jiang Jingxin was asked to bring the hand-bell to the practitioners’ dormitory. Coming before his seat he encouraged him: “Old Master! Listen for the sound of the bell, recite the Buddha’s name, put everything down, and seek rebirth in the West!” After about half an hour of assisted recitation, the Master passed peacefully. Later Layman Wu Xuzhai came as well; the offering to the Buddha in the great hall was finished, and all the great worthies came together to assist with recitation. Master Xingzhen then divided them into three groups in rotation. That night they recited the Buddha’s name until dawn.

3. After his rebirth his appearance became more excellent than before. At ten the next morning his fellow practitioners bathed him and changed his clothes and placed him in the coffin, and his complexion was finer than in life.
, in the
4th
month — recorded by Changji.

blocks.text: 13. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Suiru, His Field of Merit Complete, Took Leave of the Assembly and Went West)
The venerable elder of the south, Great Master Suiru, was of the Wang family by birth, a man of Suixi in Guangdong. He left home in childhood and was surpassingly intelligent;
Before 1931

he had traveled to study at the famous monasteries of Tiantong, Jinshan, and Gaomin. He lived for many years in the Chan hall at Jinshan and Gaomin, and after leaving the hall he served in the guest hall at Gaomin, where his virtue and repute were outstanding. When he returned to Guangdong he took up residence on Lantau in Hong Kong, stilled all conditions, and applied himself single-mindedly to advance.

Before long, the faithful of Hong Kong, admiring his virtue, would earnestly invite him whenever there were sutra lectures or seven-day retreats; and the Master, to accord with the capacities of others, gave his help in many ways, often serving as interpreter when the elder masters Juecheng, Hairen, and others lectured on the sutras — praised by all, with scarcely an equal.

The Master was versed in both the Chan school and the teachings, and all his life he applied himself to the Pure Land, taking Buddha-recitation as his final refuge and such fields of merit as keeping the precepts, giving, and releasing living beings as auxiliary practices. When Hong Kong fell, he returned south as conditions allowed, and the flourishing of Buddhism on the Leizhou Peninsula — what is called “the Buddha-land of the southern sky” — owed much to the Master’s work of teaching.
Unhappily, his karmic work was done, and in

, in the cool of autumn, he entered quiescence at Qingliang Monastery in Zhanjiang. Because his practice and vows turned back in every thought to the Land of Bliss, he was able to know his time in advance: with palms joined he greeted the assembly, charging them with nothing but the single phrase Amitabha, with no other attachment, and then quietly passed away! Apart from worn-out clothing the Master left no savings at all; Master Hairen led the assembly, and more than three hundred people including Layman Wu Kejiu, to arrange his affairs according to the Buddha’s rules. All who were present felt the Master’s virtue and could not bear that so great a matter should sink into oblivion; so they recorded this summary of it, as a word to those who recite the Buddha’s name and to all who had a connection with the Master.
, in the
8th
month — Suzhong

blocks.text: 14. Letting Go of the Body in Peace

inline.s: Original title: Elder Monk Zhenda Joined His Palms, Recited the Buddha’s Name, and Let Go of the Body in Peace)
Elder Monk Zhenda, whose posthumous name was Weitong, his style Tifan, also styled Yiren, was a son of the Hu family of Shexian in Anhui.

At about twenty he left home at Sansheng Hall on Mount Putuo. After his tonsure he pressed forward with keen resolve, and in Mituo Monastery he entered closed retreat three times, nine years in all. He was on the most intimate terms with Master Yinguang. At that time Master Yinguang was at Fayu Monastery devoting himself to the Pure Land, while Master Zhenda had founded and was building up Taiping Monastery in Shanghai; still he often went to sit at his feet.
In the last years of the Qing, Lingyan Mountain Monastery in Suzhou
was rather desolate

and because the abbot was incompetent the local gentry asked Master Zhenda to take it over, with Master Mingxu acting for him. When conditions had ripened he invited Masters Jiechen and Cizhou to serve as abbot one after the other, with his disciple Mingben as supervisor; later, when Mingben attained rebirth in the West, Master Miaozhen became supervisor, and most of the expenses were subsidized by Master Zhenda. Thus the revival of Lingyan came partly from Master Yinguang’s planning and guidance, partly from Master Miaozhen’s painstaking management, but at the source and root it was Master Zhenda’s ability to give up what was hard to give up.

Master Yinguang, residing at Taiping Monastery in Shanghai, printed Pure Land scriptures, and Master Zhenda supported him to the utmost, once personally recompiling the two volumes, primary and supplementary, of The Western Public Evidence, and the four volumes of the Fang-compiled Collection of Toil. Though he dwelt amid the dust and clamor of Shanghai, his mind was calm and diligent, and his practice was as though he were still in retreat. He also helped establish the Hu family elementary school of Huizhou and the prison reform society, and gave clothing and medicine, relieving the cold and pitying the poor. Whatever could benefit others, he never failed to promote with all his strength.
, in spring, he went to Lingyan to shut himself in retreat, and people far and near, hearing of it, vied to come and pay their respects.

, in winter, his disciple’s disciple Xingkong welcomed him down the mountain, and he stayed at Taiping Monastery. Master Miaozhen and the patrons repeatedly asked him to return to Lingyan Mountain, but he was detained by small matters and could not.
After
the
9th month,
the 19th,

Guanyin’s birthday, his appetite gradually failed and his spirits declined day by day. Chinese and Western physicians were called to treat him, but with little effect. So from the fifth day of the tenth month his monastic and lay disciples assisted him with recitation, and he was exceedingly joyful. At eight that evening he was even more delighted, joining his palms; when his disciples asked whether he saw the Buddha, he nodded again and again. At about nine on the morning of the sixth, amid the sound of the assembly’s recitation, he let go of the body in peace. At nine on the seventh he was bathed; the crown of his head was still warm and his limbs soft, auspicious signs fully manifest — surely a rebirth in the upper grades. At three in the afternoon Elder Master Yuanying spoke the Dharma and sealed the jar. He lived seventy-eight years, with sixty-one rains-retreats as a monk.
, in the
8th
month — recorded by Chuanzhi.

blocks.text: 15. Knowing the Time and Being Born in the West

inline.s: (Original title: Master Changyang Practiced Strictly and, Knowing the Time, Was Born in the West)

Master Changyang was a man of Sichuan. At sixteen he left home at Shijing Monastery in Longyi, Jianyang County, Sichuan (now part of Chengdu), and once served as its secretary. Of medium build, he constantly practiced Chan concentration, lived frugally, and kept his practice strict and pure; the crown and back of his head were both lustrous. He often urged people to recite the Buddha’s name as much as they could.
After Liberation, Shijing Monastery was put to other uses, and the Master usually stayed at Wenshu Monastery and Jinci Monastery.

, one day in the first half of the year, when the Master was living in the drum tower of Wenshu Monastery, he went in the morning to line up in the dining hall for rice gruel, and said to the monk of the hall: “I shall eat only this one meal and no more.” He returned all his remaining meal tickets to the dining hall, carried a bowl of gruel back to his room, set the gruel on the table, climbed onto his bed in the auspicious posture, and passed away, at the age of

years. After he was placed in the coffin his face was as in life, and the fourfold assembly came in an unbroken stream to gaze on him and bow. He was cremated at Baoguang Monastery in Xindu, and a tray of relics was obtained.
In October of this year, Master Changfu of Dafo Monastery in Santai County told the writer:

, before I had myself left home, I often went to Wenshu Monastery to worship the Buddha. At that time my eyesight was very poor; I could not even make out clearly the great couplet before the image of Amitabha Buddha: “Long I stretch out my hand to welcome the guests of the Sahā world and walk the road with them; long I stand on the ground awaiting the people of the world to join me and go together.” Master Chang recited it aloud for me and explained it in detail, urging me to recite the Buddha’s name more. Through his blessing, the very next day my sight returned to normal, and it remains good to this day.
, in the
10th
month — respectfully recorded by Zhang Miaoshou at Wenshu Monastery.

blocks.text: 16. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Master Dahua Sat Cross-Legged at the End: “A new realm has come.”)

Bhikshu Shih Dahua of Meifeng Monastery in Putian was of Bangtou in Xianyou by ancestral home, of the Lin family, his given name Suzhi. Of three brothers he was the second. His parents farmed, and the family was poor from his childhood; he herded cattle and picked up dung, and when he grew up he worked hard at farming and sericulture. He was honest and loyal by nature. At nineteen he was seized as a conscript; he tried several times to escape without success, and remained in the ranks for eight years with no news getting home. His family assumed he was no longer among the living, while he drifted with the army across the north and south of the great rivers. One midsummer, when plague was rife, several hundred men of the unit died within a month; the corpses of the young and strong lay in heaps, too ghastly to look upon. Human life is impermanent and a lifetime is brief — the Master’s heart was moved with pity and his grief was unending.

One day, as the Master happened to go out and return to the camp, he saw an old woman weeping bitterly by the roadside. The Master asked: “Why are you so grieved?” The old woman answered: “My son lies ill in bed, at the point of death. I sold our property for one silver dollar to get medicine at the pharmacy, but the dollar turned out to be counterfeit and cannot be used. In my urgency I have nowhere to borrow, and I cannot bear to live.” Deeply moved with compassion, the Master at once took out a silver dollar of his army pay and exchanged it with her. Overjoyed beyond expectation, the old woman thanked him again and again and went off. The Master put the counterfeit dollar in the breast pocket of his tunic and happily returned to camp.

A few days later a night battle broke out. The two armies faced each other, bullets flying like rain, and the casualties were heavy. The Master stood firm in the ranks when suddenly he felt a violent shock in his chest; he knew he had been hit and that his life was over. He sat on the ground a moment, his mind clear, then felt over his whole body with his hand — there was no blood. He rejoiced to have survived. When the fighting ended at daybreak and he changed his clothes, he found that the breast pocket had been struck and the bullet had burst open; feeling again, he found that the counterfeit silver dollar had been shattered by the bullet. The Master was struck with amazement: had it not been for this “heart-guard mirror,” he would long since have been a ghost in a foreign land

A single thought of compassion brought such a response. Thereafter the Master felt all the more that life is a dream, and the resolve to leave the dust arose in him; at last he left the ranks and went home. By then his father had died, and mother and son wept in each other’s arms at their meeting, sorrow and joy mingled as in a dream. From then on mother and son depended on each other for life; he farmed with his own hands and served her in filial devotion, enjoying the joy of family love. Time slipped away, and four more years passed. Pity the heart of a loving mother the world over: though the family was in straits, she saved on food and clothing and engaged a matchmaker to bring him a wife. The Master’s resolve was firm not to marry; he steeled himself to leave his mother and went to Meifeng Monastery in Putian to take Master Zongshou as his teacher. He was then already thirty-one. The Master was honest and sparing of words, practicing the ascetic disciplines. Before long Elder Monk Xuyun transmitted the precepts at Yongquan Monastery on Mount Gu, and at his teacher’s bidding he went to receive full ordination.

Returning from Mount Gu to Putian, he took up residence at Meifeng Monastery and served for many years as field overseer, rising early and working in the dark, taking the lead in the heavy and dirty work through all four seasons without a break. Later he also served as treasurer, meticulous in every particular, and was praised by all. Whenever he had spare time or on rainy days he recited sutras and sat in meditation; after the morning and evening services, when the assembly had gone to rest, the Master still bowed to the Buddha and repented without cease. During the Cultural Revolution, someone forced his teacher Zongshou to eat meat, return to lay life, and raise pigs; his teacher was firm in his resolve and would not comply. At each of the three daily meals he would set his steamer among the others’, but in truth it was an empty steamer going back and forth: he only pretended to eat while in fact fasting. After seven days he took to his bed and did not rise, and passed away in peace — his firm resolve is to be admired. The Master, grief-stricken, saw to all his teacher’s affairs after death, fulfilling a disciple’s duty to the utmost, and all who saw it sighed. At that time the Master too was caught in the calamity: someone forced him to pull down a Buddha image with a rope, and if he refused, his ration would be stopped. The Master feared no threat and yielded nothing to coercion. People said: “Firm and unyielding, master and disciple alike,” and praised him without end.

After the policy on religion was restored, the Master returned to the monastery, though it was by then so dilapidated as to be unrecognizable. Patriotic monks from overseas gave full support to a complete restoration, and the Master undertook the heaviest and hardest work. Even during the midday rest he would not give up his practice, either bowing to the Buddha or reciting the Buddha’s name; however weary he was, he would sit in meditation in the great hall, never slackening. In 1984 the Master was sixty-five, toiling as always; when people urged him to rest and do less heavy work, he was just as before.

In the first ten days of the seventh month he showed a slight illness, and when people urged him to see a doctor, the Master said: “Birth, old age, sickness, and death — human life is impermanent, and the span of life is fixed. There is no need of a doctor.” In the seventh month Putian was fiercely hot, and he lay on the brick floor of the dormitory for more than twenty days; his food and drink diminished, yet he recited the Buddha’s name as usual each day. On the morning of the twenty-third the Master saw Layman Lin Qingxin nearby and said: Prepare water and bathe me. Layman Lin at once attended to it. After the bath the Master said: “Thank you for drawing the water and bathing me; my whole body is light and my spirits are easy. Now I ask all the masters to assist me with recitation.” At noon, when the board sounded in the dining hall, the masters went to the offering. Someone asked the Master whether he would eat. The Master said: “No.” In the afternoon the assembly gathered to assist with recitation. At four o’clock the Master rose from the ground of himself and sat cross-legged, saying: “The old realm has gone; the new realm has come.” The assembly knew he had taken no food for many days and, fearing he had no strength to hold himself up, moved to support him lest he topple; but the Master sat there perfectly upright. After a moment no breath was heard from his nostrils. Master Miaoxu, who was present, observed him closely and said to the gathering: “Master Dahua has attained rebirth!” Master Daxiang, Layman Yongxin, and others were also present; when they came near to look, the Master had indeed entered quiescence. To pass away sitting in peace, so free and easy — all were filled with admiration. The assembly continued to assist with recitation for eight hours; the Master’s face was as in life, and when his clothes were changed and he was placed in the coffin his whole body was as soft as ever.

In sum, the Master was loyal and upright all his life, principled and never fawning; he recited the Buddha’s name and bowed to the Buddha with diligent practice. The auspicious signs at his end are truly a model for later students. I therefore make his noble character and shining integrity known to all, to encourage those who come after.
Recorded by a concealed name

blocks.text: 17. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: White Light Appeared at Master Xiangkai’s Crown at the End and Rare Fragrance Filled the Room)
The Master’s secular surname was Cui, his given name Shizhou.
by the lunar reckoning, in the
5th
month,
on the 13th

day, he was born in Fu’an Town, Dongtai County, Jiangsu. His family was poor, and in childhood his parents died one after the other. Knowing the impermanence of birth and death, he left home at eleven, kept the noon fast from sixteen, and at twenty went to Mount Baohua in Nanjing to receive full ordination, practicing austerities and study in the monastery.

he returned to his native Fu’an and founded a Buddha hall, lecturing on the sutras and expounding the Dharma to convert living beings, and was deeply revered by the local Buddhists. During the war of resistance, local ruffians named Wang Chengrong, Dong Lishan, and Ding Shaoshan oppressed the people and stopped at no evil. The Master reformed them through the education of the Buddha Dharma, so that they turned from evil to good and took refuge in Buddhism, and all came to a good end.

the Master was in Shanghai, cultivating austerities at Sangyuan Street outside the Small South Gate... Through the ten years of turmoil he endured every affliction; the Master roused the bodhi mind and vowed to suffer in place of living beings; amid adverse conditions he kept right mindfulness single and unmoved in patient endurance, and in a small thatched hut at Qingjing Yuan he still persisted in ascetic practice.

The Master studied the Lotus Sutra deeply and gained much understanding. Single-mindedly he devoted himself to the Pure Land practice of Buddha-recitation coordinated with the breath, applying himself diligently day and night. Often in samādhi he received the Buddha’s blessing. He constantly taught his disciples from Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings and Records of Excellent Words: to observe the fasts and precepts strictly, to recite the Buddha’s name with faith and vow and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, to abstain from killing and release living beings, to fulfill one’s human duties, and to diligently perform all good. Under the Master’s compassionate gathering in through word and example, many good men and believing women in the Nanshi, Zhabei, Zhangmiao, and Zhongshan North Road districts of Shanghai took refuge in the Three Jewels and recited the Buddha’s name with faith and vow.
The Master, in
by the lunar reckoning, in the
9th
month,
on the 19th
day, said to his disciple Zhang Xiuying: “From today I will receive no visitors. I will shut myself in (at Qiujiang Road

Lane) and recite the Buddha’s name for seven days; after seven days you will know the outcome.” From the first day the Master, apart from drinking water, ate nothing, silently mindful of the Buddha’s name. On the fourth day he said to his attendant disciples: “Do you remember the three essentials for deathbed recitation? You must recite single-mindedly according to the three essentials for deathbed recitation.” On the seventh day, at three in the morning, he said to his disciples: “After I pass away, keep me at home for three days, then send me for cremation. Do not weep; recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly.” At a quarter to eleven in the morning he asked his disciples to raise him up, facing west, sitting in full lotus... In a single instant the disciples saw his eyes fixed and his spirit concentrated, white light appearing at his crown; several disciples knelt together reciting the Buddha’s name. In a moment sandalwood fragrance filled the room, and the people in the lanes before and behind all smelled the rare scent. Amid the sound of Buddha-recitation the Master passed away in peace. It was then
, by the lunar reckoning, in the
9th
month,
the 25th
day. The disciples, in accord with the Master’s instruction, recited the Buddha’s name for three days.

At the memorial service Master Xiangkai’s countenance was as in life; he wore his old monastic robes, and his hands, feet, and every part of his body were exceedingly soft. He lay peacefully on his back in the hall, and more than two hundred fellow practitioners and disciples bowed to take leave of him. The body was cremated separately, and that same day they received ashes of a single snow-white color. The crematorium workers said to everyone: “We have never seen ashes so white; the Buddha Dharma really does make sense.” From the ashes the fellow practitioners picked out nearly thirty relics, white, pale yellow, and light green.

Master Xiangkai labored at his practice all his life, with true faith and earnest vows, and he recited the Buddha's name in all simplicity. The auspicious signs at his death and his foreknowledge of the time of his passing prove that his Pure Land work was accomplished, and that he was born in the upper grades of the lotus. There are many other auspicious responses which I shall not describe in detail. Among his disciples, many practiced the Buddha-recitation with such diligence that they kept at it twenty-four hours a day.
Recorded by his disciples Xue Renxing and others
(Original title: Master Kuanlü, free of illness, passed away calmly while seated)

Master Kuanlü, whose alternate style was Foxing, was a native of Xinshi Town in Deqing County, Zhejiang. His family name was Cheng Qiuxun, and before leaving home he had worked as a doctor and a petty clerk. In his twenties he became a vegetarian and took refuge in the Buddha, and he also took refuge with Master Dixian. In the early years after Liberation he came to Nanhua Monastery to help collate the Great Treasury of Sutras.
he was ordained as a monk by Venerable Xuyun,
and in 1955
he received the full bhikshu precepts at Zhenru Monastery on Mount Yunju in Jiangxi. Afterwards he traveled to study in Shanghai, Fujian, Guangdong, and elsewhere,
and in '86
he came to Nanhua Monastery, where he remained until the end. He compiled one book and had it published, the fourth volume of the Records of Pure Land Sages.

In ordinary life Master Kuanlü was meticulous, fond of cleanliness, upright in character and unyielding in integrity; whenever he saw conduct contrary to the Dharma, he reproved it to the offender's face without the least mercy. He said: “For the sake of the Dharma and the Way I do not fear to offend people; I would die content.” All his life he kept the precepts strictly, never visited nunneries and never let a woman sit in his room. He cultivated the Pure Land practice of Buddha-recitation and also recited the Lotus Sutra. Every morning he rose at two o'clock to recite the sutras, and he did not break this off even during his time in the hospital. He was always mindful of karmic cause and effect, took his food and clothing as they came, and never sought comfort. He never accumulated savings; most of his money went to giving, to releasing living creatures, or to helping young monks study at Buddhist academies, and he was forever urging others to give and to release living beings.
Master Kuanlü was the chief seat of Nanhua Monastery. In
on the 5th

of the first month, free of illness, he passed away calmly while seated, at the age of eighty-four, with thirty-six years of monastic standing. Until just before his passing his spirit was still vigorous.
On the 1st

at noon he even presided over the fortnightly recitation of the precepts, his voice strong and full. In the afternoon he showed slight ailments, a headache and a pain in the waist, and told his attendant: “I am finished.” In the evening the attendant helped him to sit in a chair,
and at about half past four in the morning on the 5th
the 11th

— he slipped quietly away. The monks of the monastery recited the Buddha's name for seven days, and he was cremated. The monks of Nanhua Monastery all said that to have cultivated to such a point was quite enough.
Recorded by Ru Ji
(Original title: Elder Monk Liyu passed away sitting upright, a strange fragrance filling the room)
This year
on the 17th
at five o'clock in the morning (the 15th
of the third lunar month), one of the great monks of our age, the Elder Monk Liyu, who had reached the age of one hundred and six, entered quiescence at Baoguo Monastery in Lezhi County, Sichuan.

The old monk was fully lucid to the very end. He calmly gave his instructions for what was to follow and passed away sitting upright. At that time a strange fragrance filled the room; his countenance was as if alive and his limbs were soft.

All his life the old monk sought neither fame nor profit, but buried himself in practice in a remote mountain village, living simply, tilling the soil and eating what he grew, and his manner of practice was austere. He also possessed a refined skill in medicine, and cured many a stubborn and baffling illness for the local people, which gave him no little legendary repute.
Dharmaghosa, 1992, ninth issue. Yan Yongkui
(Original title: Monk Yinkong, begging his food and teaching the people, passed away in peace)

The ascetic monk Yinkong of Qinglian Monastery on Mount Chao in Yuhang County, Zhejiang, was devout in his reverence for the Buddha; he once burned off one of his middle fingers as an offering. In the past the monastery had no incense offerings, so he went about the four surrounding villages begging for food, and whatever money he received he gave to the children, telling them to recite the Buddha's name aloud. That is why the children around Qinglian Monastery all knew how to recite the Buddha's name. Sometimes he also gave money to relieve those in need.
Monk Yinkong
passed away in 1977.

At the end he needed no one to assist his recitation, his body was free of illness, and he never ceased reciting the Buddha's name. By the time the assembly came down from the evening service, the old man had already departed in peace. Three days later the crown of his head was still warm. His venerable image is still enshrined in the patriarchal hall of Qinglian Monastery.
Recorded by Niandao of Shangtianzhu, Hangzhou,
the 10th
(Original title: Nun Shanhui, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, passed to the West sitting cross-legged)

The nun Shanhui, whose family name was Wang, was a native of Shashi in Hebei. She entered the Way in childhood, and at the Shifang Nunnery in Shashi she was tonsured under Master Dingche and given the Dharma name Miaocheng. In the nineteenth year of the Republic she received the full precepts at Zhanghua Monastery in Shashi, and at once resolved to travel in study, drawing near to good teachers, and journeyed throughout the Three Rivers region. In the twenty-sixth year she went with her senior fellow disciple Lingming to study the Dharma in Kham, following Guru Gongga at the Great Snow Mountains and elsewhere. Whether walking or resting, they endured three and a half years of hardship.

In the end her strength failed her, and she returned to Ya'an. Hearing that I had built He Lin Monastery and opened the Way of Love Hall, she came to ask to stay under my guidance and to rest and recover her health. Later a physician diagnosed a longtime atrophy of the lungs, against which a hundred medicines were of no avail. In
on the 27th

, at dawn, seeing that her illness had grown critical, I sent thirty-six people in three shifts to assist her recitation, and the sound of the Buddha's name was unbroken. After two days and one night she obtained the added power of the Buddha; her spirit was clear, she foreknew the time of her passing, and suddenly she rose and sat cross-legged, joyful and free in question and answer, as though there were no illness at all, and she recited the Buddha's name with the assembly. At the you hour of the twenty-eighth day she looked at the pure companions assisting her recitation, joined her palms and smiled, took leave of the assembly, and passed away. She was thirty years old. The assembly, witnessing her rebirth, so free and at ease in her liberation, were all overcome with grief and joy at once and marveled that such a thing should be. And there was much evidence of her rebirth: twelve hours after her death her whole body was cold, but the crown of her head was warm. She sat peacefully until the third day, and when they changed her clothes her hands were still joined and her whole body was soft. She was cremated on the second day of the third month; the smoke of the fire rose straight up and took five colors, pointing directly to her return to the West. Several thousand people came to watch, and all were moved to sighs without end. Now I set down the plain facts of her rebirth in the West to tell those who have the affinity to hear. May all people alike deeply believe in the Pure Land Dharma gate, that most inconceivable and special of gates, for the universal deliverance of living beings. Master Yongming said: Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice and ten thousand go. Truly this is an unchanging and supreme truth for all ages.
Chu Chan
(Original title: Nun Liande, amid a strange fragrance and the sound of music, passed to the West sitting upright)

The master was a native of Baifeng in Zhenhai; her mother's family was named Le, and from childhood she longed for pure cultivation. At eighteen she married, and before long she left her husband and was tonsured at Shizi Nunnery east of Yin County, burning off one finger as an offering to the Buddha. She practiced Chan concentration, and from the time she entered samādhi to the time she emerged was a full seven days, so that people suspected her of illness. Afterwards this was seen many times. In middle age she gave up grain, eating fruits and vegetables every other day, and never more than a single vessel's worth; yet her step was quicker than other people's, and she could carry heavy loads over long distances. Someone asked her why, and she said: “I neither plow nor weave; I live on the offerings of lay donors. Others give up their food to feed me, and my heart is heavy at this. Besides, food is the cause of suffering; if one could do away with food, why should the whole world contend?” So she forced herself to do it, and in time it became a habit, though she herself could not say why. All her life she never solicited donations, yet she would accept money or rice that was offered. In speaking with people she seemed to have no deep meaning, yet her utter sincerity was enough to move them. One year the Hall of the Heavenly Kings at Yuwang Monastery burned, and she rushed there and wept as though she had lost her own parents, grieving that the golden image should be burned and living beings come to harm.

This year she was eighty-one. When her diarrhea first began she said: “The time of my rebirth is near.” To those who came to visit her illness she spoke of the vastness of the sea of suffering and of the need to rely on the Buddha's power. On the evening of the fourth day of the intercalary fourth month, at eight o'clock, she suddenly rose and bathed, then sat cross-legged and recited the Buddha's name. After a little while a strange fragrance filled the room, and faintly the sound of drums and music was heard; then she passed away seated upright. Earlier, the old mother of the Hanlin reader Wang had been a devoted follower of the Buddha and was the master's closest friend, almost as a mother is to a son; and so the reader recorded much of the master's practice and gave her abundant praise. This account is based on a letter from the master's junior disciple Shangen and is drawn from the reader's Miscellany of the Cassia Window, together with what I myself witnessed; I am confident that not a single word of it is fabricated.
Lin Depu

blocks.text: 3. Passing to the West with a Smile

inline.s: (Original title: Nun Miaoru wrote out sutras in blood from her own veins and passed to the West with a smile)

The bhikshuni Miaoru, a woman of Yangzhou in Jiangsu, left home at the Yishou Nunnery in that city at the age of thirteen. At nineteen she went to Mount Baohua to receive the full precepts. The following year she returned to Yangzhou and stayed at Lingyin Monastery to learn the rules and ceremonies. Soon, through circumstances, she moved to Hangzhou and stayed at Longhua Nunnery on Mount Liangdao for all of eighteen years. In the end she was abbess of Wo Guanyin Nunnery on Qingchun Gate Street in Hangzhou, when she was forty-nine years old. Her brahma conduct was strict and pure and her vows were firm; she built the Hall of the Great Being. Every day she performed one full repentance of Great Compassion, recited the Kṣitigarbha Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, and the preface to the Lotus Sutra, for decades as though it were a single day. The rest of her time she devoted to reciting mantras and the Buddha's name. She once wrote out a copy of the Lotus Sutra in blood drawn from her own body, and burned off a finger as an offering to the Buddha. Ordinarily she never tired of releasing living creatures and of giving cool tea, medicines for heatstroke, coffins, and other such good works.
from the sixth day of the eighth month
she suffered from dysentery that would not heal.
On the 25th
the illness grew grave;
on the 14th
a good friend visited her illness and urged her to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. By the 19th
she saw the Three Sages of the West with her own eyes and instructed those assisting her that the sound of the Buddha's name must not break off.
On the 22nd

at noon she passed to the West amid the recitation, at the age of sixty-three. Her face was as if alive, and a smile was on her lips. Seeing that she saw the Buddha come in person and told others to assist her recitation, we may know that she was one who could be master of herself at the end. Judging by her diligent practice in ordinary times, her rebirth is certain. I myself took part in the assisted recitation, though on the day of her passing I happened to be kept away by heavy snow. Yet her lifelong lovely conduct must not go unrecorded, and so I have written this account, to prove that merit is never cast away in vain and that its fruit is never won by chance.
Mu Lian
(Original title: Nun Yuanxing, with a rich strange fragrance, attained rebirth through Buddha-recitation)

My late teacher, the bhikshuni Yuanxing, was a native of Linhai County in Zhejiang. Her secular name was Hu Ruiqing, and at twenty she graduated from a higher normal school for women, after which she taught for many years in various places in eastern Zhejiang around Ningbo. She governed herself strictly and taught with method, and the students who passed through her hands were a brilliant company of the time.
It was about 1947
that she began,
and from that time she and I taught together at the Buddhist Cidong Home for the Old and Young attached to Jingyuan Monastery in Cixi.
In the forty years that followed
we were almost never apart,
so that each depended on the other for her very life.

When my late teacher was about forty she left home at Baiyun Nunnery in Cixi, under the old nun Changde as her teacher. Afterwards she received the full precepts at Guanzong Monastery in Ningbo. In the mid-fifties, after the Cidong Home for the Old and Young closed, she was invited to my own house (Wang Family Village, Juedu Township, Zhenhai) to cultivate the Pure Land work together. On the wages I earned from teaching, the two of us lived a plain Buddhist life, leaning on one another. Morning and evening she steeped herself in practice, benefiting living beings as conditions allowed, for decades as though it were a single day.

On the nineteenth day of the first month of this year my late teacher caught a slight chill and came down with a cold. After sitting up in bed reciting the Buddha's name for several days she recovered as usual. Afterwards she felt that her strength, her eyesight, and her complexion were even better than before. Every day she bowed and recited, cooked, received guests, and expounded the Dharma, all as usual, and she talked and laughed with more spirit than ever. On the afternoon of the third day of the second month she asked me to heat water, and she wiped her body and washed her feet and put on new clothes, trousers, and socks. She even helped me wash and hang the clothes, and then told stories, walked in the garden, and did her evening service of bowing and recitation, going to bed at nine.
On the morning of the fourth she ate a bowl of glutinous rice porridge

after moving her bowels freely, and felt a little weak. At about half past two in the afternoon she sat on the bed reciting the Buddha's name, and soon told me to burn incense. She recited until about half past two,

her voice gradually sinking; and just as I was about to help her lie down to rest, I suddenly smelled a rich and strange fragrance. Wang Huanjie, Wang Houxun, and others were present too, and all of them smelled this fragrance such as they had never smelled before. Her hands, joined in prayer, dropped; a smile came to her face, and we knew that she had passed away in peace with a smile. The time was forty minutes past two in the afternoon of the fourth day of the second lunar month. Three or four hours later

her whole body was cold, only the crown of her head still warm. After twenty hours her remains were brought to the mourning hall. Three days later, when we took our leave of her body, a hundred students from the three townships of Xiepu, Juedu, and Shiqifang came to see her off, and all of them saw that her countenance was unchanged, smiling and kindly, showing the marks of a bodhisattva, more dignified than in life; and they believed with conviction that the auspicious signs were manifest and the Pure Land work accomplished, and that her rebirth in the Pure Land was attested beyond doubt. Because of this the villagers and neighbors aroused the aspiration, and many took refuge in the Buddha.

In accordance with my late teacher's testament, everything after her death was kept simple: no announcement of the death, no ceremony or display of any kind, and all her belongings given to monasteries for the use of monks and nuns. When we were sorting through her things we found a farewell letter she had written but not sent to her close kin in the world, and taken together with her bath and change of clothes on the afternoon of the third, her foreknowledge of the time of her passing is certain.
