My late teacher was eighty years old at her death, with forty-seven years of monastic standing. All that is recorded above is fact; because she did not like to speak of worldly matters, I do not know the details of her family in the world.
In the spring of 1987,
the year dingmao, respectfully recorded by Wang Ruyu of Zhenhai
(Original title: Nun Fuhui passed away in samādhi into the Land of Ultimate Bliss)

At Daxingshan Monastery in Yuanli, Taiwan, there was a bhikshuni named Fuhui, whose family name was Chen. She had a middle-school education, and after marriage bore a son and a daughter; sadly she lost her husband while still young, and, struck by the impermanence of life and the abundance of suffering and scarcity of joy, she resolutely left home. After her tonsure she labored hard at her practice, eating nothing after noon and never lying down to sleep (at night she sat and rested a little), and keeping silence, speaking not a word, for thirty years as though it were a single day. Such a spirit of diligence fills one with deep respect.

Nun Fuhui took the daily recitation of the Great Compassion Mantra as her practice, and the Great Compassion water she consecrated had remarkable effects: the sick who drank it with devotion were healed of every illness, so that people marveled at the inconceivability of the Buddha's power.

In the first few years after she left home the master ate no grain, taking only fruit and the Great Compassion water she herself had consecrated to sustain her body. She loved to sit, and often entered samādhi, remaining motionless and without rising for days on end; her fellow practitioners saw it again and again, and thought nothing strange of it.
In the first ten days of the first lunar month of 1985
Nun Fuhui entered samādhi again. Ten days passed and she had not emerged.
Her fellow practitioners recited the Buddha's name aloud,

hoping to bring her out of samādhi, but to their surprise the nun had already passed away within it. After her body was cremated, more than a thousand five-colored relics were obtained. When the four assemblies heard of it they came hurrying to gaze upon the relics, deeply sighing that the master's ascetic practice in life had not been in vain. Some also said that if she had not been cremated she might perhaps have emerged from samādhi again.
The master had thirty years of monastic standing and was fifty-six years old. All said that she was an outstanding jewel among the monks of modern times.
From the reference room of the World Institute of Religion, City of Ten Thousand Buddhas
(Original title: Nun Kuanzan foreknew the time and attained rebirth in earnest)
The bhikshuni Kuanzan was a native of Nanchang in Jiangxi and a disciple of the Venerable Xuyun. I came to know her in 1982.

At that time she was the incense-and-lamp attendant at Yaotian Chan Monastery, conscientious in all she did and exact in every particular. She was straightforward by nature, and no matter who had made a mistake or broken a rule, she would rebuke them loudly without the least mercy. In ordinary times she delighted in helping others, was gentle in manner, and warm in her dealings. Whatever the faithful offered her, no matter how much, she always handed over to the community for the support of all, never enjoying it herself. When she had saved up money she would sponsor the Rite of the Flaming Mouth, the Great Compassion Repentance, or universal Buddha-recitation for the deliverance of living beings, or go on pilgrimage to the mountains. In her seventies she still feared no hardship and made pilgrimage to Mount Wutai, Mount Emei, and the other four great sacred mountains.

As she approached eighty her strength gradually failed and her movements slowed. She still rose before three o'clock every day to adorn the Buddha hall, and she still struck the bell and beat the drum. Such labor she kept up without a break through cold and heat, the same in sickness as in health; even when ill she would not let another take her place, and to the end she did her duty and kept her post. Only when she had aged so far that she could no longer straighten her back and walked with a totter did she resign the office of incense-and-lamp attendant, yet she still came to the hall on time for the morning and evening services. I remember once at the service she wore her ceremonial robe and stood in the front row, with me behind her. I saw her head bowed and her back bent, and from a distance she looked for all the world like a black stone tablet with rounded corners. My heart ached and tears came to my eyes, but more than that I felt reverence and deep feeling. Whenever I myself fell ill and my mind turned to laziness, I remembered her, that image of a stone tablet that never ceased in its diligence.
In the spring of 1989,

when she was eighty, she fell ill. By autumn she was bloated and passing blood in her urine, and was sent to Zhoutian Hospital for treatment. I went to see her and saw that her case records showed no dangerous illness, so I urged her to set her mind at rest and take treatment. She said: “I am old and it is time to go. Everyone is busy; why must I trouble people (at the time her junior disciple Guoming was at the hospital caring for her)? Besides, if I cannot be cured for the moment and die in a hospital
my death would be contrary to the Dharma
and all the merit of a lifetime of practice would be lost.”
She firmly demanded to leave the hospital.
After leaving the hospital she suffered for about three months
and then gradually improved. On the fifth day of the twelfth month
she said to Master Facan, who lived in the room next door
“Please trim my nails for me.” Yaotian Monastery farms and practices Chan side by side and supports itself by its own labor,
and most of its members were elderly,
so everyone was very busy. Master Facan said
“I have no time now.” She said
“Let it be a karmic connection.
I have only two or three days left.” On the morning of the eighth day of the twelfth month
she still ate a bowl of the laba porridge
and in the morning
she asked the young nun who cared for her to shave her head
and bathe her,
and said
“I shall be leaving tonight.”
She ate no lunch at noon
and lay on the bed without any pain. At five o'clock in the afternoon
she asked everyone to come and assist her recitation, instructing them to bring the lead-encased bell and the small wooden fish
and to be as solemn and earnest as always.
They were reciting “The Assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the Lotus Pool Ocean,”
the Verses in Praise of the Buddha,
and the dedication of merit
and each time she stretched her hands out from under the quilt and joined her palms. When the recitation ended, before seven o'clock
everyone went back to eat. Since she was in no pain
and her spirit was excellent
and her mind perfectly clear
and she had eaten a big bowl of laba porridge that morning
the young nuns simply did not believe she would really go, and while they ate they said to one another
“Sister Kuanzan is really something.
She says she is going today, but the time has not come; even if you wanted to go, you could not.” Just then
Sister Kuanying, who lived opposite Sister Kuanzan, came running up breathlessly and said
“Hurry!
Sister Kuanzan is about to leave.” (It turned out that not long after everyone had gone
Sister Kuanzan had called out loudly to the old bhikshuni Kuanying across the way
“Fellow disciple, fellow disciple, quickly call them all to come and recite the Buddha's name and open the road for me, I am about to go.”) When everyone went over with Sister Kuanying
she could no longer speak
but her two eyes were opened very wide
and when Sister Facan reached out her hand to close them
they would not come down.
Then, after more than ten minutes of Buddha-recitation
her eyes closed of themselves and a smile appeared on her face.
The next day, when they changed her clothes for her
and put the wind cap on her head
and set her upright in the coffin
her face was ruddy
with a faint smile,
far more dignified than in ordinary life.
She was cremated on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, and truly the conditions were good.
The great monk Yicheng of Zhenru Monastery, with two other monks, was passing through Yaotian
and on the night of the fourteenth he stayed at Yaotian Monastery
and the next day he lit the pyre for Sister Kuanzan
and spoke the Dharma. The great monk said
“Having foreknown the time of her passing, she may be reckoned as having attained rebirth.” Everyone said
“Sister Kuanzan was always willing to make karmic connections in ordinary life
and so after death she had such wonderfully apt circumstances.” Three days after the cremation
Sister Huaguang went to gather the ashes
and the ashes were placed in the Haihui Stupa of Zhenru Monastery
Sister Huaguang told me that Sister Kuanzan's skull had pink
emerald green
and gold, three colors in all.
I am only setting down the facts as they were
without adding a single view of my own
In the five or six years
of my contact with Sister Kuanzan
the impression she left on me was
this: (1) patient endurance of hardship
doing her duty to the full; (2) a heart upright
and a spirit brave and diligent; (3) no thought of private gain, and care for others.
Respectfully recorded by Yao Nianzhou of Yongxiu
(Original title: The present-day holy nun, the Venerable Tongyuan, has returned in peace to the Land of Nurture)
The nun Tongyuan, a woman of rank
whose family name was Zhai
and whose given name was Yaochen.

She was born on the sixth day of the ninth month of the old calendar in Shuangcheng County, Heilongjiang. Her father Zhai Wenxuan was a provincial graduate of the late Qing and served as salt commissioner
and was governor of Fengtian Province (now Liaoning) in Zhang Zuolin's time. In Zhang Xueliang's time
he assisted in his government affairs. Her mother Li Shuhua worked in education and left home in her later years
and entered quiescence at Mount Wutai at the age of eighty-three
The master was
she graduated from the economics department of the Beijing Women's College of Arts and Sciences.
From 1938 to
she went to Beijing to hear the Elder Monk Cizhou lecture on the Avatamsaka Sutra.
she was tonsured in Beijing under the Elder Monk Cizhou. In the same year she received the full precepts at Guangji Monastery. Afterwards she studied under the nun Kaihui.
From 1941 to
she studied and lectured on the sutras at Tongjiao Monastery.
From 1953 to
she attended the nun Kaihui and her mother in their move to Mount Wutai, staying at the Xiaomaopeng and other monasteries.
she became abbess of Wulang Temple.
During the Cultural Revolution
she moved to Nanshan Temple.
she moved to Guifeng Temple.

she kept the summer retreat at the Xilian Hut in Dandong, Liaoning. For the two assemblies of lay followers she transmitted a full set of bodhisattva precepts. In autumn she moved to Dayuan Temple in the Zhongnan Mountains.
she moved to Qingliang Hut.
she established a Dharma-conforming precept-transmission center at Jixiang Hut in Qian County.
In the autumn of 1990
she made pilgrimage to Mount Emei again. She met with the Venerable Nun Longlian.
On the sixth day of the third month of 1991
she returned in peace to the Land of Nurture at Chongshan Monastery in Taiyuan. She was seventy-eight years old, with fifty-one years of monastic standing.

In her lifetime the Venerable Yuan served as a standing councilor of the Buddhist Association of China, a standing councilor and vice-president of the Buddhist Association of Shanxi Province, vice-president of the Buddhist Association of Mount Wutai, and a member of the fourth, fifth, and sixth Chinese People's Political Consultative Conferences of Wutai County.

The whole life of the Venerable Yuan took the propagation of the Avatamsaka as its guide, strict purity of the vinaya as its root, the training of nuns as its own charge, and the single-minded cultivation of the Pure Land as its home.

After leaving home the Venerable Yuan studied the Avatamsaka deeply, and for more than thirty years at Mount Wutai she never broke off lecturing and reciting it. She spread the precepts and kept the vinaya strictly pure; by word and by example she transformed a great many people without their knowing it. To restore the discipline of the Sangha she traveled north and south despite serious illness and twice transmitted the two-fold Sangha ordination. When she lectured on the Markers of the Bhikshuni Precepts of the Four-Part Vinaya during the summer retreat, monks and students from home and abroad gathered from all directions, and for those who could not attend she fulfilled their wish by means of recordings.

In her teachings to the faithful the Venerable Yuan always made the keeping of the precepts and the recitation of the Buddha's name and the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land her highest theme. She often said: “Recite the Buddha's name with one mind; this is the true cause of escaping suffering. If you can be born in the West, everything is accomplished; otherwise, when the fruits of beginningless karmic causes ripen, they are hard to escape! Birth and death and the wheel of rebirth — fearful, fearful!” Such was the depth of her compassion.

after the Spring Festival the Venerable showed illness, and knowing that her worldly conditions were nearly exhausted, she instructed her constant attendant disciples to make every preparation and to let go of all conditions.
On the sixth

(the twentieth day of the first lunar month) she bathed and changed her clothes of her own accord at Chongshan Monastery, looked around at her constant attendant disciples in sign of farewell, then closed her eyes and lay down on her right side, reciting the Buddha's name with one mind; her disciples gathered around her and assisted her recitation. At twenty-one forty that day, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, she returned peacefully to the West.

From that day through the seven weeks, at every hour of day and night, the four assemblies kept up an unbroken round of bowing and recitation in the mourning hall. Some knelt long and sobbed without being able to speak; some in their seventies bowed without ceasing; some children sang out the recitation loudly; some, gravely ill, persisted in bowing and reciting day and night. Though the ancient city was cold with spring chill, those assisting the recitation never paused day or night and seemed to gain in spirit. Such was the power of her inspiration.

Before her passing, because of ascites of the liver, the Venerable Yuan's abdomen was swollen; yet when she was placed in the coffin on the fourteenth, her abdomen was normal, the ascites had vanished without a trace, and the bedding was unstained. Truly a strange thing.
On the 14th

the coffin was carried to the transformation cave at Guangji Maopeng on Mount Wutai. Snow fell on the mountain, the road was winding and slippery, and those escorting the body felt the car struck head-on by a freight truck coming down the mountain. In their alarm they got out and saw that the two vehicles were only inches apart. If this was not the Buddha's power and the Venerable's silent protection, what was it?

At the cremation, lotuses appeared from time to time in the fire, and someone took photographs. From the ashes countless relics were obtained (more than seven thousand), and the relic flowers were of every color; all who saw them marveled that such a thing should be. In accordance with her instructions the ashes were divided into three parts: one scattered along the great road on Mount Wutai, one sent to Lingyan Mountain Monastery in Suzhou, and one enshrined on this mountain. The Venerable's one span of conditions is finished; surely she will return on her vow to broadly deliver those who have the affinity.
Recorded by the lay Buddhist Yixin
(Original title: Layman Yue Yunsheng, his face wearing a smile, a strange fragrance floating in the room)

All living beings possess the Buddha-nature and are capable of becoming Buddhas; only because they are deluded and turn against their own nature do they fall into birth and death and the wheel of rebirth without end. The Tathāgata, wishing to restore them to that original nature, teaches all manner of Dharmas in accord with their capacities. Yet to rely on one's own power of practice and in this very life reach the point where delusion is utterly exhausted and one escapes birth and death — that is truly rare in this latter age. Only by cultivating the Pure Land Dharma gate may anyone, of high, middle, or low capacity, old or young, man or woman, so long as they possess true faith and earnest vows, with a sincere mind recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. Together with doing no evil and practicing all good, at the end of life they will receive the Buddha's welcome and be reborn in the West, and not one in ten thousand will be left out. For they rely on the Buddha's compassionate power and gain this immense benefit, as one crosses the sea in a steamship, which no power of one's own could accomplish. That is why the bodhisattvas, patriarchs, and good teachers of every generation have all urged this method with all their strength, since it is the shortcut for escaping birth and death and the essential Dharma for accomplishing the Buddha Way.

Layman Yue Yunsheng was the father of Buyun. He served his parents with the utmost filial piety, delighted in goodness and loved righteousness, and was loyal and generous by nature, partial to no one. For several years Buyun had given rise to a right faith in the Buddhadharma, eating vegetarian and reciting the Buddha's name with utter sincerity and care. He therefore urged his parents to do the same, to eat vegetarian and recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West, and he explained to them from simple and easily understood Pure Land books, telling them to read them often. His father thus came to know that his own mind inherently possesses the Buddha-nature, but that delusion and karma obscure it so that he could not enjoy it; and that happily there is this Dharma gate of relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, which enables us living beings of scant good roots and poor capacities to transcend the three realms sideways in this very life and to be received on high among the nine lotuses. What greater fortune could there be? From then on his mind dwelt on it long, hoping to realize what he cherished. In the seventh month of this year he showed a slight illness; on the eighth day he rose early, and when he had finished reciting the Buddha's name he told Buyun to prepare clothes and a coffin at once, for he was about to go. When clothes and coffin were ready he bathed, dressed, and lay down. Buyun warned the family that they must on no account weep and cause him to lose right mindfulness, but should recite the Buddha's name in unison to aid his rebirth. He also urged his father to follow the sound with his mind; his lips moved slightly, and after a long while they stopped — he had gone. They recited on for another three hours before they began to weep. And his father's face wore a smile, and a strange fragrance floated in the room. When he was encoffined on the third day his countenance was as if alive, so that his rebirth may be decisively known. Day by day Buyun and the family recited the Buddha's name before the coffin, hoping that his lotus grade might rise and that he might swiftly realize the unborn, thereby repaying the toil of his parents and fulfilling the duty of a son. Recorded by the ever-shamefaced monk Shakyamuni Yinguang.
(Original title: Layman Sha Jian'an instructed his family beforehand about the funeral, his right mindfulness clear)

Sha Jian'an, whose given name was Yuanbing, was a native of Rugao in Jiangsu. His conduct and bearing, his writing and his sense of duty, were all fit to be a model for this latter age. He valued practice above words in his studies and did not esteem mere literary polish; his resolve was to fulfill his duties and he coveted no glory or favor. Thus after passing the imperial examination he stayed at home to serve his parents, hoping to fulfill a son's duty, and did not enter official life. At first he did not know what manner of man the Buddha was or what meaning the sutras held, and he followed the sayings of Han Yu, the Cheng brothers, and Zhu Xi, holding that the Buddhadharma harmed the Way of the sages and benefited neither country nor people. After the revolution of 1911, sunk in gloom and with nothing to do, he often harbored the thought of transcending this world. He tried reading the Buddhist sutras, and saw that their principles were subtle and wondrous, perfectly interfused and transcendent, and he knew at last that the Buddha is a great sage and his teaching contains inconceivable things. It was as if he had come out of a dark valley and beheld the sky, and he could not help being overcome with joy and grief at once, regretting the narrowness of decades of confinement. From then on he devoted himself to study, received the precepts, and recited them, hoping to personally realize the Buddha-nature inherent in himself and not remain forever a man of the six paths of rebirth.

the year guihai, when he had completed the sixty-year cycle, his weariness of the world grew keener. Just then Master Dixian came to Rugao to lecture on The Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra, and he attended the Dharma feast in person. Thus he came to know the Pure Land Dharma gate of sideways transcendence, the way by which the great sages of equal enlightenment and the small, ordinary beings who commit the five heinous acts may alike, here and now, rely on the Buddha's compassionate power to leave this Sahā world and reach that Land of Ultimate Bliss, each according to his own capacity entering the path. Thereupon he devoted himself to the Pure Land work, hoping for rebirth. The following year Cui Yirong came to the mountain to take refuge, and because he spoke of the layman's learning and practice, I had him bring a copy of my writings as a gift; the year after, Chen Zhengyou showed me his essay condemning the eating of meat and drinking of wine during mourning, which cited the classics and histories and argued with great clarity, and I knew that the layman's learning had deep roots and that his aspiration reached toward the sages and worthies; though we had never met, each of us had already acknowledged the other in our hearts as a kindred spirit. Last summer, hearing that I had come to Shanghai, he wished to come and see me, but illness kept him from leaving the house, and he still hoped to come to the mountain another day to ask for instruction; to the very end, when he spoke with friends, he counted it a regret. Yet having been born in the West, to attend upon Amitābha in person and follow the assembly of the ocean-wide host, never seeing a single rice-eating monk, what is there to regret? In autumn his left armpit became paralyzed, then he coughed blood, and as winter came it grew worse; Chinese and Western medicine alike were of no avail. Might it not be that by the power of his practice he turned a heavy retribution into a light one, a later retribution into a present one, and so exhausted his former karma? On the eleventh day of the twelfth month he took to his bed and did not rise, and he handed his life's writings to his disciples Xiang Benyuan and Huang Wenjun, and gave brief instructions concerning family matters. He greatly regretted that he had formerly supported turning Guangfu Monastery into an assembly hall and moving the Buddha images, and commanded his son Jin to contribute three thousand pieces of gold toward rebuilding the Buddha hall at Guanghui Nunnery in the east of the city, to atone for his former fault. He further ordered the family to take turns reciting the Buddha's name at his bedside day and night, and to do the same at the end, and not to wash or change his clothes beforehand, nor to weep; he was to be encoffined in cloth, not silk. During the mourning, whether sacrificing to the gods or entertaining guests, no wine or meat was to be used; “I have written essays condemning the world's ways, and you must not follow the evil customs”

and bring guilt upon me.” He also ordered that monks be invited to assist his recitation, that he might surely rely on the Buddha's compassionate power and be reborn in the West. A censer table was set before his bed with an image of Amitābha welcoming and guiding, and he faced the compassionate countenance, reciting with his mouth and remembering in his mind, single-mindedly and without distraction, mentioning nothing else at all. On the night of the twenty-fourth his illness grew critical, and the assembled monks all came to assist his recitation; the layman's right mindfulness was clear, and he followed the sound aloud or silently. It went on to the twenty-sixth; though no sound was heard, his mouth kept opening and closing. In the afternoon his breath grew more hurried, and the sound of the family and monks reciting together grew tense and sorrowful; at the you hour he suddenly passed away. There was a noticeable strange fragrance, and the assembly recited all the more fervently; more than two hours later the crown of his head was still warm, and not until dawn did they stop the recitation, wipe his body, dress him for the coffin, and begin to mourn. His son was able to carry out his commands without transgression, which may truly be called filial piety.

Ah! A layman such as this may be called deep-rooted from former lives, lofty in his understanding, his words answering to his deeds, within and without as one. Judging by his practice over several years, his faith and vows in ordinary times, and the scene at his death, he must surely be one of the middle grade of the upper birth. For he supported his parents with filial piety and practiced benevolence in the world, and he possessed full faith and vows and gathered his mind in pure mindfulness. Yet once reborn, he will surely ascend to the stage of non-retrogression, realize the unborn patience, and gradually practice until he perfects bodhi, and there an end. What regret or lack could remain? Here I have gathered and recorded what was told me by his disciple Xiang Benyuan, his son Jin, and my own disciple Cui Yirong, so that those who later compile biographies of the reborn and records of recluses may have a source.
Recorded by the ever-shamefaced monk Shakyamuni Yinguang
(Original title: Layman Zhao Zunren sincerely performed good works and passed away seated in Buddha-recitation)

Zhao Zunren, whose Dharma name was Peigeng, was a man of Makuang in Rugao. He was over thirty, had long been in business, and was honest and sincere by nature and decisive and straightforward in all he did. In recent years he had heard the Pure Land Dharma gate and given rise to deep faith, and day by day he made it his affair to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. He set aside his business and devoted himself wholly to charitable and public works with the utmost earnestness. Through these affairs he initiated the Jisheng Branch Association and a distribution center for Buddhist sutras, and whatever good work was within his power he never failed to do. He himself collected the street lamps of the district in the morning and set them out at night, and thought nothing of the toil. All the people of the region admired his sincerity; he moved them by sincerity and they answered with sincerity, and every subscription he urged was fulfilled according to his wish.
In the winter of 1926,

stricken with grave illness, he pressed on in his illness to promote a Buddha-recitation week to pray for peace in the world. It was set to begin on the second day of the twelfth month and conclude on the eighth, with Master Fancheng of Xifang Monastery in Juegang presiding, the funds all freely offered by the faithful, and more than forty people joining in the recitation.

Though the layman bore a grave illness, his recitation grew all the more diligent, as though he had no illness at all, and at seven o'clock on the evening of the sixth he passed away seated in the recitation of the Buddha's name. Those in the assembly recited all the more earnestly to aid his rebirth. Several hours later the crown of his head was still warm, and his countenance was no different from when alive. Here one sees that the power of Amitābha's vows and the power of living beings' minds are both inconceivable. Truly, the Buddha-nature of suchness is inherent in all beings; it waits only for conditions to awaken it. As when a seed has been sown in the ground, at the first timely rain it sprouts at once. Yet the people of the world use the power of the Buddha-nature inherent in them to race daily through greed, anger, and delusion, through killing, stealing, and lust. It is like placing the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel, which rains down treasure at will, in a privy, where it can be of no use at all. Is this not pitiable! Hearing of the layman's manner, one ought to die of shame.
(Original title: Layman Ding Bingwen, earnest in faith, vows, and practice, foreknew the time of his passing)

Ding Bingwen was a man of Rong County in Sichuan. He lived at the west gate of the county town and ran a pharmacy. In those parts many people smoked opium in those days, and he too had taken up the habit. Later, influenced by clansmen, he aroused the aspiration to study the Buddha. Because of his former habit of smoking he went to bed very late each night, so he often washed his face and rinsed his mouth in the middle of the night and only went to sleep after reciting the Buddha's name with utter sincerity.
in the fifth month,

he told his family: “On such-and-such a day I shall go to be reborn in the West.” His family thought he was speaking carelessly and paid it no mind. When the day came he fell ill and took to his bed; that evening he asked his family to change him into new clothes and lift him into the main hall to sit, and he indeed looked as though he were about to die. Only then did his wife say in astonishment: “Our second son boards at the middle school; how could he hurry home in the middle of the night to be present at the end? I beg you to wait until tomorrow!” He nodded and agreed.

The next morning a messenger was sent to tell the second son to come home. He sat in the middle of the main hall, and his sons and daughters-in-law knelt before him. He said: “You should kneel to either side, not in the middle, and block my road.” So they knelt to either side and recited the Buddha's name in unison. Before long he passed away in peace.

In life this Layman Ding Bingwen had nothing else that surpassed other men; he could simply believe deeply, vow earnestly, and practice with all his strength. It was by relying on faith, vows, and practice that he at last attained rebirth in the Pure Land. The sutras say that even a man of the ten evil deeds, reciting ten times at the end, may attain the lowest grade of rebirth; how much more he, who for years had not broken off the recitation of the name — how could his vow go unfulfilled? Knowing how he attained rebirth, all of us who study the Buddha ought to apply ourselves well to the recitation of the Buddha's name.

Note: This was recorded by Mr. Huang Shuyun of Rong County. The old layman Huang was a great Pure Land worthy of modern Sichuan, of broad learning, lofty virtue, and strict and pure precepts. He founded the Rong County Buddhist Monthly and established a Buddhist study society, and for a time many people came under his influence and took up the study of Buddhism; it was by following him that Layman Ding Bingfang studied the Buddha and attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
Transcribed and translated by Zhang Miaoshou, upāsaka of the bodhisattva precepts,
in October 1989
at Wenshu Monastery

blocks.text: 5. Foreknowledge of Rebirth in the West

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Gu Haitao foreknew his rebirth in the West and took leave of relatives and friends)

Gu Haitao was a man of Rong County. He had formerly studied Daoism, and in recent years, on the advice of his teacher Liu Rongzhou, he turned to the study of Buddhism and devoted himself to the Pure Land work, reciting the Buddha's name at fixed hours day and night without fail. Several months earlier he had predicted that he would be reborn on the sixth day of the ninth lunar month of this year (

), at six o'clock in the afternoon. In early autumn he and I were still rushing to build a brick pavilion with walls on three sides at Zhaofeng Mountain south of the city. At this time he went back to his old home in the countryside and told his son Gu Xinghua to oversee the work. One day Xinghua dreamed at night that his father said to him: “When the pavilion is finished, name it the Pavilion of Rebirth in the West; I am about to attain rebirth.” Waking, Xinghua was alarmed and prepared to go back to the old home to visit him, and by chance found in a desk drawer a handwritten note his father had left beforehand, which said exactly what the dream had said.

Xinghua hurried home, but his father had already gone to the homes of relatives and friends in Rong County and Yibin to take his leave, saying that he was about to go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When the day came he had only a slight illness and meant to go to the Pavilion of Rebirth in the West. Afterwards his family dissuaded him and he did not go. At the end he told his family to recite the Buddha's name and see him off to rebirth. Then he passed away with a smile on his face. After his whole body had grown cold, the crown of his head remained warm for as long as twenty-five hours. When the relatives and friends who came to offer condolences heard Xinghua describe it all in detail, for a time all the Buddha-reciters of the whole county gave rise to great faith in rebirth in the West.
Recorded by Huang Shuyun,
in the winter of 1934
(Original title: Layman Wang Agou gave instructions about family matters and was reborn in the West that day)
Layman Wang Qingmao told me: In the years of the Republic,

there was a merchant on Qingtai Road in Hangzhou whose childhood name was Wang Agou. Past sixty years of age, he made his living from salt, and for more than thirty years he ate vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name. One day he suddenly called his family together, had them stand in a circle, and told them: “I mean to go today.” He then handed over all the affairs of the household, settled and clear. He further instructed his family: “After my death you should follow the Buddha's teaching and cremate me.” When he had spoken, holding a fly whisk in one hand and a book in the other, he passed away in peace, his countenance as if alive, and all who heard of it near and far came to bow in reverence.
Xiu Lun

blocks.text: 7. Passing Away Seated, Holding the Rosary

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Yang Deqia burned incense and worshipped the Buddha and passed away seated, holding his rosary)

The layman was a farmer's son from the northern countryside of Wuxi, named Yuquan. Of four brothers he was the eldest. At fourteen he came to Suzhou to learn the silk and satin trade. When his training was complete he set up his own shop at Tianhou Palace Bridge, and then brought his brothers out one by one and welcomed his parents to be supported in the proper way. He fulfilled filial piety and brotherly love to the utmost, by natural disposition. His mother believed in the Buddha, and he attended her on pilgrimages to Mount Putuo, Mount Jiuhua, and other famous mountains. When his parents had passed away and his sons and daughters were grown, he reverenced the Buddha all the more devoutly and took refuge with the old Master Yinguang, who granted him the Dharma name Deqia, and he went on to receive the bodhisattva upāsaka precepts. Whenever a master lectured on the sutras, or there were assemblies for lotus-society recitation, he took part in them all, and he gathered like-minded friends and founded the Xiangguang Lotus Society within the Tianhou Palace, with regular sessions of Buddha-recitation and releasing living creatures, for many years as though it were a single day.

In recent years, as he approached seventy, his vital force gradually declined and he often suffered from diarrhea, though treatment with Great Compassion water was quite effective. In the eighth month of this year the diarrhea returned, and when his children and grandchildren urged medicine on him he would not allow it, saying: “For one who recites the Buddha's name, if his worldly conditions are not yet exhausted, he will recover even without medicine; if his worldly conditions are finished, what can medicine do to prolong his life?” Whenever friends came to inquire after his illness he asked them all to recite the Buddha's name to aid him and spoke of nothing else. Though his bodily strength failed him and he lay in bed much of the time, he still often patted the quilt with his hand as though striking the Dharma instruments and recited the Buddha's name aloud, with no other concern. Then on the night of the eighteenth, at nine o'clock, he had his sons help him sit up; when he had rinsed his mouth and washed, he lit candles, burned incense, bowed, and gazed at the Buddha's image without letting his eyes leave it for a moment; then he sat upright, holding his rosary in his left hand and a stick of sandalwood incense in his right, and recited the Buddha's name aloud, reciting more and more softly until at last no sound came, while his fingers told the beads as before. It went on past midnight, and he passed away sitting peacefully with his eyes closed. The time was the early zi hour of the nineteenth day of the eighth month
the year xinsi,
on the 19th

at the early zi hour, he passed away, and he was sixty-eight years old. His children and grandchildren, all following the Buddha's teaching, held incense and recited the Buddha's name as they knelt to see him off and aid his rebirth in the West. On the morning of the twentieth he was placed in the coffin in the lotus posture, his body soft as cotton. On the fifth day of the ninth month the coffin was carried to Lingyan Mountain at Mudu for cremation. On the sixth the bones were examined: they were pure white and yielded a great many firm relics, glittering and bright, exceedingly rare. The remains were placed in a porcelain jar with the firm relics together inside, and enshrined in a position in the common stupa of the four assemblies at Lingyan, that he might constantly hear the Buddha's name and his lotus grade rise ever higher. The layman's firm faith in life and single-minded practice were every one of them causes for rebirth in the Pure Land; his right mindfulness clear at the end, and the auspicious responses obtained at the cremation, prove beyond doubt the fruit of certain rebirth in the West: merit is never cast away in vain, and the fruit is never won by chance. The Buddhadharma is inconceivable, and the Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the West is the most inconceivable of all the inconceivable. Now the layman has borne witness to it. May those who have the mind to seek liberation take note.
Shen Misheng

blocks.text: 8. Knowing the Time and Passing While Seated

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Wu Chensi Knows the Time and Passes While Seated, Manifesting Many Auspicious Signs)

The layman's name was Chensi; his Dharma name was Dechang. He was a man of Lianhe township, Nan'an county, Fujian. His family was poor, and at seven he lost his father. Before he was twenty he followed his elder brother Zhuqing to the Dutch East Indies, to the port of Cirebon, to do business. He buried himself in hard work, and was in no way like the men of the marketplace. He served his mother with filial devotion and his elder brother with especial respect. Though he traded in a foreign land, every two years he would once return home to see his mother. Later, when he brought his mother abroad to be with him, he was able to wait upon her day and night. But because she could not grow used to living among overseas Chinese, he soon gave up his occupation and took his mother home, serving her morning and evening for many years. When his mother fell ill and could no longer comb her hair or wash her face, the layman did it for her with his own hands. Though there were maidservants, he said that carefulness was not to be compared with his own.

At first the layman did not know the Buddha. At home he recited the Ming Sheng Jing daily, and admired the way Guan Zhuangmu served his elder brother in ritual. When he spoke with his elder brother he would always stand with hands folded in respect, and for forty years he was as constant as on the first day. He was a man of plain and unadorned simplicity, and his heart was set on kindness. From youth to old age, from his village to lands overseas, wherever he went, whenever there were floods or droughts, pestilence or years of famine, and the masses were in distress at the seasonal sacrifices, he took their troubles to heart as though they were his own. Hence when people came to ask him to comfort orphans and support the aged, relieve widows and pity the poor, give medicine and provide remedies, build bridges, repair roads, give coffins, release living creatures, revere and conserve written paper, or open up farmland waterworks and public burial grounds, and even to make offerings to the Three Jewels, there was no request he did not carry out with his own single strength, or together with others. In this way he also moved his friends and transformed his fellow villagers, so that these undertakings were all the more extended. Thus Mr. Wu Guangping of Jinguang entrusted the layman, over several years, with six or seven thousand silver dollars to be used in relieving the poor of the Anhai region at the New Year, and kept it secret from others. Mr. Lian of Chenchun in Nan'an, on the layman's behalf, repaired bridges and distributed relief for ten or twenty years, never daring to complain of toil or weariness; this is clear proof.

In that year, at the age of fifty, he brought forth the mind of renunciation. As for his business affairs at home and abroad, what he owed to others and what others owed him, whether repaid or not, he let be; and he did not count the considerable losses. From then on he kept a vegetarian diet and served the Buddha, taking refuge under Dharma Master Yinguang and devoting himself to the pure karma. When he heard that the monk Xuyun was dwelling at Yongquan Monastery on Mount Gu, his admiration grew; he gave alms and offerings, and when Xuyun went on to Caoxi he still thought of him from afar without cease. When the greatest Vinaya master of the age, Dharma Master Hongyi, spread the Dharma in southern Fujian, the layman was enamored at first sight and sighed that such a man was rare. He served and supported him to the utmost of his ability. Whenever he met elders of the various mountains, he drew near and made offerings with unfailing earnestness and gravity, never letting an occasion pass. In all his life, seeing one good deed or hearing one good word, there was none to which he did not hold fast with all his heart. And he was ever earnest in telling others what he had gained in his own mind. For himself he was extremely frugal: cloth clothes and vegetarian food, and in forty years he never had a fine garment made or set out a single snack. He delighted in reciting the Diamond Sutra, the Medicine Buddha Sutra, and others, sometimes reciting them himself and sometimes asking others to recite, tireless through the years.
Then one day, setting aside all the sutras, he told his relatives and friends that he must devote himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation and seek rebirth in the West. And so it was that on
September
th,

, at three in the afternoon, he passed away seated at his lodging on Gulangyu, aged sixty-two by worldly reckoning. At the end he knew beforehand that the time had come, and there were fifteen kinds of auspicious signs, which Layman Wang Deyi recorded, and which I will not repeat here. By his dying command his body was cremated at Ziyun Rock in Xiamen. When the people of Xiamen and Gulangyu heard of it, several thousand came at once to gaze up at him in admiration and praise. Because they saw that the layman's study of the Buddha had borne fruit, there were many who were moved to bring forth the bodhi mind. Strangest of all, the layman's honored wife, Madam Chen, had never believed in the Buddha; yet on the night before his rebirth in the West she heard heavenly music sounding in the sky nearby, and thereupon brought forth faith. She keeps a vegetarian diet now and recites the whole Diamond Sutra. His second wife, Madam Lin, and his eldest daughter-in-law, Madam Lin, likewise, on the night before his rebirth in the West, saw with their own eyes the Three Holy Ones of the West come in person to receive him, the golden countenances of the Buddha and bodhisattvas clear before them. For this reason every member of the household, great and small, after the layman's rebirth, brought forth the bodhi mind and pressed forward with courage. In
, in the
rd month

, I returned from the Philippines to Quanzhou one stage at a time; and while waiting for a ship I was lodged, through the kindness of my nephew by marriage Mianyi, at his home for more than half a month. With my own eyes I saw the layman's family, who recite together twice each day: men and women, old and young, striking the wooden fish and the chime, chanting, reciting, and bowing, their deportment perfectly ordered. From this I felt that the layman, who all his life cultivated himself and transformed others, had now accomplished it; and so he brought about a Buddhist family. Every member of that household, great and small, is a seed of bodhi. Generation after generation of descendants will carry it on: how could the merit and blessing they obtain be conceived? How splendid! He may well be called a model for the lay community of our Fujian.
Ye Qingyan

blocks.text: 9. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Zhang Huiming, the Buddha Dharma Not Being Vain, Passes to the West in Peace)

The old layman Huiming, whose personal name was Luming and whose courtesy name was Pingzhi, was a man of Baokan township, the sixth district of Zhenjiang county. In the former Qing dynasty he entered the local academy; he was intelligent and upright, and in virtue and letters he surpassed his fellows. More than half the famous scholars of the whole county came from his school. He had two sons and one daughter. In his later years the old layman studied the Buddha, delving deeply into the inner scriptures, and he gained much understanding.

, when he took refuge under Great Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Huiming. After the master's instruction he became still more diligent, giving his whole heart to the Pure Land. He was good at exhorting everyone he met, and no small number of people in the whole county were stirred by his persuasion to bring forth the mind of Buddha-recitation.

, when the old layman was already seventy-five, his second son Zhongwen suddenly died of illness. The old layman well knew that worldly things are illusion and human life impermanent, and that grief is of no avail; he ought rather to redouble his effort in Buddha-recitation. From then on, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he never for a moment parted from the Buddha. That autumn, on
th month, on the
20 th

, he felt slightly unwell and his food and drink fell off a little, but in his movements he recited the Buddha's name as usual, and morning and evening he still bowed as before. Then he said to his daughter Shangu: “The human body is hard to obtain; do not let it pass in vain. You should exhort others to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and only so escape the round of rebirth.” Shangu at once invited Layman Xu Peiliang and others to come day and night to his home to assist in reciting the Buddha's name. On the

th, in the morning, the old layman suddenly glared and said sternly to them all: “Do not recite the Buddha's name; be off with you.” Hearing this, Shangu knew there was a demonic obstruction, and stepped forward shouting: “Be off with you! My father is a man of Buddha-recitation, lofty in virtue; you cannot obstruct him. Away, away!” The old layman then lowered his eyes and said no more, and in a moment he was reciting the Buddha's name as before. And he said: “My child may be called filial. From now on you must know that the Buddha Dharma is not vain.” And so he again recited with the others. On the

th, his voice grew a little softer; at the hour of xu his lips moved slightly, and still following the others he silently recited the Buddha's name, and passed to the West in peace. Everything was done according to the Buddha's regulations and the old layman's own long-standing wish, in which he had charged the whole household beforehand, grandchildren, boys and girls alike, that they were not to weep. Some six hours after his passing, when they attended to dressing him and wiping him down, his whole body was cold through, his face as though alive, and the crown of his head still warm. In his lifetime he had made a couplet himself: “The years I regret were squandered; happy that in late life I turned toward the West, / Only then knowing that reciting the Buddha makes one a Buddha, resting on faith and vow alone. / If sons and grandsons prove worthy and filial, I hope they will early devote themselves to the Pure Land; / Resolved to seek rebirth, they shall attain it, and together leave the round of rebirth.”

Bingcheng returned home before the Mid-Autumn Festival and heard my cousin Shangu and Layman Xu Peiliang and the others relate the whole affair in detail, and so he set it down according to the facts.
Li Bingcheng
(Original title: Guan Jiongzhi, Defender of the Nation and Protector of the Dharma, Received by Guanyin)

Jiong had been much afflicted by illness these past two years, and in the spring had once vomited several cupfuls of blood. The physicians examined him and learned that cancer had formed in his intestines. On the day before the Dragon Boat Festival he suddenly fainted for more than ten minutes, and from then on his illness grew daily more severe. On the morning of the second of July at seven o'clock he summoned Puchu to his bedside and said: My mind is very pure at this moment, I can put everything down, and I am single-mindedly seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. I feel that seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is not difficult; already I am drawing nearer step by step. In my illness I have often visualized the lotus pond on Mount Putuo and the image of Great Being Guanyin in the front temple, and several times I have seen them in dreams. I only wish the Great Being to save me from suffering and hardship and to receive me into the West — this great matter of birth and death I must trouble you to assist. He also told Puchu to take from the Buddha hall the will he had written the year before and to sign it as witness. He said himself that from now on he could put down all family affairs. He went on to say that during his illness he had not kept the vegetarian fast purely, and he deeply repented of it: all the many offenses he had committed since beginningless kalpas he now repented. Then he summoned his children one by one and admonished them, and charged the family not to weep. Puchu asked whether he wished them to invite Dharma friends to recite the Buddha's name at his side, and what he thought of it. He answered: Very good; you may recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva together. Puchu then went to invite Dharma Master Desen and the monks Haipeng and Foxin of the Pure Karma Society, Layman Qiao Xunru and others to assist in the recitation, and the family too gathered round and recited with them. When Dharma Master Desen arrived later, he told them to change to the Buddha-name of Amitabha. Old Jiong said: We will still recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva to receive him into the West; it is no different from Amitabha, and the collected writings of Old Dharma Master Yin say the same. There is no need to change. Puchu feared this might give rise to obstruction, so he told Master Desen that in his illness old Jiong's visualization of Guanyin was the more practiced, and that they should follow his wish; the master consented. Then they invited Dharma Master Xingci to come and speak the Dharma. Master Xing instructed him to recite the name of Guanyin Bodhisattva and to think of Guanyin Bodhisattva, for mind would then be sealed with mind, and he would surely attain rebirth. Old Jiong smiled and joined his palms, and said: I ask only to be reborn with my karma, even in the borderland or a phantom city; that too would be my joyful wish. He said again that the recitation was too fast and he could not follow it clearly, so Master Xing led the assembly in reciting slowly, for about two hours. When the master took his leave, old Jiong said: Hearing the master recite the Buddha's name has been a great help to me. I beg the master to stay and not go. Master Xing, because he was returning to Fazang Monastery to expound the sutras, stayed a little longer and then left.

In the afternoon, Laymen Ding Guicen, Huang Hanzhi, Yang Xinlian, and Yue Huibin, fellow cultivators from the Lay Buddhist Grove, and the monks of Fazang Monastery arrived one after another. Old Jiong joined his palms and thanked each of them, and recited the Buddha's name with the assembly, his face joyful and his manner serene. He said to Layman Ding: Layman, I now put everything down and am resolved upon rebirth. He said to Mr. Lu Deshen: Everything in this world is false. Then he turned and asked Puchu: Has the will been signed? Puchu told him it had. He laughed and said: Now I have done another false thing. At this time his temperature had reached 103 degrees, yet his mind was not disordered; all called his calm composure rare. Then Puchu had occasion to go out, and by the time he returned it was already evening. The family told him that old Jiong had called for him more than ten times. He hurried to him, and old Jiong said: At this moment I have many deluded thoughts. Guanyin Bodhisattva appears in every land without exception — why has he not appeared to me yet? Puchu answered: The bodhisattva is within your own mind. Never mind whether you see him or not; only cling close to Guanyin Bodhisattva, and you will receive the bodhisattva's empowerment. Then he brought a statue of the four-armed Guanyin and placed it before the bed. When old Jiong saw the image he joined his palms and cried aloud: Homage to the Great Compassionate, Great Merciful, Vast and Wondrously Responsive Guanyin Bodhisattva. Then he said to Mr. Liu Sufeng: I have been to the lotus pond and did not see the Great Being; I turned back, and I fear there is an obstruction of karma. Please recite the Great Repentance Text for me. Puchu, on his behalf, visualized the bodhisattva sending forth light to receive him, and recited the bodhisattva's name with all his heart.

After about an hour, old Jiong suddenly cried out joyfully: The Great Being has come! He told the family to kneel before the bed, and said: Guanyin the Great Being is in the lotus pond, surrounded by lotuses. At this moment my body and mind are happy beyond measure. The electric lights are all gone from my sight, but I see the Great Being most clearly. Puchu said: Then only look at the Great Being with all your attention, and that is well. Old Jiong joined his palms and cried aloud: Homage to the Great Compassionate Guanyin Bodhisattva. He looked around and said: Whoever wishes to be reborn may come and be reborn with me. At this time there were some twenty Dharma friends assisting in the recitation, all joyful and full of praise. From then on his gaze was fixed on empty space and he spoke no more. At two in the morning Puchu withdrew to rest a little. At dawn he hurried to look at him, and old Jiong said to him: Do not stand on ceremony with me; say a word to me. Puchu asked him to put everything down, recite the Buddha's name with one mind, and seek rebirth in the West. He answered: Yes. Dharma Master Xingci then arrived together with the monk Xingru, and he could still raise his hand in greeting. Master Xing told him to close his eyes and recite quietly. At first he still opened his eyes and looked upward; the master himself struck the chime and led the assembly in reciting the bodhisattva's name, neither hurried nor slow, pure mindfulness continuing without interruption. Gradually they saw his gaze draw inward and his lips and jaw move slightly, and knew that he too was reciting along with them. At about eleven his breath came slightly faster, yet he was very calm and showed no sign of pain. At half past eleven, when Master Xing was about to leave, he spoke to him again: Let go of the ten thousand conditions, and with one mind seek rebirth in the West. He answered: Yes. The master asked: Do you hear the Buddha-name clearly? He said: I do. Half an hour after the master left, his breathing gradually grew fainter, and from faint it ceased. It was
th month, on the
rd (the twentieth day of the fifth lunar month), at twelve twenty at noon. The family all knelt and recited the Buddha's name; any who wished to weep withdrew. From the
th month, on the
2 nd,
to the morning of the

th, for three days and nights, the sound of the Buddha-name was unbroken. After his breath had ceased, Puchu felt his hands and feet, which were both cold, while the crown of his head was warm; the forehead had grown cold first, and the crown was still warm. Eleven hours later, when Mr. Lu Deshen felt his crown, it was still warm. Though he had been ill and confined for a long while, when he came to the end of life he may be said to have been clear in mind and distinct in right mindfulness. Such being the signs, judged by the scriptures and treatises, one may conclude without doubt that he was surely reborn in the Pure Land.
Zhao Puchu

blocks.text: 11. Passing to the West with the Buddha

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Mao Shouxiang, Doing Good and Serving His Parents, Passes to the West with the Buddha)

In the first month of spring in the jiazi year of the Republic, I was a guest in Nanchang and joined the Jueji Buddha-Recitation Grove, vowing to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. In the late autumn of the bingyin year I took refuge from soldiers in my home village. My son's father-in-law, Layman Mao Shouxiang, took the Pure Land scriptures and treatises from my trunk, read them, and loved them. One day he asked me: “The Amitabha of self-nature — what is the use of reciting the Buddha's name? The Pure Land of mind-only — what is the use of seeking rebirth?” I answered him: “How can mind-only be recognized? How can self-nature be realized? There is a Dharma gate for it, a skillful means. Of skillful means, none excels Buddha-recitation: from one recitation you arrive at no-recitation, and only then can you recognize your own mind; from seeking rebirth you arrive at no-birth, and only then can you realize your self-nature.” He asked again: “Buddha-recitation as a Dharma gate is indeed a skillful means; may I hear of the work of beginning?” I said: “One who recites the Buddha's name must first possess true faith: faith that Amitabha Buddha is a Buddha already accomplished, and that one is oneself a Buddha not yet accomplished — and that a Buddha not yet accomplished, relying on the protection and reception of a Buddha already accomplished, may easily perfect himself. This is called true faith. Then one must make a great vow, vowing that at the end of this present life one will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and realize the patient acceptance, and thereafter be able to deliver living beings and accomplish perfect enlightenment. This is called the keen vow. Then one must resolve to put it into practice in earnest, setting a daily lesson of reciting the Amitabha Sutra, the Rebirth Mantra, and the name of Amitabha Buddha for a certain time, and practicing it to the end of life without interruption. This may be called true practice. These three, faith, vow, and practice, must be complete without deficiency. Add to this doing no evil, practicing every good, abstaining from killing, and eating vegetarian food, striving in the pure karma — this is the supreme skillful means of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate, whereby one's mind responds and is in accord with the Buddha's compassion, and one is surely received by the Buddha and reborn in the West; and then mind-only and self-nature are naturally and personally experienced.” The layman heard this and was greatly awakened. From then on he kept a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha's name, day and night at the six periods, pressing forward with courage; his deep roots from former lives and the firmness of his mind and nature were truly beyond my reach.

At five the layman could read a text once and recite it from memory. At twenty he married Madam Bao, who died of illness after a miscarriage, and he did not marry again. Though he had graduated in law and politics, and had helped establish the Qinan Primary School, he would not take credit for any accomplishment. Whenever there was a charitable undertaking in the region, he would donate generously, yet fear that others might know. Only in serving his mother, the Lady Dowager Wu, morning and evening, did he take his joy in filial care and cherishing her wishes. From her sixties into her great old age the Lady Dowager's liver energy was often unregulated. The physicians said she should take Korean ginseng. Each time he would place the ginseng in a small porcelain pot and slowly decoct it over a water jar and oil lamp, never closing his eyes all night, sitting and waiting until the flavor was strong before offering it to her: for twenty years as on the first day.

When he brought forth the mind of Buddha-recitation, the Lady Dowager had already long since passed away. He asked me to buy for him a small plot of land at the Lesser Tianchi on Mount Lu, and there he built a pure hermitage to serve the Buddha. When frost and snow came down, the empty mountain was still and had no dwellers
and the layman resolutely dwelt there alone

cutting his own firewood and drawing his own water, cooking and eating by himself, exactly like an ascetic dhuta. In the mountain there was a poisonous snake that became a demon and troubled the layman. He lay unconscious for three days and nights, his life hanging on a breath; then he lifted up right mindfulness, took a knife, and cut off the index finger of his left hand, writing the character “Buddha” in the blood he sprinkled, and the demon was quelled at once. Afterwards he traveled among the famous places of Mount Putuo, Hangzhou, and elsewhere, and his Way advanced the more. He took refuge at Jian'ou in Fujian, helping his family manage a medicine business. Though amid a hundred pressing affairs, he recited the Buddha's name with one mind as before. On New Year's Day of this year (

), which was the layman's fiftieth birthday, I, being related to him by marriage and also his fellow lotus friend, wrote out the Heart Sutra in seal script on a horizontal scroll and sent it to him as a birthday gift. On the day of the Double Ninth, just as I had finished my morning lesson, sparrows clamored outside my window and my heart suddenly stirred greatly: I thought that I had long had no word from the layman. At once I sent off a letter to inquire. Two nights later I received the telegraphic obituary from his second son-in-law, Yixun. The layman had on that very day sat with closed eyes, raised his right hand as though welcoming someone, and followed the Buddha to the West. Thus in the unseen, mind was sealed with mind — such was their accord. This ought to be recorded, to mark the karmic bond.
Huang Lüsi
(Original title: Old Layman Shi Yanshi, Returned from Death, Believes in the Buddha, Spreads the Dharma, and Releases Living Creatures)

Old Layman Yanshi was my adoptive grandfather. His family had lived for generations in the southwestern corner of Fukang township, the sixth district of Chongming. In youth he studied for the examinations and for several years taught in a school, and the pupils he trained were very many. Then at the age of twenty-seven he fell ill and nearly died, his breath stopping for a full day and night. Just as the family were preparing coffin and shroud, he revived and told them: I came to a place that seemed very dark, and there were two men there. At first they told me to go inside; then I heard someone within say, Shi Yanshi's time has not yet come — let him return quickly. And so I came back to life.

Moved by the impermanence of human life, he abandoned the Confucian path and took refuge in the Buddha. Buddhism in our Chongming was then just sprouting, and believers were very few. But after my adoptive grandfather labored to exhort people, and printed and gave away moral books, spreading the teaching with energy, believers greatly increased. That Buddhism in Chongming has come to what it is today is not a little owing to my adoptive grandfather's efforts. He was diligent in spreading the Dharma, and earnest in his own Buddha-recitation. Morning and evening lessons he kept without a break, summer or winter. When there were rites for the dead, sacrifices to ancestors, exorcisms to avert calamity, or other Buddhist services, and he was invited to lead and to preach, he would not decline even in wind and rain. In expounding the Buddha Dharma he took the Pure Land scriptures and treatises as his warp and the Dharma words of Old Master Yin as his weft. Whenever he came to speak, ordinary men and women who heard him and gave rise to faith, and who of themselves asked to take refuge in the Buddha's gate, were truly numerous. Moreover, though past seventy and widowed young, and though his household was comfortably off, he kept no servants, and most of the household's small affairs he did with his own hands — he had much of Master Yin's manner. On ordinary days he took especial delight in releasing living creatures, and each year saved them by the tens of thousands. We looked forward to his long enjoying a great age, to transform the foolish and the stubborn everywhere.
Who would have thought that the Buddha would suddenly call him away, and that he would pass to the West on
March
th,

1944, with many auspicious signs? I therefore record the facts as follows, as a report to the comrades of the Buddha's gate. My adoptive grandfather's eldest daughter, Huizhen, who married into the Zhang family, lived more than ten li away. This New Year she dreamed that someone told her: Your father has passed to the West on
December

th, she woke in astonishment. But the time had already passed, and though she told the clan what she had dreamed, no one paid it any attention. Who would have known that he would indeed pass to the West on
March

th, and that the number twenty-eight had all along been foreordained? This is the first sign of rebirth in the West: the foretelling of the time of return. In Fukang township there was a Buddhist believer named Dong Guoliang, who had long upheld the Buddha's precepts strictly and had passed to the West the previous winter. On the day before his rebirth, he stopped breathing for several minutes, then came back and told those in the room: I have already been to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; my lotus throne is there, and Shi Yanshi's lotus throne is there too — his is higher than mine. For a time it was told as a fine tale. This is the second sign: the foretelling of the lotus throne. My adoptive grandfather, at the point of death, was clear in spirit and fresh in mind, talking and laughing as ever, constantly telling others to recite the Buddha's name and reciting along with them himself. He also charged them that after death he should be dressed in a monk's robe, since it was right to manifest the monk's appearance. At the end he lay on his right side, propping his cheek with his right hand and covering his body with his left, just like the auspicious lying posture of our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. After his rebirth in the West, his whole body grew cold through, while the crown of his head alone was warm. His complexion was as in life, and his joints were soft. He sat upright in the longevity urn, still and lifelike. When the residents near and far heard of the wonders and came to look, the roads were blocked, and none could cease from sighing in admiration. This is a rough account of the auspicious signs of his rebirth in the West; judged by the scriptures and treatises, one may conclude without doubt that he went straight to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I have therefore made this record, to spread it abroad in the world, earnestly wishing that readers may deeply know the supreme and unrivaled excellence of the Pure Land Dharma gate, and together bring forth right faith.
Recorded by Lu Huiyi

blocks.text: 13. Knowing the Time and Taking Leave of Kin

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Xu Kunyang Knows the Time and Takes Leave of His Kin, Rare Fragrance Filling the Room)

My late maternal grandfather, Mr. Xu Kunyang, all his life went out to the various temples to recite the Buddha's name, and would not break off in cold or heat, wind or rain. When people invited him to recite, the merit money he received he deposited with the Buddhist society for such good works as repairing bridges and paving roads; and so it had been for more than thirty years. But he did not understand the principle of the Pure Land, and sought only blessings in the next life. I earnestly exhorted him, saying that Buddha-recitation would surely bring rebirth in the West, the enjoyment of all joys, and eternal freedom from all suffering. He said: I am an ordinary man; how could I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? I said: In the Records of Rebirth there is Zhang Shanhe, who made his living slaughtering oxen; at the end of his life he met a good teacher who taught him to recite the Buddha's name, and he attained rebirth. How much more, then, when you have never done such a trade in all your life — you will surely be reborn. Hearing this, Mr. Xu's faith and vow arose at once. Afterwards his practice grew more earnest; and in the sixteenth year of the Republic, on the fourth day of the first month, he knew that his time of rebirth had come and took leave of all his relatives and friends. My late father and my mother both recited the Buddha's name to see him off. After his passing a rare fragrance filled the room and did not disperse for a long while, and by this we know for certain that he attained rebirth. Fearing that among those who recite the Buddha's name in the world many seek only blessings, I have made this record in particular, as an exhortation to those who recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West.
, in the first month, supplementary note made at the Avatamsaka assembly.
Chen Jingquan

blocks.text: 14. The Buddha Comes to Receive Him

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Chen Zihong, at the End, at Ease, Received by the Buddha)

My late father, Mr. Zihong, in youth studied Confucianism and medicine, and delighted still more in Buddhist learning. Each day he recited the Diamond Sutra, and morning and evening the Amitabha Sutra and the ten breaths of Buddha-recitation, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land: for more than twenty years he never broke off. From

, when he was sixty-one, he suddenly contracted a wind ailment. On the fourth day of the fourth month asthma was added, and he sat long without lying down. On the night of the fourth day of the fifth month, at ten o'clock, he said: The master has come. Asked who the master was, he said: Amitabha Buddha. At eleven o'clock he said again: Many monks have come into the house. After twelve, I led the household in reciting the four-character sacred name of Amitabha Buddha to assist him. My little son Shunnian also stayed at his side. I had grown somewhat drowsy, and dreamed of monks wearing black haiqing robes, truly several of them. Now I too have always loved Buddhist learning, and if I met with monks I would surely talk at length. But at that moment my mouth was stopped and I could not utter a single word; it must have been the holy assembly appearing before him to receive my late father into rebirth. On the afternoon of the sixth day my late father said that the suffering of his illness was wholly gone and his mind was very much at ease. I sensed something unusual and told the whole household, great and small, to stand in a circle holding incense and reciting the Buddha's name to see him off; and in no long time he passed away. In ordinary life my late father could not keep the vegetarian fast, and I fear his grade was not high. The weather was already hot, yet when he was placed in the coffin there was not a single fly, and he looked as though asleep. In this there is not one word of falsehood. May all who see or hear it bring forth pure faith and together form the surpassing karmic bond of the West.
, in the first month, at the Avatamsaka assembly, speaking with Dharma Master Mingde, I supplied this account.
Jing Quan
(Original title: Layman Yang Yide, Palms Joined in Buddha-Recitation, Passes Peacefully to the West)

Yang Wenlan, whose Dharma name was Yide, was a man of Wuxing in Zhejiang. His father was Jingting and his mother née Lu; both were kindly and served the Buddha. From childhood the layman received his family's instruction; he was courteous and yielding, respectful and frugal, kind and beneficial to others, and he cultivated the Pure Land with devotion for more than thirty years. His family and children all took refuge under Great Master Yinguang. This summer (

) the layman's eating fell off and his spirits declined, and his sons and daughters grew anxious. They therefore asked Dharma Master Desen to write to Lingyan and have a Buddha-recitation retreat of seven days established for him, with the prayer that if his remaining years were not yet exhausted he might soon regain ease, and that if his allotted span had ended he might go straight to the Land of Peace. On the eighteenth day of the tenth lunar month the layman rose in the morning and recited a scroll of the Amitabha Sutra; when his recitation was done he suddenly told the family: The Saha world is boundless in suffering; I am going to the West. The family then telephoned Xinlian to ask, on his behalf, four Dharma friends from the Lay Buddhist Grove, four nuns from the Bliss Hermitage, and Layman Hu Songnian of the Buddhist Fellowship to assist in the recitation. The household members too divided into shifts and recited the sacred name of Amitabha Buddha with the rest. At twenty past ten on the morning of the nineteenth, amid the sound of the assembly's assisting recitation, he joined his palms, recited the Buddha's name, and passed peacefully to the West. At five in the afternoon the crown of his head and his forehead were still warm. The next day at the encoffining his whole body was soft and his face as in life. All these things are truly auspicious tokens of rebirth in the West. I record them now in particular to tell my fellows. You should know that in the Pure Land Dharma gate ten thousand practice and ten thousand go; the ancients truly did not deceive me, and everyone ought to believe it deeply.
, the
rd month. Recorded by Xin Lian

blocks.text: 16. Letting Go of the Body in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Laywoman Wu Huixiang Sees the Great Being Descend and Follows Her Away)

The laywoman Wu Huixiang was a lotus friend of the Lay Buddhist Grove at Chema Lake. She was sincere by nature and diligent in Buddha-recitation. Whenever a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat came round she pressed forward with courage and never slackened in the least. During this year's Kṣitigarbha retreat she was slightly unwell, yet she bowed and recited as usual, bearing her illness. After the retreat broke up her illness increased day by day, and though physicians were called to examine her, nothing took effect. Physician Zhi knew her illness might be past curing, and so invited the grove's assisting-recitation group to come and recite. The laywoman faced the Buddha and listened attentively, her mind not the least disordered. One morning at dawn she gazed intently into empty space and smiled, saying: “The Great Being has descended; I shall follow her and go.” She passed away on
, on the

th day of the month, at the hour of zi, released from the body, aged sixty-one by worldly reckoning. The family gathered to assist in the recitation, and all saw her let go of the body in peace, wholly free of suffering. Physician Zhi was bound to her in the closest friendship and knew her best; and so he moistened his brush and wrote this down, that the world may know that the merit of Buddha-recitation is truly not in vain.
Ma Zhiyi
(Original title: Layman Wang Yuchun Sits Facing West and Passes in Buddha-Recitation)

My late father, Mr. Wang Yuchun, courtesy name Jingwen, was born on the seventh day of the sixth month of the second year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and his family had lived for generations at Xiuyan. He began as a farmer and later took up commerce. When he reached his fiftieth year he returned to live at home, making it his business to teach and raise his children. My late father in ordinary life delighted in doing good, and was by nature upright and generous, and he believed deeply in the Buddha. At fifty-three he led my mother and my brothers in bringing forth the mind to eat vegetarian food. Those who could not keep the precept, however, he did not force. Later, because my fourth brother and I studied the Buddha Dharma, my late father came to know deeply that the one Dharma of Pure Land Buddha-recitation is the sole supreme and unsurpassed shortcut for leaping over the three realms and escaping the round of rebirth outright, and that it is easily practiced by those who live at home. And so with reverence he cultivated the Pure Land, holding to the Buddha's name alone, in the hope of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of life. In his ordinary recitation he was most sincere. Not only did he never miss a day; he did not forget it even in dreams.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eighth lunar month of this year, my late father suddenly wished to go to my eldest brother's house (the place was called West Mountain, with no neighbors near, some two li away), and so my brother came with a cart to fetch him. When he arrived he was as usual, except that at supper he suddenly ate much less; by the next morning he took no food at all, yet he had no illness. Afterwards he suddenly said to my brother: I feel my body is rather weak, and I shall not be long in this world — and I shall not wait until the ninth month. At the time my brother, because he had no illness, paid it little attention. In the afternoon he went to my mother and told her of it. My mother too, because he had no sickness, did not think it so. But when my fourth brother heard it he was greatly alarmed, and said: This is our father's foreknowledge of the time, because he is about to be reborn in the West; we must prepare quickly. He urged my mother to gather his clothes and bedding, and carried them there in haste. When he arrived he comforted him and asked: How does my father feel now?
