You may quiet your mind and recite the Buddha's name, and take no thought for other matters. He answered: I have no other illness; I simply do not want food and drink. Then he closed his eyes and said no more. Later, seeing that he had fallen into deep sleep yet his fingers moved without cease, they called to him softly and asked. He said: When I am not talking, I count the recitations on my fingers and recite the Buddha's name. Do not disturb me again. Afterwards a telegram came from my fourth brother: Father is gravely ill; come home quickly. I hurried back to Andong, but when I arrived there was no cart going to Xiuyan; there was nothing for it but to set out the next morning with my wife and little children and return to the village together. As we reached the gate I happened to meet my mother. I asked at once: How is my father now? She said: He has gone to your brother's house. So I went there at once. When my late father saw me he asked: Do you know that something has happened? I have no other illness; I only do not want to eat. I held back my grief, comforted him, and asked: How does my father feel now? Do you still recite the Buddha's name as before? He said: I recite; I can never forget it even for a moment. Then he closed his eyes and said no more, and silently recited the Buddha's name. And so we divided into shifts and recited aloud to assist him, hoping he might go straight to the Land of Bliss and escape the round of rebirth outright. After twelve that night, at the hour of zi, my late father suddenly rose, sat upright facing west, and passed away in Buddha-recitation. Reckoning to his birth, he had enjoyed the age of eighty. My brothers and I, and all who were at his side in the house, knelt facing west and recited the Buddha's name, assisting aloud, and only at dawn did we begin to prepare the funeral rites. At first, when my late father had just risen and sat up, he still counted recitations on his fingers for a long while, and only then did his fingers grow still. After a further time his jade chopsticks hung down — that is, two streams of mucus — and then he let go of the body in peace and passed. More than a day after his death he still sat upright as though in meditation, his face as in life. And so we encoffined him in a seated shrine and conducted the funeral rites in pure vegetarian fashion. We also took a photograph of him seated in transformation, to keep his memory and to strengthen the faith of those who cultivate Pure Land Buddha-recitation. It was taken thirteen hours after his rebirth.
Wang Chaohuan
(Original title: Layman Xu Yuelin Knows Three Days Beforehand and Passes Away Smiling in Buddha-Recitation)

The Precepts Sutra says: Be filial to father and mother, to teachers and monks, and to the Three Jewels; filial piety is the Dharma of the highest Way, and filial piety is called the precepts, and is also called restraint. Great Master Lianchi said: The grace is heavy as a mountain; five tripods and three victims are not enough to repay it. Only when one's parents are freed from the dust of defilement is the child's way accomplished. From this we know clearly how seriously Buddhism weighs filial piety.

In our Huai region there was a Layman Xu Ruitang, whose great-uncle Xu Yuelin had formerly been employed at the Zhang Yuantai salt warehouse at Liuhe in Huai'an. Seeing that his great-uncle was advanced in years and had no one to serve him broth and medicine, the layman brought him home, cared for him filially, and exhorted him to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. Layman Yuelin had in early years taken refuge under Dharma Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Huizhen. Some months before, he had contracted a grave illness, and medicine and physicians were of no avail. The layman stayed at his side day after day, reciting the name of Amitabha to aid his rebirth. Three days before the end he already foreknew the time, and said of himself: I shall wait three days and then go to the West. He told the whole household, nephews and grandchildren, to recite the Buddha's name together and by no means to grieve. And indeed, three days later, he passed away smiling in Buddha-recitation. Looking at the manner of his end, wholly free of pain and affliction, we see clearly that the effect of Buddha-recitation is trustworthy and well attested. And Layman Ruitang, in his filial respect and full observance of propriety, was able still more to exhort him to rebirth through Buddha-recitation — this is the greatest filial piety of all. Alas, human life is a dream, worldly things are impermanent, the three realms are a burning house, and the five turbidities scorch and sear us. If one does not recite the Buddha's name and seek to escape, in the end there is no way to gain liberation. The sutra says: Reciting Amitabha Buddha once with all one's heart can wipe away the heavy offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death. Now, seeing Layman Yuelin's rebirth through Buddha-recitation and such auspicious signs, we believe the more firmly that the Buddha has not deceived us. Earnestly may all our fellows believe deeply and practice earnestly, and share together in the victory.
, the
st month. Zhang Xiaoci
(Original title: Layman Yang Bingquan Foreknows the Time and Passes Away Sitting, at Ease)

My late elder brother Bingquan was eight years older than I, and I once studied under him. He was of keen and unusual nature, and in childhood was unlike ordinary boys. When he read a book he grasped it at once, and in his conduct he was courteous and well-mannered, so that from his earliest years his teachers esteemed him highly. At seventeen he was enrolled as a doctoral student. He was by nature much given to doing good, and delighted in printing and giving away moral books, and above all in relieving the poor. When he kept a school and taught pupils he earnestly instructed them in filial piety, brotherly respect, propriety, and righteousness. He would also recount historical cases of karmic response, to make clear that cause and effect never fail — this I heard as a boy together with my schoolmates. At twenty-four my brother passed the provincial examination; beyond his studies he still gave his mind to the inner scriptures. After the wuxu year of the Guangxu reign, troubled by the daily decline of the nation's affairs, he gave himself earnestly to the business of ordering the world, and had no leisure to read the Buddhist scriptures. But once the roots of goodness had sprouted, there was sure to come a day of growth and flowering. Hence after his fiftieth year he again delighted in reading the scriptures, and went further to settle his mind in the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha's name with faith and vow, and with this he urged me on as well.

, my brother was serving in the capital, and with Layman Mei Xieyun and others he organized a Buddha-recitation society, gathering the community at Wanshou Temple once a week at fixed times to recite the Buddha's name, while his own daily lesson of recitation was also most diligent. He constantly upheld the precept against killing with all his strength. After he took up the Buddha's teaching, when the family kept the New Year they used no meat in the offerings to the spirits, and sacrificed to the ancestors with vegetarian dishes only. One year at the end of the twelfth month a clansman came with a gift of two chickens. He declined them, but the man would not take them back, so he repaid him with other things and sent the chickens to the monastery that releases living creatures, to be kept there. In ordinary life he was very frugal for himself, but for relieving the poor and releasing living creatures he spared no expense; for my late parents delighted in doing good and giving alms, and my late brother, having received this family instruction in childhood, followed and practiced it, and to old age it grew only more steadfast.

Early on, when my brother was lodging in the capital, he bathed. When the bath was done he felt unwell, and so went to bed to rest, and suddenly fainted. His nephews, seeing it, were frightened and sought a physician. Before the physician came my brother had revived. Asked what ailed him, he said: Nothing; I only feel tired. That evening a cat disturbed him and he could not sleep peacefully; longing for rest, he sat upright facing west with closed eyes. At about eleven he seemed to fall into deep sleep, and after a time he woke. He told the family: I am about to be reborn in the West; do not be alarmed and do not grieve. Then he set his affairs in order and told his niece Xiaoci to write out his testament. He also had a long-distance telephone call made to notify his two nephews, Xiaozhang and Xiaokai. And he charged them not to send the news to his two younger brothers by wire, which would only make travelers alarmed and sorrowful. His dispositions made, he had people invite the eight bhikṣuṇīs of the nunnery east of the house to come and assist in the recitation, to see him into rebirth. When the nuns arrived he spoke to them himself: Please divide the eight of you into four shifts, each shift reciting the Buddha's name for one period of two hours, rotating thus, and for a day and a night do not let the sound of the Buddha-name be broken. At this time the whole family had gathered. Seeing his state, there were those who could not keep from weeping. He charged them earnestly: I am about to be reborn in the Pure Land. This is a chance that comes once in a thousand years, and it is not easily obtained. Do not imitate the grief of ordinary people, which would disorder my right mindfulness and drag me down. You should each restrain your sorrow and help me recite the Buddha's name; that is better by far than weeping. Then he took up the book The Last Stage of Life, written by Great Master Hongyi, and charged them to conduct his funeral according to it. He further charged that after his death they must by no means wail, nor move the body; only after twelve hours might they wipe the body and change the clothes, and he was to be encoffined in old garments. The coffin must not cost more than a hundred yuan; there was to be no public mourning, and the funeral was to be without display. The family consented as best they could. At this time nothing was heard in the house but the sound of Buddha-recitation, while my brother sat with closed eyes and silently recited with them, waiting for the time to come. Toward ten at night the family still had both a Western and a Chinese physician examine him. The Western physician said there was no sign whatever of mortal illness; the Chinese physician likewise said his pulse was calm and even and that he would not go at once. Then my sister-in-law brought in a decoction, and my brother said: My rebirth in the West is at hand; what use is this? He said again: I have no pain at all; I shall simply go like this. You should keep my words well in mind, and only recite the Buddha's name to see me off; you must not wail. With these words he closed his eyes and silently recited the Buddha-name as before. At midnight he opened his eyes and said to my sister-in-law: The time has come; I am going. She said: When the two boys in the capital get the telephone call they will certainly hurry back; why not wait for them? He said: Wait a little, then. When the clock struck two he again opened his eyes and said: I cannot wait any longer; I am going now. And so, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, he passed away sitting, at ease. The next afternoon, when mourners came to look at the body, he was still sitting upright in his chair, his face as in life. His four limbs were already cold, while the crown of his head alone was warm. The Small Pure Land Text of the Song-dynasty Master Ciyun, “Repentance Master,” says: “If at the end of life one knows beforehand that the time has come, and the body is free of the suffering of illness, the mind free of greed and attachment, the intention undefiled and not inverted, then one enters samādhi” — my late brother truly passed through that very state. Those who assisted in the recitation at the time all witnessed it, and none could cease from sighing that it was rare. When those near and far heard and saw it, it was passed about as an even stranger tale.
My brother died at the hour of chou on the
23rd day of the
5th
month
of
by the lunar calendar. His worldly age was sixty-three.
Yang Ping
(Original title: Layman Xu Zhiyi, Buddha-Light Filling the Room, Lotuses Rippling)

The layman's surname was Xu, and his personal name Jianzhang. His Dharma name was Huizhang, and he was a man of Xiangshan in Wu county. He believed in the Buddha from childhood and aspired to rebirth in the Pure Land. He once wrote a poem cherishing the Pure Land, containing the line “single-mindedly one phrase, Amitabha,” and so he took Zhiyi as his style name. He was by nature pure and generous, of mild temper, fond of stillness, sparing of speech and laughter. In youth he studied the Confucian books with his grandfather and father. His grandfather served the Buddha with the utmost reverence, bowing and reciting morning and evening, and so without knowing it he was steeped in it and had long possessed faith. Copying the Diamond Sutra as a calligraphy exercise, when he came to the lines “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should one contemplate them,” he would stop his brush and gather his spirit, as though thinking of something — his wisdom from former lives was surely there.
In
, the fifth month

, when the layman was seventeen, he heard that Dharma Master Yinguang was dwelling at Lingyan, and so went to pay his respects. He told of his own resolve to bring forth the mind and study the Buddha, and asked to be granted refuge. Old Master Yin praised him, and gave him the Collected Writings and the Record of Excellent Words and other works to take home and study. From this his faith grew firmer and his practice more earnest; he kept a vegetarian diet and cultivated purely, his whole mind galloping toward the West. Though he had not received the precepts, he upheld the five precepts most strictly, and especially the precept against killing: even mosquitoes, horseflies, fleas, and lice he did not dare to injure. When he saw others about to injure them he would find a way to save them. When his father and elder brother had silk garments made for him, he simply laid them aside and would not wear them. In cloth clothes and vegetarian food he practiced austerely and purely. He saved his pocket money and gave it all to the spreading of the Buddha Dharma and to such good works as relieving those he met. His filial piety, friendship, benevolence, and compassion were indeed his heaven-given nature. When he had nothing to do he would sit quietly and silently recite the Buddha's name, exactly like an old monk dwelling in the mountains. Because the mixed entanglements of a household are troublesome, and life at home is not so pure and single-minded as leaving home, he often had the wish to leave home. But because his parents were still living, and to comply with their wishes, he could not bear to go far away. Such was the purity and depth of his filial thought.
The layman had suffered from atrophied lungs for years, and his strength was rather thin and weak. On the
20th day of the
7th
month

, his elder brother, Mr. Caizhang, came and said: “Zhiyi has passed to the West. There are two letters left, in his own hand; the dates he asked someone else to fill in. One is for Master Huikong, with a request that it be forwarded. One is for the master.” I took and read it: “Reverend Master, your disciple passed to the West on
the 17th of the
7th
month
. Much have I received from your instruction, and I shall repay it hereafter. Zhiyi bows.” The farewell letter brought boundless feeling.
On the 27th

, I went to see the layman's father, Mr. Zhaoqi, and received from him this full account: “On the night of the fourth, Zhiyi dreamed that three monks told him: ‘You cannot stay here; you may come away with us.’ On the fifth he wanted to return to the village, and so on the sixth he went down to the countryside with him.” He said to me: “The scriptures and books deposited at Baoguo Monastery are all entrusted to Master Huikong to be given away and distributed as karmic bonds.” On the seventh he charged me not to go out, and asked monks to recite the Buddha's name, for he delighted to hear the sound of the Buddha. On the eighth he asked Master Changxiu to come to the house to recite the Buddha's name. In the morning he asked for paper and brush, and lying in bed wrote out his farewell letters. One was for the master, one for Master Huikong, and one concerned household affairs. When he had finished writing he handed them to me and said: “Fill in the date on the day of rebirth. When the breath is cut off at the end, do not at once feel and move the body; you must wait until eight hours have passed. During the seven periods, the repentance rites may be simple; one precept-keeping monk to recite the Buddha's name will suffice. My mother is kind and loving, and if she grieves and weeps for her son, my heart will be uneasy, and I fear my right mindfulness will be disturbed; please do not let her be at my side. Yesterday I already saw the Buddha and the great lotus flower; I once sat upon the lotus, rippling in the seven-jeweled pond. There are still a few days of worldly karmic bond left, and then I may go. Earlier I intended to go to Baoguo Monastery, not to nurse my illness, but truly to be reborn in the West there. But I am not a monk, and there might be inconvenience.” At eight or nine in the evening his mother was at his side assisting in the recitation, and saw a blue Buddha-light fill the whole room. On the ninth someone comforted and exhorted him: “Among the eminent monks and great worthies of old there were those who left home because of illness. Let the layman pray to the Buddha and make a vow that if he recovers he will leave home, in order to obtain a swift cure.” Zhiyi said: “There is no need for that. You should know that I am now resolved to be born in the Land of Bliss.” When a pure friend comforted him, Zhiyi said with a stern face: “Please do not speak worldly words; I beg you to recite the Buddha's name for me.” And he charged the family to recite the Buddha's name together, saying: “Let the sound of the Buddha-name be unbroken, and my mind is glad.” Of himself he bravely bowed to the Buddha in bed, about forty bows. When the bows were done he lay quietly at ease. On the sixteenth he refused food and drink. That evening, when he rose to urinate, his mother asked: “Do you need the quilt?” He said: “It is still early.” Afterwards he said to his parents: “The night is deep; you may go to sleep in peace.” At twelve, when those assisting in the recitation and those keeping the night watch took refreshment, Zhiyi said: “Please give some refreshment to my mother.” His mother asked: “What do you need?” He said: “I need nothing; you may go to sleep in peace, the hour is not early.” At half past twelve the night watcher lifted the curtain to look at him, and felt that his hand was already cold; he at once called me and his mother to look. We saw his bearing calm and composed, one hand pressed to his breast, the other stretched straight out, like the posture of the Buddha receiving and guiding. Only his breathing grew slowly lower and lower, never hurried, and with no phlegm or panting; and we gathered the community to recite the Buddha's name for him. And Zhiyi, seeing his mother at his side, said: “Only recite the Buddha's name, and please do not weep.” After that his breathing grew lower and fainter, faint to the point of not a thread of breath remaining, and he had calmly and peacefully let go of the body. Yet still one hand was pressed to his breast and the other stretched straight out, calm and composed, as though entered into samādhi. It was one o'clock in the morning of the seventeenth. Eight hours after death, when they felt his body, it was soft, and the crown of his head was still warm. At the encoffining he wore the haiqing robe and draped the precept sash, to fulfill his wish for the monk's dress. So much his father related in detail.

The layman lay ill for more than seventy days, and from first to last he never felt the suffering of illness as his own. His spirit was clear and composed; from this we may know his ordinary practice and its fruit. The depth of his samādhi and wisdom may likewise be glimpsed. When he had taken to his bed and could not rise, he did not talk of worldly things but pressed forward with courage, bowing to the Buddha, reciting the Buddha's name, and asking others to assist in the recitation: this is indeed a model for those who cultivate the pure karma and aspire to rebirth in the Pure Land. He saw the Buddha and the great lotus flower; his mother too saw the blue Buddha-light; he foreknew the time and serenely showed his passing, and the crown of his head was still warm. That he was reborn in the West is already sufficiently proved. And such are the evidences of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate, enough to stop the mouths of the obstinate and the slanderous, who may no longer revile it as superstition. I have therefore recorded the facts, to tell those who come after. The layman died on
the 17th of the
7th
month
of
, at the age of twenty-two years.
Ming Kai
(Original title: Layman Yu Zhizhao Bathes and Changes His Clothes, and Charges Them Beforehand to Assist His Recitation)

The layman's surname was Yu and his name Zhizhao; he was a man of Yujiahui, outside the Genshan Gate of Hangzhou. His family was comfortably off, and he was by nature kind, so that whenever he saw anyone in urgent difficulty he would help them to the utmost of his strength, and his fellow villagers all praised him. His family had served the Buddha for generations; from the time of his ancestors there had been an Avatamsaka society, and every year they recited the sutras, and so it had been for many years. When the layman was in his teens he already recited with the assembly, and most devoutly. Moved by the Buddha's empowerment, he often conceived the thought of leaving the world. He would think to himself: within this world, why is there suddenly an “I”? Before I was born, where was I? After I die, where do I go? And the six paths of rebirth, rising and sinking without certainty, are most perilous. Everyone in the world is like this — why are they not afraid? He did not know what good Dharma could free him from this root of suffering. Such was the layman's view before he took refuge in the Three Jewels. Afterwards he suddenly had a dream in which he saw two men come and say that the Great Emperor of Mount Tai had sent them to arrest him, and that at the tenth hour he was to go to the underworld. In the dream he at once charged his family to prepare for his funeral. Thinking of the agony when a man dies and his consciousness leaves the body, he was terrified awake. And he awoke to the truth that human life is always a Nanke dream; and so he went to the hermitage of Puji Nunnery, bowed to Dharma Master Mingde, and asked for the Dharma of swiftly ending birth and death and forever escaping the round of rebirth. The master said: If you would escape rebirth and forever enjoy peace and bliss, you cannot do it without cultivating the Pure Land Dharma gate and seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. He was graciously given several Pure Land scriptures and treatises and the name Zhengzhu. From this the layman's faith and vow were complete, and he vowed that in this life he would seek rebirth in the Pure Land. He took the Diamond Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, and the six-character great name Namo Amitabha Buddha as his daily lesson. When he chanced to be a guest in another land, he recited silently as well. And when he met those with the karmic bond, he exhorted them by this Dharma too.

, in the spring, he contracted dropsy. By the eighth month his illness had grown grave, and he knew that his worldly bonds were nearly ended, so he recited the Buddha's name with one mind. When pain came he added the recitation of Guanyin Bodhisattva, and at once his mind was at peace; such was the spiritual response again and again. At the end of the tenth month he firmly resolved to return to his village, and gave clear instructions concerning the affairs of the household. He said also: If I cannot rise, help me recite the Buddha's name, and on no account weep, which would disorder my mind for rebirth in the West. His wife too had taken refuge in the Three Jewels, with the Dharma name Zhengyan, and she understood the principle and practice of the Pure Land quite clearly; day and night she nursed him in his illness and recited the Buddha's name constantly. The layman repeatedly urged that new clothes be made quickly, because the clothes he wore felt too small. On the evening of the twenty-eighth of the winter month he asked for water to bathe, and changed into the new clothes, saying: These clothes are very good; I can bow to the Buddha in them. And he smiled slightly. His wife asked him why he smiled. He answered: The bitter root of my birth and death is cut off from this moment; why should I not smile? On the afternoon of the twenty-ninth he asked: Is there sun outside? His second son said: Today is overcast; the sun is hidden by clouds. The layman said: I see a very great brightness. The time of my rebirth has come; recite the Buddha's name aloud, all of you, so that I may hear it. When he had spoken, he recited the Buddha's name with the assembly. Thereafter only his lips moved, and in less than five minutes he passed away at ease, wholly free of pain. He was forty-one. The assembly recited the Buddha's name for two more sticks of incense before they began to mourn. Such a state at the end is truly rare; the hardship of his lifelong study of the Buddha has now brought him real benefit. When relatives and neighbors saw it, none failed to call it wonderful, and all said that Buddha-recitation has such benefits that they too wish to recite constantly, and in time may hope for rebirth in the West. Ah, the layman may be called one who benefits himself and others, teaching the Dharma in his own person. Earnestly may all living beings of the Dharma realm cultivate the pure karma together and be born together in the Land of Bliss: this is the essential thing.
Qin Kunquan

blocks.text: 22. Passing to the West in Peace

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Xu Yuxiang Sits Facing West and Passes to the West in Peace)

Layman Xu Yuxiang was a man of Jiangcun, the third district of Jinshan county, Songjiang. After his wife died when he was thirty he lived alone, and had no children either, and so he ate vegetarian food and recited the Buddha's name. In his thatched hut he set up a Buddha hall, and morning and evening he burned incense, bowed, and recited. By day he farmed for his food, and so it was for decades as on the first day. When he grew old and both eyes went blind, he made his living by twisting grass rope, ragged as a beggar, yet cheerful and content, never seeking help from others. This spring, in the second month (that is,

), on the day before the Great Being's holy birthday, he still carried his grass rope on a pole into the market to sell, and bought incense with the money before returning, as healthy as ever. At midnight on the twentieth the neighbors still heard the sound of Buddha-recitation and the wooden fish. The next morning (that is, the morning of the twenty-first) the neighbor Gao Yude, because there was sickness in his house, wished to go to his Buddha hall to burn incense and draw a lot; but there was no answer when he knocked. Going inside, he saw the old man sitting upright facing west, making no sound at all: he had already passed to rebirth in peace.
Jue Lian
(Original title: Layman Zhou Daxi, a Great and Lofty Jeweled Lotus Thronging the Descending Buddha)

Layman Zhou, courtesy name Ruifu, was a man of Suzhou. At No. 2 Erma Road, Taozhu Lane in Shanghai, he kept the Yikang Silk House. Through the occasion of buying silk I came to know him. Later, seeing that his house had a copy of the Diamond Sutra, I asked him why he held to the sutra. He said it had been given him by relatives, and that he did not understand it very well either. Seeing the man to be sincere and trustworthy and possessed of good roots, I told him of the Pure Land Dharma gate, because for those who live at home it is the most convenient and the most timely, and one may rely on Amitabha's vow-power to be reborn with one's karma and be freed from birth and death. If one holds the Diamond Sutra and dedicates its merit toward rebirth in the West, that too is inconceivable; but if one holds the Diamond Sutra alone and seeks thereby to end birth and death, then it is by no means easy. The layman's roots from former lives were deep; he at once expressed his belief and acceptance, and straightway gave up wine and meat to show his resolve. From then on, whenever he met anyone, he urged them to recite the Buddha's name and eat vegetarian food; his mind of self-benefit and benefit to others was admirable.

Last autumn he also invited me and several others to take refuge together under Dharma Master Desen. From then on his pure karma advanced day by day and his faith grew firmer. His wife and his daughter were both disciples of Master De as well, keeping a vegetarian diet and reciting the Buddha's name. In less than half a year they had brought about a Buddhist family. Seeing such progress in him, I rejoiced in my heart. But truly, “when the Way advances a foot, the demon advances a fathom.” The layman, burdened by his relatives, suffered a setback and seemed to give rise to a mind of retreat. So I told him that when adverse conditions come, that is precisely the day for cultivating practice and repaying one's debts. When the debts are done, blessings arrive; when bitterness is at its extreme, sweetness comes — and that time cannot be far off. He should endure and pass through this difficult gate, and redouble his Buddha-recitation, and only so could he swiftly dissolve his former karma. Unhappily, forced by his circumstances, in the end he could not lighten his afflictions, and so his original tuberculosis and his hemorrhoids and other old complaints flared up violently again. At this time evil conditions were many, and all said that the cause of his illness lay in his vegetarian diet and its lack of nourishment. If he should be enveloped by the demon and actually begin eating meat again, I heard of it with unutterable grief; for the layman was an educated man, one who could well have been a help to the Buddha's gate, and unhappily he had fallen into demonic obstruction and thrown away his former merit. This was not yet to be lamented; but the very foundation of his whole family's faith in the Buddha might perhaps be shaken by it. Thinking of this, I did not scruple to be unmannerly, and from the standpoint of a fellow student I told him that the fault of eating meat would surely bring him into the three evil paths. Since you are a son of the Buddha, I said, how can you be so unwise? Hearing it, the layman showed a little repentance, and said that Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth with one's karma, and that even if he ate meat he might still be received by the Buddha. I said: That is your great mistake. To be reborn with one's karma means that one must not create new karma, and that with old karma not yet exhausted, one may then receive the Buddha's empowerment. But if one is without shame or conscience, with former karma piled up like a mountain and new offenses added besides, deceiving oneself and deceiving the Buddha, wholly at odds with the Buddha, how can one evoke the Buddha's compassion? There can be no principle of rebirth in that. Stirred by this, he felt great shame, and made his vow anew, telling his wife to bring no more meat, and to remove the meat-based medicines. But only a few days after he had begun eating meat again, his illness moved into his throat; though hungry within, he could not swallow food or drink. And he said to his wife: I have become a hungry ghost in appearance; regret is too late. Hearing it, I comforted him, saying: In the Pure Land Dharma gate even the five heinous offenses and the ten evils, when the signs of hell have appeared — if one can truly repent, give rise to a mind of shame, and recite the Buddha's name with courage — may still receive the Buddha's descending compassion, which turns hell itself into a lotus pond. The layman nodded deeply in belief. On the fifteenth day of the fourth lunar month his mind and spirit fell into confusion. The next day, when Lady Jiang of the Longfu Hermitage at Mudu happened to come, she joined the two of us in urging his household that all assist in the recitation. His wife and daughter, believing deeply without doubt, recited together with one voice and spoke of nothing else. And I again and again had him lift up right mindfulness and recite the Buddha's name with one mind; and he received it with utter sincerity, quietly reciting along, earnestly vowing rebirth in the West.

At about twelve on the night of the sixteenth he said: I see two peacocks and a lotus seat, tall and great, thronging the descending Buddha; but the lotus is too high to climb. I at once told him to give rise to a mind of shame, redouble his repentance, and vow that after rebirth in the West he would return by his vow to deliver living beings everywhere in repayment of the Buddha's grace; and then he might sit at ease upon the lotus throne. He nodded, joined his palms, and bowed to me again and again, showing his belief and compliance. Then he asked the time. His wife asked whether he foreknew the hour of his passing. He signaled with his hand: a quarter to nine. Later, when it was past seven in the morning, he asked for paper and brush, as though he had something to say. But his spirit was too faint and weary to form characters, and when he tried to speak his voice was too fine to be heard clearly. So I said: If you have anything to say, you may pray to the Buddha for empowerment to help you make a sound. And he did cry out aloud: No meat; no opening of the white. I asked again whether he had any last affairs. He shook his head to show that he had none. I then told him that the time had come, and that he should follow the Buddha straight to the West. He nodded again and again, then placed his right hand over his breast and stretched out his left like the Buddha receiving and guiding, and passed away at ease. It was exactly twenty minutes to nine, on the morning of
, on the
4 th month, on the
th

, so it was. I at once had his wife and daughter recite the Buddha's name aloud and burn incense in farewell. At about ten, when they felt his whole body, it was all cold, only the crown of his head hot. At half past one in the afternoon, when his crown was felt again, it was still warm, which shows how inconceivable the Buddha's power is. And it is rare indeed that his wife and daughter understood the Buddha's principle and did not imitate any of the vain practices of the world, but wholly followed the pure conduct of attending the dying, aiding his right mindfulness and completing his rebirth in the West. Stranger still: only a few days after the layman broke the precept and ate meat, the illness shifted to his throat, and he could not swallow his food, becoming a hungry ghost in appearance — proof enough that karmic retribution never fails. Afterwards he repented deeply, redoubled his Buddha-recitation, and in the end received the Buddha's compassionate guidance and manifested many auspicious signs, going straight to the West — which shows all the more that the Buddha's vow is not vain. Note that the layman had cultivated for only a short time, and had broken the precept midway, so that the signs of hell appeared; yet through Buddha-recitation he turned sinking into rising. Such a victory no other Dharma can compare with, apart from the Pure Land Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the West. From this one sees that to believe the Buddha's words and rely on the Buddha's power is, compared with relying wholly on one's own power, as far apart as heaven and an abyss. And a Buddhist household is a deep source of help, to which we too should give particular attention. I am ashamed that I have no learning and no literary grace; I only wish that cultivators of the Pure Land may speedily bring about a Buddhist family and carry on after Layman Zhou, so that even with shallow practice, by relying on all these aiding conditions they may evoke the Buddha's power to receive them into rebirth in the West, and not fail at the last step. This is the essential thing.
Tang Huaixi
(Original title: Layman Yi Huiming Foreknows His Rebirth and Passes Away Sitting Upright, Smiling)

Old Layman Yi Huiming was a man of Jinsha in Nantong. All his life he was in business, and his word was his bond. At first he was deluded by the planchette. I constantly urged him to eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha's name, devoting himself to the Pure Land, and I sketched the essential meaning of the Pure Land for him. The layman believed deeply without doubt, took refuge under the Great Master of Lingyan, and gave up practicing the planchette. In
the community proposed and established the Jinsha Buddhist Lay Grove, and the layman had a part in it. In the winter of

he received the precepts with me at Shousheng Chan Monastery at Pincha in Dongtai, and then went to the grove to cultivate exclusively, pressing forward without slackening. Whenever there was merit to be made, such as releasing living creatures, giving coffins, printing sutras, or making Buddha images, he would generously open his purse, transforming himself and others, for ten years as on the first day.

On the first day of the winter month of the old calendar last year, just after his morning lesson, he suddenly felt a slight dizziness in his head and eyes. He joined his palms to me and said: At the hour of shen the day after tomorrow, I shall return to the West; I earnestly beg the whole community of the grove to assist my rebirth. On the day (that is, the third), Gu Degui, Zhang Huijie, and all the grove friends came, and the layman recited with them, his lips moving without cease. At the hour of shen he broke into a smile
and passed away sitting upright
The next morning
the crown of his head was still burning hot
That day happened to be the second anniversary of Master Yin's passing
in the afternoon

they dressed him and set him cross-legged, and his whole body was soft. When he was placed in the shrine, his face was as in life and his smile was still there, and those who saw it sighed that it was rare. His worldly age was seventy-five. Ah, a man like the layman, foreknowing the time and with auspicious signs so clear, may serve as clear proof of rebirth in the West.
, the
rd month. Hu Huiche respectfully records
(Original title: Layman Zhang Jingshan, Guanyin Foretelling It, Passes Away with Palms Joined)
, the
th month. Recorded by Yishan

The layman's name was Ruzhen, his courtesy name Jingshan, his style name Bao'an; he was a man of Fangqiao in Yuyao, Zhejiang. There were four brothers, and the layman was the youngest. In youth he studied the Confucian books; by nature he was mellow and good, filial in serving his parents, frugal and hardworking, loyal and honest without deceit. Grown to manhood he went into business, kindly in his dealings and resourceful in planning. At forty-two, moved by the turmoil of the nation's fortunes and the floating clouds of worldly affairs, he wished to abandon business altogether and give his whole mind to the Pure Land. But it was no easy thing to wind up the shop's affairs, and hard to shake off the dusty bonds, so he had no choice but to cultivate at home. He turned the shop into a lotus society, reciting the Buddha's name while carrying on business. He and his partners and their families all gave up wine and meat and devoted themselves to the pure karma. At every fifth watch he would recite the name of Amitabha several hundred times aloud, and so it went for nearly three years.

Since last summer his body had been weak and burdened with illness, lingering for more than a year. On the first day of the ninth month of this year he wrote inviting me to his home. Seeing his illness to be grave, I gave him a sharp warning: Why not put down the ten thousand conditions, refuse medicine and physicians, and recite the Buddha's name with one mind, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land? For one who recites the Buddha's name, to be able to recite in ordinary times is not so good as to be able to recite in illness. You have been ill a long time without recovery; what is there to fear in death? You should rather set your mind toward the Buddha's land, never parting from Amitabha in thought after thought, and vow to seek the Pure Land, never forgetting the Land of Bliss from moment to moment. Know deeply that the Saha world has many sufferings, and the Land of Bliss has immeasurable joy. Recite the Buddha's name with one mind, in the hope that Amitabha will receive you and bring you across to the other shore. The layman heard it and joyfully accepted. He at once refused medicine and physicians and all worldly bonds. And he had a note written out and pasted on the wall, to show all who came: I am resolved to recite the Buddha's name with one mind, to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, to leave the round of rebirth, and to end birth and death. All relatives and friends who visit my sickroom are earnestly begged not to talk of worldly matters, but to recite Amitabha the more, and help me toward rebirth in the Pure Land; my gratitude will be endless.

From then on, every day he asked several monks of the Guanzong Monastery to stay at his bedside and assist in reciting the Buddha's name, day and night without cease. On the morning of the eighth he suddenly saw Guanyin come and tell him: On the eighteenth you may reach the lotus assembly. The layman counted on his fingers and found there were still ten days; though he told others of it, in his heart he had not decided. On the fourteenth he saw Guanyin come again and say: On the eighteenth you will be born in the West; the date is exact. And so his mind was settled. He then told his son to write and urge me to come to Yuyao before the seventeenth, and to invite several more people who recite the Buddha's name to assist together in the recitation, seeing him off to the West. On the morning of the sixteenth he closed his eyes and saw the surpassing realm of the Land of Bliss, pure and adorned, present before his eyes. On the seventeenth he saw it again, and said: My birth in the West is certain. That day I set out from Ningbo and reached Yuyao at noon. I found his mind and spirit clear and fresh and all his faculties keen. Perfectly as usual, he said to me: I do not hang my heart on any of my affairs in the least, but my thought of being born in the West I never forget; perhaps I shall go at eleven tonight. The Dharma masters who assist in reciting the Buddha's name should rest more by day, for the night is hard work. Recite the Buddha's name the whole night through to help me. At nine that night, when the whole family and all the masters had gathered in the room reciting the Buddha's name, he himself called for a haircut, bathed, and changed his clothes

and when all was done he sincerely made his vow, lay quietly reciting the Buddha's name, and waited to be received. At twelve, when he did not see Amitabha come to welcome him, he raised his hand to count and changed the time to nine the next morning, saying to those present: I have good news: I see two boys carrying a pair of white silk lanterns, exceedingly bright. On the eighteenth, at eight in the morning, he asked for water to wash his face, and had his clothes and bedding set in order and his body laid straight; he lay quietly reciting the Buddha's name for half an hour, then suddenly stretched his hand out from the quilt, reverently joined his palms, and made the gesture of bowing to the Buddha three or four times. Then he gazed again at the image of Amitabha and told his son to face west and recite the Buddha's name. At twenty past nine he passed away at ease, wholly free of pain. Two hours later, when his whole body was felt, it was all cold, only the crown of his head exceedingly warm. His family all restrained their grief and recited the Buddha's name, and no sound of weeping was raised. At the encoffining his four limbs were soft and his face as in life. Reviewing all the layman's auspicious signs — foreknowing the time ten days beforehand, beholding the realm of the Land of Bliss in between, joining his palms in homage at the end, and the crown of his head growing cold last when his breath ceased — all are certain proof of his birth in the West.
(Original title: Old Mr. Wang Repeatedly Crying, Amitabha Buddha, Come Quickly and Save Me)

On the twenty-sixth day of the fourth lunar month my younger sister sent someone to say that her uncle, old Mr. Wang, was gravely ill and asked me and my fellow brother-in-law Mr. Zhou Linpu to assist his recitation. When Mr. Zhou and I reached his home (in the village of Nizhi on Dai), the old man lay gasping on his sickbed and had already taken no food for three or four days. Seeing the two of us come, he joyfully joined his palms and bowed. Fearing that the old man's heart was heavy with love for his family, I made skillful means to exhort him: “Old uncle, you must recite the Buddha's name with one mind and seek rebirth in the West. Do not be tied to your family. Once you are tied, you cannot attain rebirth, and you will have to go to the hall of King Yama. Once in the underworld you lose your freedom and cannot look after your family at all. Only by being born in the West do you gain spiritual powers and perfect ease, so that you are not separated from this place even while separated. The worlds of the ten directions are still before your eyes — how much more your family and all those with whom you have karmic bonds? Therefore at this moment you must put everything down for the time being and strive for rebirth; only after rebirth is there any real possibility of looking after your family.” The old man said resolutely: “I will not bother about them anymore.” Afterwards, whatever exhortation was given he joyfully heard and accepted, his answers firm. Again and again he cried: “Amitabha Buddha, come quickly and save me.” That night they recited in shifts, and the sound of the Buddha-name was unbroken the whole night through.

On the morning of the twenty-seventh the suffering of his illness had melted away; he lay peacefully with closed eyes, quietly listening to the sound of the Buddha. From time to time his mouth moved slightly, as though reciting. At one in the afternoon his face suddenly turned outward, and amid the sound of Buddha-recitation he passed away in peace. Four hours later I felt his whole body; it had grown cold through, while the crown of his head was still warm. At half past nine that night, when they changed his clothes, his four limbs were soft and his face clear and moist; the whole family rejoiced, for this is certain proof of rebirth in the West.
, in the intercalary
th month, on the
th day. Respectfully recorded by Gu Huasun of Daishan, Dinghai
(Original title: Layman Yu Jingda, the Three Holy Ones Come to Welcome Him, and He Passes Away in Peace)

The layman's style name was Yecai and his Dharma name Jingda; his family had lived for generations in Nizhi village, Daishan, Dinghai. The family were farmers, and he was sincere and plain by nature. In dealing with others he was modest and self-effacing. He had a rough grasp of letters and loved to urge people to recite the Buddha's name. Later he joined the Right Faith Buddha-Recitation Society and took refuge under Great Master Xiufu, and hearing his instructions clearly he came to understand that the Pure Land Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation is a shortcut in cultivation. From then on he kept his lessons morning and evening, never breaking off in summer or winter, thinking of nothing but the Buddha and seeking nothing but the Pure Land.

Last winter he happened to catch a slight illness, but his mind was quite clear, and all day long he still chanted the Buddha-name aloud. By the fifteenth day of the first month of this spring, when I and Layman Mao Wujing and others went to inquire after his illness, we urged him with the principle of delighting in the Pure Land and loathing the Saha world, of taking up and letting go. The layman then cited the words of an ancient worthy: The three realms are like a cage, and my body is like a bird. For the flavors of the world I truly have no greed or attachment; but I regret that we country folk of this rustic place toil all day for food and clothing, and even with some cultivation have not attained one mind, and I fear rebirth in the West will be hard to hope for. Then Layman Yue Hongsong told him: Layman, do not misunderstand. You must know that the Pure Land Dharma gate is the supreme wondrous Dharma, all-pervading for the three capacities, wholly gathering in both the sharp and the dull. From the equal-enlightenment bodhisattvas above, who vow to seek rebirth, down to the perverse and evil ordinary man, for whom even ten recitations bring horizontal transcendence. Now you have cultivated for many years; you are not perverse or evil, and your merit exceeds ten recitations — how could you fail to be reborn? Then Layman Zhou Linpu told him of the actual proof of Mr. Yu Mingsheng of the same county, who attained rebirth with ten recitations. Hearing it, the layman said joyfully: Now that I have received this instruction, it is like building a high wall and laying a firm foundation, so that there is no more danger of collapse. All praised it as good, and assisted him in reciting the Buddha's name. At eight on the night of the twentieth the layman suddenly recited aloud the holy names of the two bodhisattvas Guanyin and Mahāsthāmaprāpta himself. Asked why, he said: Because I have already received the two bodhisattvas come to welcome me. Asked again whether he saw Amitabha Buddha, he said: He is seated on the golden terrace. Presently his breath came faster and faster, and amid the sound of Buddha-recitation he passed away in peace. It was

, the twentieth day of the first month, at the hour of xu; his worldly age was fifty-six. Eight hours later the crown of his head was still warm. On the twenty-second, when he was placed cross-legged in the shrine, his four limbs were soft as in life. Those who came from far and near to look all sighed that it was rare; such auspicious signs are indeed clear evidence of rebirth in the West. I have made this record of the facts in particular, wishing that those in the world who would escape the sea of suffering of birth and death may deeply believe that in the Pure Land Dharma gate ten thousand practice and ten thousand go, and that it cannot be compared with the other Dharma gates that rely wholly on one's own power.
Hong Minzhou

blocks.text: 28. The Three Holy Ones Come to Welcome Him

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Song Yunzhong, Golden Light Filling the Room, the Three Holy Ones Come to Welcome Him)

Layman Song Yunzhong loved painting from childhood, and at thirteen his father, Mr. Yulin, had him study under the famous painter Mr. Hang Jingying. The layman had a genius for art, studied with diligence besides, and his attainments were profound. Mr. Hang believed in the Buddha, and the layman was steeped in his influence. In the winter of the twenty-fifth year of the Republic, when Great Master Yinguang was expounding the Dharma at the Shanghai Dharma Assembly for Protecting the Nation and Averting Calamity, Mr. Hang led the layman and his fellow students to beg the Great Master to confer the three refuges; the layman received the Dharma name Zhen'gen, and was then twenty-one. He ate vegetarian food and recited the Buddha's name, keeping morning and evening lessons, his heart turned toward the pure realm. At twenty-six he married Miss Li Menghua, and entertained the guests with a vegetarian banquet at Gongdelin. Miss Menghua followed him in believing in the Buddha, and the couple were deeply devoted.

Two years ago the layman fell ill with his lungs and entered the hospital. For close to two years he was there, and seven ribs were removed, yet he was not cured. So he came home to nurse his illness, and recited the Buddha's name the more diligently. With the coming of winter his illness gradually grew grave. On the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month of this year I went to comfort him. The layman said: The suffering of illness is very great; when shall I return to the West? I said: In former days Dharma Master Xuanzang too suffered illness at the end, and a heavenly being told him: Master, for the karmic offenses of having harmed and vexed living beings through measureless kalpas, you now rely on the power of the Three Jewels and are turned to light recompense, and in this suffering of illness it is wholly finished. The layman's illness is likewise so. Amitabha's great vow says: “For the heavenly and human peoples of the worlds of the ten directions who in former lives did evil, if they hear my name, repent and do good, uphold the sutras and precepts, and vow to be born in my land, at the end of life they shall not pass through the three evil paths, but shall straightway come to be born there.” Therefore those whose evil karma in former lives was heavy and whose pure karma in this life is light receive the sufferings of illness before the end of life, to dissolve the evil karma, and at the end of life are born straight into the Land of Bliss. If their former evil karma was light and their pure karma in this life heavy, then before the end there is no more suffering of illness. This depends on whether a man can diligently cultivate the pure karma or not. Hence for a Buddhist to suffer illness at the end is precisely heavy recompense turned to light, a good omen before rebirth; the world does not understand it, and so falls into doubt and confusion — truly a mistake. What is called former life, this life, and the life to come is no other than yesterday, today, and tomorrow. This body comes driven by the power of the good and evil karma of former lives; while the recompense is not yet exhausted, how could it go? It is like a man who has business here: while the business is unfinished, how can he go elsewhere? Or like a prisoner whose term is not yet full: how can he leave prison? This body is the prison; the consciousness is the prisoner. When the prisoner's term is full, even if he wished to stay in prison, he could not. When the karmic recompense of this life is exhausted, the spirit-consciousness departs, and it cannot be kept. Layman, set your mind at ease and wait, holding the Buddha-name without forgetfulness. I also told his family: Where there is life there must be death, just as where there is day there must be night, going round and returning again — who can escape it? Though a life last a hundred years, in the end there must be parting. What is to be lamented is that after death each goes according to his karma to receive recompense, and there will be no set time for meeting again — that is what is pitiable. Now that Mr. Yulin and your worthy household can all recite the Buddha's name diligently, you shall afterward go together to the Land of Bliss and be companions in the Dharma forever, with no more parting; and so when this body of recompense is given up, it is rather a cause for rejoicing — why grieve? When the visit was finished I took my leave.

At ten that night his family had all gone to bed. The layman called out: Get up, get up! I am going to the West; please assist my recitation. The family gathered around the bed reciting the Buddha's name. The layman clapped his hands and called on Amitabha Buddha, telling the family to recite along. After a long while, he saw golden light fill the room and the Three Holy Ones of the West descend to welcome him; the layman then joined his palms, called on Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva once, and passed away. It was one in the morning of the twenty-ninth. Three days later, at the encoffining, his whole body was soft, and those who saw it sighed in wonder. The layman's whole family was steeped in the Buddha's transformation; his younger brother Yungong, eighteen this year, a graduate of the telecommunications college, serves the Buddha with especial diligence. The layman was a man of Jiading in Jiangsu, and lived at No. 202 Dongjiadu Street, Nanshi, Shanghai; his worldly age was twenty-nine.
, in the lunar
th month, on the
th day. Recorded by Chen Hailiang
(Original title: Old Mr. Zhang Youmei, Assisted in Recitation at the End, an Auspicious Rebirth)

To be reborn in the West and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression is a matter hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas. To die with the mind not inverted, in the auspicious sleeping posture, with the crown of the head warm at the end, is certain proof of rebirth in the West. Now here was a sixty-eight-year-old old man who had kept only the six vegetarian days, and only when gravely ill resolved to enter the lotus society and recite the Buddha's name; yet amid the sound of assisting recitation he obtained this rare auspicious sign. Was it that he had long since planted good roots under measureless millions of Buddhas? Or that the Pure Land Dharma gate is so supremely excellent that, beyond Chan, Vinaya, and Esoteric teachings, it displays this extraordinary efficacy? This must not go unrecorded, to strengthen the faith of those who are beginning to cultivate the Pure Land Dharma gate, and as an exhortation to those who do not know it.

Zhang Youmei was a man of Liushutou in the eastern district of Jiangyin. His family were scholars for generations, and Youmei also studied medicine. He was modest and gentle, and never haggled over the size of his fee; those who sought his treatment came one after another, and he had no leisure in the day. His village was about three li from Beiguo, and at Beiguo there was the Jigui Lotus Society. Youmei's eldest son, Mengliang, kept a vegetarian diet and served the Buddha, promoting the Lotus school with all his strength, and very many followed him in faith. Youmei at first clung obstinately to the Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu view of refuting the Buddha; then, from stories of karmic cause and retribution, he came to believe a little, and so kept the six vegetarian days.
, in the

th month he fell ill with quinsy, and the assembled physicians were helpless. He then had himself registered at the lotus society and named himself Juewu. He said that when his illness was cured he would enter the society and recite the Buddha's name. His son Mengliang, day after day, asked pure companions to recite the Buddha's name and release living creatures for him. He said that whenever he heard the sound of the Buddha he felt his mind grow clear. On the twelfth his illness grew grave. I said to him: Brother, now you must put everything down and silently recite Amitabha Buddha; Amitabha Buddha will naturally come to receive you. He could not speak, but nodded his head. At once his lips began to move, reciting the Buddha's name without cease. At that time in the next room the sound of the Buddha-name rang out clearly. Toward dusk he said: My mind is very clear now; the weather is hot, let everyone rest a while. On the thirteenth, at about six or seven in the afternoon, his illness grew more urgent, and I warned his wife and daughters not to weep before him and disorder his mind; for a son or daughter's first duty to a parent is to set his spirit at peace. Death is the most bitter thing in a human life, and one should let him not feel its bitterness but know only rebirth in the Land of Bliss. Then some twenty pure companions were gathered, and the four-character Buddha-name was raised aloud. At about ten, his whole body was cold; some three hours after his breath had ceased the Buddha-name was stopped and mourning begun, and his body still lay facing west in the auspicious posture. His friend felt his warmth, and only the crown of his head was warm. At about eleven, his second son, named Xiang, and his son-in-law Zhou Changshou, both university graduates who had not believed at first, were struck with wonder.
Ming Xi
(Original title: Layman Qian Bingjun Sees the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Is Assisted in Reciting the Buddha’s Name at Death)

Qian Bingjun, courtesy name Hengfu, was a man of Nantong. He lost both parents in childhood, and was by nature simple, sincere, and filial. Growing up, he entered school, mastered letters, and then went to Luzhou to study machinery. He once worked at the Dasheng No. 2 Mill, and later became director of the Gongfu Electric Light Plant of the Reclamation and Herding Company, also serving as a staff member of the company; it was thus that I came to know him. In his dealings with others, he remained respectful even after long acquaintance. In managing his livelihood he worked diligently and spent frugally, and his family thereby attained modest comfort. In

, in June he fell ill with a throat ailment. The doctors were of no avail, and he was in grave danger. On the urging of a good friend he constantly drank Great Compassion water, and his illness gradually healed. From this, seeds from former lives were perfumed and awakened within him; he took refuge in the Buddha and adopted a vegetarian diet, fixing a daily course of Buddha-recitation. Later he went to Suzhou and took refuge with Master Yinguang, the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, who gave him the name Huishi. From then on his views grew ever more correct, and he recited the Buddha’s name with greater diligence. In matters of the Buddhadharma he shrank from no toil and feared no difficulty, and did all he could to bring them to accomplishment.

In the end, called forth by former karma and brought on by toil, his lung disease grew worse day by day. Though medical treatment was of no avail, he never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name. In the last ten days or so before his death, I invited Master Xinjing and several laymen such as Xi Chaozai to take turns reciting the Buddha’s name daily. If his allotted span were not yet exhausted, we would seek to avert calamity and prolong his life; if his allotted span were already exhausted, we would assist him in reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth. Through the Buddha’s response, he indeed enjoyed a spell of excellent spirits. He said: I saw my teacher, Master Yinguang, and I saw the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, with all its adornments and all its radiance; from that time my mind opened ever wider. He told people, “Even if I did not recite the Buddha’s name, I would not much cling to worldly affairs — how much the less, then, as one who does recite it.” He also gave instructions concerning the family affairs to follow his death, arranging them in the greatest detail. On the evening two days before the Double Ninth of this year, I suddenly heard that the layman’s illness had turned critical and that he was calling for me to assist in recitation; but because communications were cut off, neither Master Xinjing nor I could get there. Fortunately his wife, Madam Peng, who also kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and honored the Buddha, led the children and the household in reciting the Buddha’s name for him, and the layman passed away peacefully. The next day, hearing the news of his death, I went to inquire how he had been at the end. They told me that his family had all been able to help by reciting the Buddha’s name, that they had restrained their tears and wept only silently, and that there were no particular auspicious signs. In my humble opinion, if at the moment the layman relinquished his retribution his family could refrain from weeping and help him by reciting the Buddha’s name, then thoughts of affection would not arise and right mindfulness would be clear of itself; although there were no remarkable auspicious signs, by this cause and condition he may, I believe, have attained rebirth. The layman lived fifty-two years, born at the hour of the dragon on the seventh day of the first month, and died in
, on the seventh day of the ninth month, at the hour of the rooster. I am ashamed that I have no literary talent, and being by nature remiss, I have been late in writing this record for him.
Xing Deheng

blocks.text: 31. Seeing the Lotus and Attaining Rebirth

inline.s: (Original title: Yong Guiping, Sincere in His New Faith, Sees the Lotus at Death and Attains Rebirth)

Mr. Yong Guiping was a man of Yongjia Town in Hanshan County, Anhui. His family was poor and he did not finish his schooling. At twenty he gave up study for business. Through the help of his maternal uncle he was recommended to an egg factory in northern Anhui as an accountant. As he was quite capable, he was soon promoted to manager. It happened that the First World War broke out, business prospered abnormally, and the family fortunes grew steadily more ample. His first wife bore two daughters, both of whom were married off in turn. After this upheaval he moved to Wuhu.

Because the times were troubled and his dwelling never at peace, he had often heard that Guanyin’s responses are inconceivable and that reciting the Guanyin Sutra can avert disaster; and so he recited it daily, praying for the removal of his karmic obstacles. Later, through frequent visits with Cui Siqiao, the son-in-law of his friend Mr. Wang, he first heard the Buddhadharma. Layman Cui urged him to cultivate the Pure Land practice alone, whereby one may forever escape the sea of suffering: with deep faith and earnest vows, holding the Name and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will surely at the end be received by the Buddha and reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there to enjoy immeasurable bliss. At first hearing, Yong could not believe or understand it, thinking that Buddha-recitation was the doing of foolish men and women, and that the Land of Ultimate Bliss was no more than an expedient teaching of the Buddha. Later, after Layman Cui had gently and patiently opened his understanding, he questioned him again, saying: Do you know whether the Saha world truly exists? This Saha world is in fact amassed by the deluded karmic power of living beings. Since the deluded karmic power of living beings can conjure a world out of nothing, then Amitabha Buddha, perfect in immeasurable merit, amassing a Land of Ultimate Bliss by the power of his great compassionate vow, should be all the more certainly believed without doubt. Hearing this, Yong’s faith and understanding opened at once. Layman Cui also gave him the Ten Essentials of the Pure Land to read and recite. From then on he studied with ardor, utterly unlike his former self, keeping the ten fast days each month and reciting the Buddha’s name single-mindedly morning and evening, vowing to be born in the West.

Who would have thought that at the beginning of the eleventh month of that winter he suddenly fell ill and could not rise; medicine and physicians were of no avail, so he summoned no more doctors and simply recited the Buddha’s name with one mind. He said to his wife: Now I recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly, and I have no pain; moreover, I have a good place to go. Hearing this, his wife wept without ceasing. Yong said: “I am not dying now — I am only moving to another place. It is as if this house were already ruined and one moved elsewhere to live; why grieve? Your weeping now makes my worldly feelings grow; if through this I were to fall, how could your heart bear it?” He added: I once heard people speak of the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation and could never bring myself to believe it. This autumn, in

, in the seventh month, thanks to Layman Cui’s guidance, he brought me to believe, accept, and practice it; I am endlessly grateful to him. Then, early the next morning, he urgently instructed his family: On my behalf, go to Old Master Xinyan of Gongdelin and seek refuge. When the refuge certificate arrived, he held it and read it through once, showing great joy. He then asked his family to support him to sit facing west, and told them all to assist in recitation together. Before long he said joyfully: A lotus flower has already appeared before me — I shall certainly be born in the West. His wife said to him: You have only resolved on this for a few months — how have you reached such a state? Yong said: This is not something you women can know. In practice, sincerity and unremitting effort are what matter; why speak of whether the time was long or short? It is well that you have kept a vegetarian diet for many years; (pointing at his wife) if you can recite the Buddha’s name with one mind, in the future you will surely meet me in the West. I may be able to come and deliver you — that too is not impossible. Having spoken, he still sat upright, palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name, until at midday he passed away. More than ten hours later, when his body was encoffined, his face was as in life, his four limbs soft, and the crown of his head still warm.
Fo Long
(Original title: The Parents of Layman Chen Xiangquan Pass Away at Ease on the Same Day)

My mother, of the Wan family, taboo name Weiyi, style name Shigu, was originally from Tianmen in Hubei, and moved to Bingkeng, a place eight li from Huangpen Town across the river from Anqing. In youth she received her family’s teaching, was well versed in the rites, and was gifted with intelligence; she was the third and youngest daughter, the most beloved of my maternal grandfather. My grandfather loved the Buddha all his life, and so my mother, taught by him, believed in the Buddha from childhood.

At eighteen my mother married my father, and bore five sons and four daughters; in rearing her children she spared herself no toil, and in keeping herself and managing the household she was upright, frugal, and sparing.

My late father, of the Fu family, style name Zhigong, taboo name Shaolan, was the eldest son of my grandfather Weibin. His original home was Sanqiao Town in the western countryside of Anqing; because my grandfather carried on business in Shanghai, the family lodged there for nearly a hundred years. As there were many children, the burden of livelihood was not easy, and added to this were frequent moves and a life of drifting uncertainty; so the children could not be sent to school, and all the books my brothers and sisters read were what we gained at home under my mother’s goading and instruction.

My mother was most devout in serving the Buddha. Though life was unsettled, the dwelling narrow and unclean, and the household chores heavy and toilsome, yet morning and evening she reverently bowed and burned incense before the holy image of Guanyin and silently recited the name of Bodhisattva Guanyin, and never once did she let a day pass without doing so.

When the Shanghai War broke out on August 13, my father happened to be in Hong Kong and had not returned (at that time our family lived at Laoximen in the southern city of Shanghai). Amid the panic of gunfire all day and unending rifle shots, when all the neighbors had fled and left the place empty, my mother could still sit calmly cross-legged, reciting the holy names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, fearing nothing. So firm was her resolve in the Way.
, in 1940 my mother redoubled her diligence, striving bitterly in the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation. Every day she rose at dawn, lit the oil lamps

, and in reverent attire went before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to bow and make offerings, to plead and repent, closing her eyes and joining her palms, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Amitabha Sutra, the Universal Gateway Chapter, the Ksitigarbha Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the White-Robed Divine Mantra, the Cundi Mantra, and others, practicing as taught. From 40 until 43
when she passed away, throughout these four years her heart of utmost sincerity, her profound heart, and her heart of dedication and vow
surpassed even what they had been before. In her spirit of vigor and valor, even in bitter winter or sweltering heat she would never consent to slacken for a moment.

Though my mother never fully received the precepts in her life, on the second, sixth, and ninth months and on the new and full moon days and the birthdays of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas she kept the fast. Whenever she saw a neighbor kill a chicken or a duck, she would join her palms toward it and recite the Buddha’s name, or recite the Rebirth Mantra, praying for its deliverance. Even at the sight of an insect or a mosquito in danger, she would always find some way to save it.
41, when the cost of living in Shanghai soared and it grew hard to make a living there, she accompanied my parents back to the old home, lodging at Bailin Yangya House in Yanshan Township, Anqing.

My late father had originally no faith in Buddhism. Seeing my mother recite the Buddha’s name and bow to the Buddha, he neither slandered nor hindered her. My mother then urged him to recite the Buddha’s name exclusively — with such sincerity, letting the sound continue unbroken, so that no thought should pass in vain; it is simple and easy to practice. From then on, whenever my mother recited, my father would recite aloud along with her. And so my parents would often sit facing each other, talking and laughing: “When I go to the West, I shall surely take you with me.”

, in mid-August (that is, half a month before her death), my father suddenly said: “I dreamed of a golden man with a red face standing before me.” My mother also said: “In the night I dreamed that three monks came into our house, shaved my head and gave me the precepts for me, and then told me to set out.” With that my mother woke with a start. Three days later my father fell ill, and my mother too felt slightly unwell. So she said to Peiqing with a smile: “Tomorrow I shall take your father out, one before the other, to look at the mountain scenery.” She also said: “After I am gone, do not weep, I beg you. If you weep, you will make me feel heavy and miserable all over. If you recite the Buddha’s name, I shall feel light in body, peaceful and free of trouble.” At the same time she took out all the deeds, contracts, notes, and account books for the farmland and handed them over to Peiqing, instructing him: “You must not lose these. When your brothers come home, hand them over to them.”

On the day of her death, my father said: “My illness is already better. Daughter, you may add more oil to the lamp in my room; wait a little, then come and see me again — tomorrow I shall be able to go out.” After a short while my father had already departed this life. My elder sister felt her heart cut as with a knife, so grieved she wished not to live; yet still she dared not wail aloud. My mother, in another room, suddenly said with a laugh: “How is your father?” She answered: “Father is already better.” She asked again: “Which direction is the West?” Then she said: “There are too many people in the room, too much noise and confusion.” And again: “Daughter! If not now, when will you recite the Buddha’s name to aid my return to the West? Do not grieve; recite the Buddha’s name quickly, and when I have gone far you may mourn as much as you like.” Having spoken, she closed her eyes and sat cross-legged. My elder sister assisted in recitation at her side, and my mother, smiling, passed away seated at ease. At that time my father’s body was not yet cold, and my compassionate mother had gone with him to the West.

My father lived fifty-seven years and my mother fifty-eight. It is a pity that our home village was then in a region surrounded and watched by the enemy and the puppet forces, where human affairs were tangled and conditions harsh; none of us brothers could hurry back to see them off to rebirth in the West in person. This is a lifelong regret.
Chen Xiangquan

blocks.text: 33. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Shen Zhifen Bids Farewell by Letter, to Meet Again in the Land of Lotuses)

Layman Shen, taboo name Youlie, style name Bowei; Zhifen was his Dharma name. He was by nature generous and kind, never tiring of doing good. Fond of the Buddhadharma, he kept the Diamond Sutra for more than twenty years. Then, six years ago, he met in Shanghai the venerable Chen Wuwo and Layman Chen Hailiang, who gave him Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings to read; only then did he know that the Dharma gate of the Pure Land can transcend the three realms crosswise and bring accomplishment in this very life. He resolutely gave rise to faith, asked Layman Hailiang to seek the three refuges from Master Desen, and, lodging in Shanghai, firmly resolved in faith and earnestly cultivated the Pure Land practice. He bowed and recited, diligent without slackening, and kept a lifelong vegetarian diet. When guests came, his talk was of nothing but the propagation of the Pure Land, or the responsive traces of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he touched on no other matters. Because of this, very many people gave rise to faith and took up the practice of Buddha-recitation. The layman practiced himself and transformed others; his heart for spreading the Way was urgent. He once said that if the times should become peaceful, he would invite fellow practitioners to found a Lotus Society on Mount Lu, as a means of leadership. How earnest was the layman’s vow-power! When the War of Resistance was won and communications between Shanghai and Hankou were restored, the layman’s worthy son (that is, the layman’s son; “worthy son” is an honorific for another’s son), Layman Huiqing, brought him to Hankou to care for him. The whole way, devastation met his eyes on every side, and he was deeply moved to sorrow; he vowed to be born early in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and then to return quickly to the Saha world to save living beings far and wide. After arriving in Hankou he bowed and recited all the more earnestly in his lodging. Every Sunday he would go to the Wuhan branch of the Permanent Memorial Society of Master Yinguang, where, under the guidance of Master Yuanche, he cultivated together with fellow Lotus friends.
This year (

1946) in the third month, a slight illness lingered, his food and drink gradually diminished, and his emaciation increased day by day; yet he still did not relax his Buddha-recitation in the slightest. Once in a while he would rise and sit a little, and when he could not hold up he would lie down again. In the sixth lunar month, because his room was narrow and painfully hot, a sedan chair was prepared and he moved to the Qingji Pure Temple. There the buildings were spacious and his body and mind were somewhat eased. Moreover he constantly heard the sound of the Buddha’s name, which sustained his right mindfulness. For this temple was a place in Hankou devoted exclusively to the cultivation of the Pure Land. After he had stayed in the temple a long while, his illness showed no worsening, but his food and drink grew ever less. Yet he could still rise and sit for a short while. From
July

onward he suddenly stopped eating and drinking, and only occasionally sipped a little warm boiled water.
