In the winter of the renwu year, on the fifteenth day of the tenth month, she passed away seated.

For twenty days before the old lady passed away she ate nothing at all, drinking only boiled water. Again and again she told her son and daughter-in-law to wash the clothes, shoes and socks she ordinarily wore, saying: “On the fifteenth I am going to the West.” Her son and daughter-in-law thought it nonsense and made no answer. On the fourteenth her daughter came to visit her, and she urged her again and again: “I cannot stay long; tomorrow I am certainly going. Quickly wash my clothes and shoes for me.” Her daughter did as she said. On the morning of the fifteenth she rose, bathed and changed her clothes. Toward evening she said of herself that the Buddha had come; at that moment a rare fragrance filled the room, and she passed away sitting cross-legged in a bamboo chair. Though her breath had ceased, her body did not fall over; the family set a door plank on wooden stools and placed the bamboo chair upon it, and there she sat cross-legged for two days and nights before her remains were placed in an earthen jar and buried. On the twenty-second of that month, at the Buddha-recitation assembly at Longhua Nunnery on Mount Daluosi, I heard the laywoman Zhang Shenglian say that this was the account given by the layman Xu Lianyin of Yunfeng Villa. The next day I went to Yunfeng Villa on Mount Wu to ask him, and it was indeed so. I have set down the essentials in order to tell all who recite the Buddha’s name. Through the ages, all the good teachers who have spread the Pure Land teaching have said: in the Pure Land Dharma gate, those of the highest wisdom and those of the dullest understanding gain the greatest benefit. Those of highest wisdom penetrate deeply to the source of the Dharma and so know how surpassing and supreme this gate is — men such as Zhiyi, Yongming and others, who could therefore be greatly wise as if foolish. Relying on Samantabhadra’s Ten Great Vows of the King of Vows, they diligently cultivated the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, leading each one back to the Land of Bliss. Those of the next grade, whose wisdom cannot penetrate the inner chamber, often think themselves clever and are half doubting, half believing

like Cao Luchuan, and the general run of recent men who love to vaunt themselves and delight in talking mouth Zen. They are in fact inferior to the lowliest foolish men and women, whose thoughts are simple, who once believing believe forever, and who yearn with a true heart. Reciting the Buddha’s name in their ignorance, they secretly commune with the Buddha’s wisdom and unknowingly accord with the wonder of the Way, gaining boundless benefit and tasting it for themselves. Now I bring forward the affair of old Mrs. Deng as proof, and my faith is the more confirmed and evidenced, in the winter of the renwu year (
), on the twenty-sixth day of the tenth month.
Recorded by Jie Ting

blocks.text: 15. Passing Away with a Joyful Smile

inline.s: (Original title: Laywoman Zhang Huichao, Filial, Kind, Diligent and Thrifty, Passes Away with a Joyful Smile)

Zhang Huichao of the Song family was the wife of Layman Song Huihe of Duojiazhuang in Yaoshan, Hebei. Her maiden name was Lan, and she was by nature diligent and thrifty. Because her husband’s relatives had for the most part taken refuge with the venerable Master Yin and honored the Buddha and practiced Pure Land, she too gradually came to faith. From the winter of

she began in earnest to recite the Buddha’s name. But with many children and grandchildren and a household none too well off, she toiled without rest. Add to that the turmoil of the times, which increased her anxiety and fear, and so exhaustion brought on illness and her heart-qi was gravely depleted. In the present year (that is,

), on the twentieth day of the first month, Huihe saw that her illness was growing worse, and invited Huiyang to instruct her and assist her recitation. He told her to put down all ten thousand entanglements and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind, and gave her blessed Great Compassion dharmāraṇī water to drink. Thereupon her illness eased, her body grew calm, and she devoted herself wholly to reciting the Buddha’s name.

On the second day of the second month she knew she would not rise again, and said: “My body is already free of illness; only my life cannot be prolonged. I charge you, my children, not to weep, but to recite the Buddha’s name together.” On the third, Huiyang, being a connection by marriage, again came at her summons, and saw that her breathing was somewhat labored and hard to bear. So he consoled her, saying: “All your life you have been filial, kind, diligent and thrifty, honoring the moral order and fulfilling your duties — you may be called a perfect woman within the women’s quarters. Of the three blessings of pure karma set forth in the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, you already possess many. For such a person, to recite the Buddha’s name and dedicate the merit toward rebirth in the West accords wholly with the compassionate vows of Amitābha Buddha. Now we all assist your recitation; you must cast off body and mind entirely and single-mindedly recite along as you listen. If your remaining lifespan is not yet exhausted, you will surely recover quickly; if your allotted span is at its end, you will certainly be received and guided by the Buddha and reborn in the West. To leave this Sahā world and be born in Ultimate Bliss is a matter for the greatest rejoicing. When the Buddha comes to receive you, your brother will surely attend the Buddha and come with him (her brother Zhang Huibing was the first person in the district to be reborn in the West).” Hearing this, Mrs. Zhang at once showed a joyful smile, and her mind and spirits grew clearer still. After supper he again told her proofs of rebirth, to direct her aspiration, and led all the family members in assisting the recitation by turns. An image of the Buddha Who Receives and Guides was hung high before her bed for her to gaze upon. She said, “Excellent, excellent! Let everyone recite the Buddha’s name together — the sound is very fine.” Again she charged her family not to weep; then, holding a cup and drinking, she set it down unhurriedly, laid her two hands together, and leaning over the table passed away. There was no phlegm, no labored breathing; her bearing was utterly peaceful. Of the twenty-four people in the house, not one wept; they all recited the Buddha’s name aloud in unison, Huihe most earnestly of all, and stopped only after about three sticks of incense had burned. Five hours later they wiped her body and changed her clothes: her hands and feet were soft, her face wore a joyful expression lovelier than in life, and hot vapor rose from the crown of her head, as everyone could see. Late into the night, four inches above her crown, the heat still scorched the hand. When the coffin was moved on the fifth, they lifted the lid and looked again: her face was ruddy, far better than in life, and her finger joints could still be flexed and stretched at will. Because of these auspicious responses, her close and distant kin, and many villagers who had never believed in the Buddha, were greatly moved and clicked their tongues in wonder. They all declared that the Buddhadharma is subtle and inconceivable, and that everyone ought to abandon the crooked and return to the upright, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. Moreover, her youngest son’s wife (that is, Huiyang’s own small daughter), at the time of her mother-in-law’s death, looked up and saw above the image of the Buddha Who Receives and Guides a golden halo the size of a teacup. All the above Huiyang personally heard and saw, without the least embellishment. Auspicious signs such as these are ample proof of rebirth in the West beyond doubt. That a foolish village woman such as this, having but lately conceived faith and aspiration, should at once gain such benefit — first, because the Lord of the West, the greatly compassionate Father, made his forty-eight vows and this Dharma gate is surpassing and supreme. The Contemplation Sutra says: for one who has committed the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, when the marks of hell appear at the end, if he meets a good teacher who teaches him to recite the Buddha’s name, then whether he recites ten times or only once, he instantly wipes out the karma of hell and is lodged in the lotus pond. Mrs. Zhang was not a committer of the five heinous crimes or the ten evils, yet her faith had but newly sprung up; judging the greater by the lesser, this too proves that the words of the sutra are not false. The ancients said, “Ten thousand practice, ten thousand go” — this belongs to the Pure Land gate alone, which relies on the Buddha’s power, and is by no means to be compared with other common teachings that rely solely on self-power. Second, because her close and distant kin all assisted the recitation properly, with no interference or obstruction of any kind, she had such a smooth passage. My teacher, the venerable Master Yin, often said: if you would have no obstacles at the end, you must in ordinary times explain to your family the harm of interference and the benefit of assisted recitation, and must see that your kin are all able to assist — only then can rebirth in the West be assured. Assisted recitation is a matter of the utmost importance. Layman Huihe, though his household was not well off, was able to create such a Buddhist family and bring his wife the real benefit of deliverance in this very life. It is my deep hope that Buddhists throughout the world, rich or poor, noble or humble, may hear of this and follow the example, yielding to none in doing good.
(Original title: Zhao Xiude and His Mother — a Mother’s Kindness and a Son’s Filial Piety, Both Born in Ultimate Bliss)

Layman Xiude was a son of the Zhao family of Xingtai city in Hebei. He served his mother with the utmost filial piety, treated others with sincerity, and was honest and gentle by nature. He had taken refuge in the Three Jewels and strictly observed the five precepts. In midwinter of

his mother, the Lady Li, fell gravely ill; the whole family recited the Buddha’s name, and auspicious signs appeared again and again. At the end she earnestly charged the layman: “Recite the Buddha’s name well, and for three years let the sound of the Buddha’s name not cease.” Having given her charge, she lay down in the auspicious posture and passed away in peace. Three hours later not only was her body soft and the crown of her head warm, but her whole face was ruddy with light. By these auspicious signs her rebirth in the West is surely proven.

After his mother’s death the layman conducted everything according to propriety. Moreover he carefully kept his mother’s command: for three years, walking, standing, sitting or lying, the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceased. Every day he rose at cockcrow and went to the foot of the Yuanzhao Pagoda to walk around it to the right while reciting the Buddha’s name. When he walked the roads, if tiles or stones happened to lie in the way he would kick them clear, lest they hinder others’ steps. On fast days he would go to the Kaiyuan Monastery, to the hall of Śākyamuni Buddha, to strike the chime, light the lamps and tend the incense. Whoever he met, he urged to recite the Buddha’s name. He once exhorted someone: “Recite the Buddha’s name, recite the Buddha’s name — the Land of Ultimate Bliss is our home.” He held the Buddha’s name with the utmost single-mindedness and diligence. He kept his mother’s command with perfect sincerity and care. By

, in the eleventh month, he said repeatedly that his mother’s charge was fulfilled and that he would soon return home. But because former karma could not be evaded, he had to suffer pain. Presently a slight illness appeared, and when it came on his chest and back ached, exactly as he had said. One day, forcing himself despite his illness, he went to the Kaiyuan Monastery to worship the Buddha and to the Guanyin Hall to make his bows. Returning home, he closed his eyes and his mouth, and neither looked nor spoke again. He only sat upright in a chair with a smile, his left hand moving as if telling beads and reciting the Buddha’s name, and peacefully passed away. Four hours after his passing the crown of his head was still warm, his four limbs were soft, and a rare fragrance lingered for days. It was

, the first day of the twelfth month; he was fifty-six. Mother and son recited the Buddha’s name and were reborn in the West one after the other — truly, of the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation it may be said, “Ten thousand practice, ten thousand go.”
Recorded by Jin Guo
(Original title: Ms. Zhong Zhongqin Believes in the Buddha and Through Assisted Recitation Gains Rebirth)

Ms. Zhong Qin, whose courtesy name was Zhongqin, was generous and upright, content with coarse fare and able to endure hardship. My late parents recognized her worth, and because I had passed thirty without an heir, they followed the Confucian rites and gave her to me as wife, entrusting the household affairs to her. From then on she drew water and pounded rice and raised the children, diligent and earnest, thirty years as one day; her constitution was always weak, so that work never left her hands nor illness her body. Though she loved the Buddha and delighted in hearing sutras, she often regretted having no leisure to hear more.

In the spring of the bingzi year she once fell gravely ill; medicine and physicians were of no avail, and when the family called her she did not answer, for her ears heard nothing, her eyes saw nothing, and her breath was entirely gone. I asked others to recite the Buddha’s name for her, and in the middle of the night she suddenly revived in peace, saying that she could hear nothing else, only the sound of Buddha-recitation, clear and distinct, entering her ears phrase by phrase and delighting her heart. She added that a moment before, four men in black robes had come and shone a lamp on her face; they looked once and went away, and she had been greatly frightened — had we seen them? The others told her they had not. Before long a sound of weeping came from the house next door: the old woman who lived there had died. The lady thus came back to life, and it is now eight years since. In these eight years her faith in the Buddha has grown ever firmer and her worship of the Buddha ever more diligent; her room is kept in solemn order, reverent and clean.

Lately her illness came on again, and she knew she would not recover. Forcing herself despite her illness, she bathed, made obeisance before the Buddha, and led the children in sacrificing to the ancestors. Hearing that a certain Dharma master was at the Yaoshi Nunnery lecturing on the Essentials of the Amitābha Sutra, she wished to go and listen, saying that though her body was ill, the sutra must not go unheard. Her family, seeing that her strength could not sustain it, gently persuaded her and she gave it up. Afterwards she gradually sank toward the end, yet her mind and spirits remained very clear. She only felt that day and night her idle thoughts were stirred by the sound of the wind and of insects on every wall. So I divided day and night, and always spent some hours before her, assisting her recitation. While reciting, the lady’s body and mind were at peace, and sometimes she would rise into the cross-legged posture or form the Amitābha mudrā, praising and thanking me. But as soon as I left, she would again prattle of household matters, gazing around at the family, her heart too grieved to let go, and so she could not avoid distraction and torpor. This is ample proof that when anyone is at the point of death, assisting their recitation certainly brings them no small benefit. For as long as right mindfulness is held, for so long are a hundred delusions dispelled — of this one may be certain. Yet if one would hold that right mindfulness firm, it is not easy without the strength of long familiarity with recitation. For thirty years my plain and bitter life has been sustained wholly by this lady’s care. In this illness of my eyes her nursing was especially untiring in every detail. The reason I recited devoutly for her these days and nights is that I thought to repay her, to bear witness for her, and thereby to bring the matter to its close. It went on until half past eight in the evening of the eighteenth day of the ninth month, when her hands and feet turned cold and her breath ceased. Three hours later the warmth at her crown dispersed and her consciousness departed. Then we bathed and changed her, to finish with this illusory body of hers in this world. The lady bore a son, Xinran, and a daughter, Pingping; her daughter-in-law was Jin Cen and her grandson Tianbu; all took refuge in the Three Jewels and devoted themselves to the Dharma gate of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Recorded by Zhang Yiliu

blocks.text: 18. Knowing the Time of Rebirth in the West

inline.s: (Original title: Laywoman Zhang Huadao, Diligent and Thrifty, a Protector of the Dharma, Knowing Her Time, Passes Away and Is Born in the West)

Old Mrs. Zhang was a farmer’s daughter of Chixi township in Jiaxing, and the mother of the Abbot Kaizhi of Qizhen Monastery. She was kind and benevolent by nature, fond of work, sparing in her own living, and to the end of her life she joined diligence and hardship with delight in giving. In her early years she heard the sound of Buddhist chanting, loved it, and at once took up a vegetarian diet and served the Buddha. Her second son, the Venerable Kai, was steeped in his mother’s teaching from boyhood, and his innate wisdom increased, so that he often showed a wish to leave the world; his mother accordingly had him shaved and dyed as a monk at Qizhen Monastery in their township. At that time the aged Master Lianren was abbot, restoring the monastery and reviving every neglected undertaking, so that the Buddha’s way flourished greatly. The Venerable Kai was the youngest of all, ranking among the aged Lian’s grand-disciples, and yet he alone won his deep appreciation. The old lady too took refuge with the aged Lian, receiving the Dharma name Huadao. After her husband’s death, wearying of the dust and noise of family life, she went to live at the Guangsheng Chan Cloister at Ruifeng Bridge in her township, where she tilled three mu of her own land with her own hands and gave all the produce to the community, living by bitter effort and refined practice. The cloister had fallen into ruin over the years, and the old lady would knock her wooden fish in the middle of the night to collect funds and gather workmen. Near and far, moved by her sincerity, vied in lending their support. She built a Guanyin Hall of three bays, repaired the remaining buildings and paved the riverbank, spending more than three thousand pieces of silver in all; when it was not enough, she emptied all her own scanty savings to make it up. That the monastery stands renewed and gleaming is the old lady’s doing.

the aged Lian passed away. Two years later the Venerable Kai succeeded him as abbot. At that time a hundred affairs at the monastery awaited attention, and the abbot was young, so that disorder was always feared. The old lady then moved into the monastery and daily oversaw a hundred and eight tasks. She was ever watchful to keep the pure rules in order, to carry on and exalt the Dharma teaching, to correct and reform declining ways, and to establish firmly the norms of the monastery. That the Venerable Kai carried on the aged Lian and traced his line back to Yun Gu was the old lady’s teaching. Once in the monastery, she made it her own duty to work the fields and gardens herself, toiling the year round and never borrowing the strength of hired laborers. The vegetables of the monastery kitchen all came from her and were never bought outside. She used to say: “My merit is thin; if I eat without working hard, calamity will surely come upon me.” When in old age she could no longer bend to plant, she would kneel to water and tend the crops, and though exhausted she never rested — and only death ended it.

In the late spring of this year, when I paid my respects at Qizhen Monastery, the old lady was already ill in bed. I was given my fill of the vegetables she had grown, plump and tender, sweet and fragrant beyond ordinary vegetables. The old lady was thrifty yet loved to give: all her life she wore worn-out clothes and straw sandals, ragged as a beggar. Whatever garment was at all whole she would give away to the poor. The Venerable Kai had prepared burial clothes for her and locked them in a chest, but when later he looked, one piece was missing — she had given that away too. She especially pitied and respected poor monks, and often charged the Venerable Kai to treat them well. When their patched robes were torn she mended them with her own hands, and sometimes made new clothes for them. When spring came warm they would ask to buy them from her; when winter turned cold she would give them away again. Whenever she saw good men and women eating vegetarian food and reciting the Buddha’s name she was filled with joy and reverence. She loved to establish Buddhist assemblies, and in the nearby villages of Guangsheng Nunnery, Songzi Nunnery and other places she was always the one to advocate and invite. Now at Qizhen Monastery, laymen Qian Binchu, Zhang Yifeng, Wang Fujun and others have taken the lead in forming a Lotus Society and gathering a life-releasing assembly, reading, reciting, expounding and teaching, practicing themselves and transforming others, so that those who come at the news gather like clouds and follow one upon another, and Buddhist influence blazes forth in great prosperity. Of late it has spread to Tianrenzhuang and other towns as well — again the merit of the old lady’s broad ferry of compassion.
In the guiwei year of this year (

), on the thirtieth day of the third month, she showed illness and could not rise. She refused medicine and would not take it, and yet had no suffering of illness. Her mind and spirits were clear, and she spoke to the Venerable Kai of matters after her death: a plain burial, no accepting of condolences or offerings, no reckless spending of the community’s goods, and cremation the next day. She only earnestly charged and exhorted him to spread the Buddhadharma and cultivate all merits. At daybreak on the twenty-third she said: “Tomorrow I shall be born in the West; I charge you to recite the Buddha’s name and see me off.” The Venerable Kai at once invited fellow practitioners of the lotus to assist the recitation without a break. In the small hours of the next day she passed peacefully to the West. She was seventy-eight. The old lady had labored in the fields all her life, her hands horny with mud and grime. Yet at her death her countenance was pure and clean, radiant and gentle. She was cremated on the eighth day of the fourth month, and three days later, when the ashes were examined, the bones were pure white, streaked here and there with the five colors. Those who came from far and near to look all exclaimed in wonder without cease.
Recorded by Zheng Yinda
(Original title: Laywoman Pan Mingzhi — Rare Fragrance Filling the Room, Two Jade Chopsticks Hanging Down)

The laywoman, whose Dharma name was Mingzhi, was a granddaughter of Chen Xinquan, the circuit intendant of Jinhua. In childhood she was versed in poetry and letters, and in maturity she studied the Buddhadharma; from youth she would not eat the five pungent plants. At nineteen she married Shenzhuang, the third son of the Hanlin scholar Pan Yaoru of Changle. In the dingyou year, when the Hanlin scholar went out as prefect of Kui, Shenzhuang attended him and Mingzhi went with them. They had been at Kui only a few months when she was struck by grave illness (she contracted a serious disease); the physicians were all at a loss, and clothes, coverlets and a coffin were even made ready for her. Suddenly she dreamed of Bodhisattva Guanyin, who gave her a cup of pure water, whereupon her illness turned for the better and she was soon pronounced cured. From this her faith in the Buddha grew firmer still. In the gengzi year Shenzhuang sat for the provincial examination and brought her home with him, and once home she recited the Buddha’s name tirelessly. In the jiayin year Shenzhuang died, and their adopted son Fu was still in swaddling clothes; for the sake of the greater right she endured her grief and forced herself to raise him. Their daughter Mingwen had married Chen Guoguang, full nephew of the Duke of Letters Chen Wenzhong, who also loved the Buddha but was without emolument. In the dingmao year Guoguang too departed this life, and the mother and daughter, alone and desolate, were struck by the scene before them and awoke to the truth of birth, aging, illness and death — that such is the way of the world for the most part. So they took a wife for the adopted son, handed over all household affairs to them, and mother and daughter together entered the Buddhist Women’s Society, resolving for good to plan for what lies beyond the world. Her son and daughter-in-law, who knew the way of filial piety and had the manners of a great house, went to the Society and earnestly begged her to come home so that they might support her. Some years later she contracted an intestinal illness and was brought near to death. Again she dreamed of a wondrous person who gave her cinnabar, just as at Kui she had dreamed of Bodhisattva Guanyin giving her water, and again she recovered without medicine. This is ample proof that she had karmic ties with the Buddha and deep good roots; and her present practice was utterly sincere and earnest. Though her body was in the home, her mind had no worldly entanglements; she kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, decades as one day.

This summer her waist ached from time to time, and with autumn her stomach and intestines hurt sharply at night, yet she never let the prayer beads out of her hand. When the illness came on, her daughter would bow to the Buddha and pray in anguish, and by dawn it would gradually ease; this went on for two months, and she never took medicine. To those who urged her, she would say: “My former karma is heavy; I may as well finish out this karmic body — what good is medicine? The two great monks Jiexian and Xuanzang, who had climbed to the holy heights, could not escape suffering at the end; how much less we ordinary beings.” On the thirtieth day of the eighth month she returned again to the Buddhist Women’s Society, and with the members assisting her recitation morning and evening, her pain now eased and now grew worse. At the last she vomited worms for several days and could take no food or drink. In the tenth month I returned to Shanghai from Yan and only then learned of her condition, and knew that she must be born in the West. So I wrote a couplet in her memory: “Plum blossoms on the ridge — an offering to the Buddha for your return to the West. Incense and fire between sea and sky — alas, I shall long owe the karmic debt of expounding the sutras.” In the first ten days of the eleventh month the mail finally reached her, and she could still read the lines I had written. She said to the members of the Society: “If I cannot be born in the West, how shall I answer my teacher’s hopes?” and she had her family write a letter thanking me. She also composed a couplet for herself: “Ten thousand thoughts turned to ash, I return to the Buddha’s land. Not one speck of dust, I go to the West.” She had her son write it out, and charged him to go home and fetch the certificate she had received when she took refuge with me, and place it in the shrine. On the eighth her spirits were still sound, and she held fast to the Buddha’s name. At the fifth watch of the night she told her daughter Mingwen to bathe and change her; after a short rest, at dawn, she wished to sit up, and though the others urged her not to, she insisted and they helped her up. Hardly had she settled on the seat when a rare fragrance filled the room; two jade chopsticks hung down from her nostrils, the crown of her head stood out, and her two eyes drooped their lids as she passed away seated cross-legged. It was

, the ninth day of the eleventh month; she was seventy-four. A day and night later she was placed in the shrine casket, her hands and feet soft and the crown of her head still warm — all proofs of rebirth in the West. The casket rested at the Buddhist Women’s Society, and on the twenty-first she was cremated at Chongfu Monastery on the northern ridge and that same day placed in the stupa. From the ashes beneath the casket grew grass with green leaves and purple stems. Among the remaining ashes were found many relics. Her family wrote to ask me, and I cited the sutras: for one who has recited the Buddha’s name all his life, at the approach of death, if right mindfulness is truly manifest, the body free of pain, the face wearing a smile, a rare fragrance filling the room, heavenly music resounding in the sky, warmth appearing at the crown, the hands and feet soft — all these are signs of rebirth in the West. Mingzhi had them all; her rebirth is beyond doubt. As for grass with green leaves and purple stems growing from the ashes, though no record can be cited for it, it is likewise an omen. Long ago there was a mynah bird that learned to speak and called on Amitābha; when it died and was buried in the ground, a lotus grew from the earth. If even a bird that recited the Buddha’s name was so, how much more a human being? I therefore record it to spread the word abroad.
Recorded by Yuan Ying
(Original title: Layman Yu Yuanming Passes Away Sitting Upright Amid the Sound of Buddha-Recitation)

The laywoman of the Yu family, whose personal name was Zaizhang and whose Dharma name was Yuanming, was a native of Yi County in Anhui. Of pure and good nature and a firm believer in the Buddhadharma, she was the second wife of Mr. Shu Zhufen of Pingshan in the same county. Three years after her marriage her husband died of illness; the laywoman mourned beyond the common measure and vowed to keep her chastity. From then on she recited the Buddha’s name ever more devoutly, and went on to keep a lifelong vegetarian diet. In

she received the five expedient precepts and the bodhisattva precepts. She often urged the faithful in the village to recite the Buddha’s name with one mind and seek rebirth in the West, and so many were moved by her that the village came to organize a Buddha-recitation society. In recent years the laywoman suffered from a wind ailment in her feet and could not walk well, so every day she lay in her room reciting the Buddha’s name, as diligent as ever. Everything was attended to by her husband’s younger brother’s wife, Zihui, who also believed in the Buddhadharma and had lived and eaten with the laywoman for more than twenty years, as close as sisters. The laywoman’s kindness toward others may be seen in this.

, after the middle of the twelfth month, the laywoman’s illness grew grave and she took to her bed. On the twenty-first, sunk in a stupor, she suddenly felt herself walking in open country, with green hills and blue waters delighting her eyes. Far off she saw a boy come to welcome her; arriving at a temple, a monk came out and sprinkled pure water over her whole body, and she felt instantly cool throughout. The monk then told the boy to escort her to the West, and she saw with her own eyes the majestic Three Holy Ones; Bodhisattva Guanyin, holding a lotus flower in her hand, gave it to the laywoman, told her to sit within the flower and recite the Buddha’s name, and personally gave her the prediction, granting her the lowest grade of the highest birth. When the laywoman woke, she told the whole matter to Zihui, Daqing, Guizi and Ruchang, four fellow practitioners. Hearing it, they sighed deeply and their zeal for practice welled up of itself. The laywoman’s heart was open and clear, and she did not feel that she was ill. At half past nine on the night of the twenty-third, amid the sound of the great assembly’s assisted recitation, she passed away sitting upright, her face wearing a smile. She was forty-nine. When the neighbors heard, they all came to look, and exclaimed that such a thing had never been. This shows that reciting the Buddha’s name truly has inconceivable merit; I therefore briefly record its beginning and end.
Recorded by Lu Zhirui
(Original title: The Maiden Ma Yanan Passes Away in Peace Amid Assisted Recitation)

The maiden Ma Yanan, whose Dharma name was Chaocui, was the daughter of the physician Ma Guanqun. From childhood she was quick-witted, lively and clever. She first entered the lower primary school and then a private school, and was quite diligent. Earlier, after Layman Guanqun had recovered from a grave illness, he aroused the resolve to study the Buddha’s teaching. That Chemahu came to have a Pure Land practice center was due first to Mr. Ma’s initiative. He had taken refuge with the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, the Venerable Master Yin Guang, and was granted the Dharma name Zhiyi. Seeing her father recite the Buddha’s name every day, Yanan also came to know the Buddhadharma; without being taught she could recite the Amitābha Sutra and the Great Compassion and White Robe dharmāraṇīs, and she sang well the six-line praise of the Willow Branch and Pure Water. From childhood, moreover, she revered Bodhisattva Guanyin and loved to recite the Bodhisattva’s holy name. Her father, seeing that her wisdom roots were planted from former lives, also asked the Venerable Master Yin to take her in, and she received the Dharma name Chaocui.
Layman Guanqun fell gravely ill
and called again and again for Yanan, but she did not answer

when he lit a candle and looked, he found her kneeling below the seat of Guanyin in the family shrine hall, holding the Bodhisattva’s holy name and praying for her father. The next year her mother’s illness grew more critical still, and Yanan tended her broth and medicine, weeping morning and night, washing her face with tears. She also vowed before the Buddha to keep a lifelong vegetarian diet, and even begged to borrow ten years of her own life to save her mother. That a girl of fifteen should have such filial devotion is rarely seen among people.
Little did anyone expect that in

she would catch a severe cold compounded by stagnation of qi and contract typhoid pneumonia. The whole family was alarmed and knew not what to do. Layman Guanqun nursed her with all his heart, reciting the Buddha’s name and the Great Compassion dharmāraṇī on her behalf. Though she gradually turned from danger to safety, her constitution was from then on depleted, already showing signs of consumption. After that came wind-cold and diarrhea, with scarcely a quiet day. In the beginning of the eighth month she contracted dysentery, passing more than a hundred times in a night, and this went on for nearly forty days, after which she took to her bed and could not rise. Her father knew her illness had become incurable, and invited fellow practitioners to recite the Buddha’s name in supplication. In the end, because her former karma had ripened to its fixed result, her span could not be extended. At dawn on the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month Yanan suddenly said her heart fluttered as if about to stop, and thinking it was hunger she asked for broth and gruel. Layman Guanqun, seeing her expression change, knew that the hour of relinquishing her karmic body had come, and at once invited the members of the group to assist her recitation. Yanan said her breathing was labored and she could not recite. Layman Guanqun urged her to listen attentively to the Buddha’s name. Yanan answered meekly, without the least attachment, and with her ear turned to listen, at times forcing herself to recite along. He also showed her the image of the Three Holy Ones of the West, and Yanan fixed her gaze upon it. Layman Guanqun and the others told her to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and Yanan nodded again and again. Thus for about ten minutes her breath gradually grew faint, and amid the sound of her friends’ recitation she passed away in peace, at the age of seventeen. The assisted recitation continued until the hour of shen that afternoon, stopping when the warmth had left her body. At midnight they bathed her and dressed her: her limbs were soft and her face as in life. All the fellow practitioners of the lotus said that to win such auspicious signs at the end is, by the records of history, indeed a clear proof of rebirth. They marveled at the rarity of it, and their recitation grew the more diligent. Though this maiden had some good roots, had she practiced other Dharma gates relying solely on self-power she could never have gained such great benefit. Master Yongming said: “No Chan, but have Pure Land — ten thousand practice, ten thousand go.” The maiden proves it, and shows fully how surpassing and supreme the Pure Land Dharma gate is, beyond comparison with other gates. I therefore record it especially, that those who insist on self-power alone may know how much the Buddha’s power can be relied upon.
Recorded by the Deathbed Recitation Assistance Group
(Original title: Fang Deren’s Mother, Her Face Covered with Smiles, Palms Joined, Reciting the Buddha’s Name)
My late mother, whose personal name was Dechao, passed away in the year
, in the
ninth
month, on the
twenty-second

day, at the hour of yin. She lived to be eighty-six, forty-nine years after my late father’s death. My mother came to my father at twenty-four and bore him five sons, of whom I am one, and one daughter. When my father passed away, my fifth brother was only two. Her nursing and care, her toil and labor, may well be imagined. All her life she was honest, kind and gentle; she never spoke deceitfully to anyone, and never used harsh words or an angry look toward those beneath her — not even toward her children. I at first knew nothing of the Buddhadharma, but I believed in cause and effect. It happened that a friend, Mr. Zhou Jiguang, gave me the collected writings of my late teacher Master Yin; the discussions of cause and effect in them accorded deeply with the principles I had long held, and so I came to faith. My late wife Deci and I begged Mr. Zhou to write a letter of introduction, and we took refuge with Master Yin at the same time. The Master did not reject us as ordinary and dull, but received us in compassion. So we set up a Buddha hall and recited the Buddha’s name devoutly on the one hand, and on the other respectfully wrote to thank our teacher. Presently his reply came, giving us detailed instruction and charging us to eat vegetables and abstain from meat, to increase our good karma. On the first day of the first month of the twenty-first year [of the Republic], following his instruction, we began a lifelong vegetarian diet. In the ninth month of that year I went with my late wife on pilgrimage to Mount Putuo, and before the Fanyin Cave we saw with our own eyes the full figure of Amitābha Buddha coming to receive and guide, moving to the left and forward. We stood watching for some time, and even as we were leaving it had not vanished — truly, its spiritual response is inconceivable. From Putuo we went on to Shanghai, and thence to Suzhou to pay our respects to our teacher and report all that had happened; he praised us without cease. Later, when I returned to Hubei and reported it to my mother, she was overjoyed to hear it, and she too took refuge with Master Yin.

My late mother had always eaten a partial vegetarian diet, and in her declining years she was never able to cut off meat and fish entirely. But from that time on, every day when no one was in the room, she would sit quietly and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind, whatever the hour. My mother had always been healthy and had never walked with a staff. In the sixth month of last year she had one spell of dizziness, and after recovering, though she could still rise, sit and walk, her spirits gradually declined. On the first day of the ninth month she took to her bed and could not rise again, yet her body and mind were at ease with no suffering of illness whatever — only her food and drink fell off sharply. On the seventeenth she stopped eating altogether. So we invited ten bhikṣuṇīs from the Hankou Old Lay Buddhists’ Grove to our house, where they recited the Buddha’s name day and night in shifts, and the family joined in aloud. On the morning of the nineteenth I respectfully prepared a petition and burned it before the image of Amitābha Buddha in my mother’s room. At the end of the petition it said: “If her allotted years are yet to be enjoyed, I dare pray that safety be quickly granted; but if her lifespan is at its end, then I beg that she be graciously received and guided — even the lowest grade of the lowest birth is my wish.” At that time my mother’s mind was clear; her burial clothes were already put on properly. Though she lay on her back, her face was covered with smiles, and with palms joined she recited the Buddha’s name in a low voice. She drew off her gold finger ring herself. Sons, daughters-in-law, grandchildren and great-grandchildren stood around her, and she had not one word of attachment. At the beginning of the hour of yin on the twenty-second her mouth still moved as if reciting, while her breath gradually grew faint. We then recited the Amitābha Sutra, and as the third repetition of the Rebirth Dharani was just finished, she passed away in peace facing west. Two hours after her breath ceased her whole body was cold, yet the crown of her head was still warm. Judging by the sutras and their commentaries, with such a death one may know that rebirth in the West is beyond doubt. Yet I still recite the Buddha’s name daily and dedicate the merit to my mother, hoping her grade in the lotus may rise.
Recorded by Fang Deren
(Original title: Laywoman Zhang Jueming’s Fellow Practitioners Assist Her Recitation, and She Is Reborn with Palms Joined)

Laywoman Zhang Jueming, whose Dharma name was Zhaojue, was a native of Pinghu in Zhejiang. In the last years of the Qing she graduated from the teacher-training class of the Shanghai Wuben Girls’ School, surpassing her fellows in literature and art, and taught at the Wuxing Girls’ School. After marrying into the Shen family of Wuxing, she supported her husband and taught her children, and served her parents-in-law with filial piety, all in accordance with propriety. In ordinary times she studied painting, music, poetry and calligraphy, and was accomplished in them all. Her running-and-regular script resembled Zhao Songxue’s but was more vigorous, with something of Chu Henan’s brushwork; her small seal script was strong and beautiful; her poetry was close to the Song and Yuan. In painting she excelled at fine detail, and with the two women Fang Zhiyuan and Shen Youkui she once produced a joint collection, The Three Friends of Winter, gathering poetry, calligraphy and painting, with a great wealth of fine work. In middle age she contracted typhoid fever, which left her somewhat hard of hearing. Falling gravely ill again and again until near death, she dreamed that Bodhisattva Guanyin came down to save her and recovered; and so she took refuge in the great Dharma and settled her heart in the Pure Land.
In the spring of 1934

she took refuge with Master Yinguang. On the first day of the fourth month of the twenty-sixth year [of the Republic], she respectfully welcomed Layman Fan Gunong to Wuxing to lecture on the Amitābha Sutra, a Dharma affinity most excellent. On the Buddha’s birthday, when the service of merit was completed, she asked Layman Fan to introduce her, and went with him to the Baoguo Monastery in Suzhou, where at the seat of Master Yinguang she received the five precepts. From then on she practiced herself and transformed others with unremitting diligence. She once composed a song in praise of the Buddha, wrote out the Heart Sutra in her own blood, and copied the Diamond Sutra in regular script as offerings. She painted the image of the Three Holy Ones of the West and a portrait of Master Yinguang, had photographs made and gave them away, and all who received them aroused the resolve to recite the Buddha’s name.
In the winter of 1937

when the Incident occurred, she went into seclusion on Mount Mogan and reverently read the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. She then lived in Hangzhou, and apart from morning and evening recitation did nothing but read the Ten Essentials of Pure Land and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind. She once said that to recite the Amitābha Sutra once was like making a spirit-journey to the Land of Ultimate Bliss once. She wrote two verses: “With zeal and constancy I keep the Buddha’s name — a thousand years of darkness blaze to light. Deluded thoughts die as conditions fade; the turbid waters instantly grow bright. The six dusts’ tangled shadows, all astir, cannot remain a single instant in my sight. The taste of Sahā palls and thins away; in Ultimate Bliss I roam in spirit’s flight.” At that time she sought out plum blossoms on Solitary Hill, enjoyed the scenery of the Qixia Cave, and called upon the Venerable Zhiyin. She climbed Mount Ziyang and gazed at the Qiantang River, and was well able to set worldly things aside. In her leisure she wrote poetry and prose expounding the principles of the Pure Land teaching, which appeared in the semi-monthly Awakened Sentient Beings, the semi-monthly Buddhist Studies, and the monthly Honghua. In his later years Master Yinguang lived on Mount Lingyan, and the laywoman corresponded with him for instruction, receiving much molding and refinement.
, in the
fourth

month, she went to Shanghai on business and called upon Master Desen and Layman Fan Gunong to ask for instruction. Layman Fan said: “A practitioner must look upon the world with the Buddha’s eye before he can attain ultimate liberation.” The laywoman deeply grasped his meaning. Master Desen said: “Among women I know five who have wisdom, learning, poetic and literary skill and many talents. One, I fear, has already been born in the West; of one I do not know whether she lives or has died. The other two both delight in talking of the profound and mysterious and do not attend to practice. She who can honor the aged Master Yin’s teaching and devote herself single-mindedly to recitation is you alone. I earnestly hope you will set your heart on the ground, put down every trick and device of body and mind, treasure this one practice of holding the name, and do it in earnest, so that you may gain true benefit. In the future you will uphold the Dharma and be a pillar among women, leading them all back to the Pure Land — thus you may repay the aged Master Yin’s compassionate grace.” This was compassion received at its utmost. From that autumn she suffered from chills and fever, lighter by day and heavier at night. Through winter into spring, for five months, medicine and physicians were of no avail. Fellow practitioners of the lotus, at their Dharma assemblies, each made obeisance and prayer for her, hoping to expiate her former karma.
, in the
third

month, the laywoman knew she would not recover and gave instructions for her affairs. She left orders that she be laid in a monk’s robe and that all the final rites follow the Buddha’s regulations. On the twenty-sixth day of the third month she asked that fellow practitioners be invited to assist her recitation for rebirth. The laywoman joined her palms and recited silently, and bade her second daughter wash her hands and cut her nails, saying: “With nails this long, how can I see the Buddha?” At the hour of xu on the twenty-eighth (the fifth day of the third lunar month) she passed away in peace, her countenance calm and gentle. Before and after her death the sound of the assembly’s recitation never stopped. On the thirtieth, at the encoffining, Master Shengen was respectfully invited to speak the Dharma, and the assembled friends recited sutras and the Buddha’s name to speed her westward journey. Within the seven weeks the assembly recited the Buddha’s name together twice. From her remaining funds her children set aside ten thousand yuan for merit: one portion for offerings to the monks, one portion to hold a Buddha-recitation week on Mount Lingyan, and one portion to help build the memorial stupa for Master Yin. The images of Buddhas and bodhisattvas she had worshiped in life were moved to the nunnery for offerings. Her coffin is to be cremated this winter. She was fifty-seven. She had seven children, all plain and honest, knowing propriety and of some accomplishment. The laywoman had planted virtuous roots in former lives and practiced with keen precision, truly receiving the true transmission of the aged Master Fayu. Well may it be that at the end she departed with such ease, her one mind bound for the West — is she not one of whom it is said, “Merit long accumulated, never retreating from bodhi”?
Recorded in 1944
, in the
sixth
month, on the
eighth
day.
Recorded by Qu Hannan
(Original title: Laywoman Liu Peiyuan Holds Fast to the Very End and Thus Finishes Her Life)

Ms. Liu, whose personal name was Peiyuan, was a native of Jingjiang in Jiangsu. In childhood she was versed in poetry and the rites, and could recite much of the Four Books and Five Classics. When a little older she studied at the Cuimin Girls’ School and the Jiangning Women’s Normal School, learning fine arts and excelling in household management. At twenty-three she came to preside over my household, sharing hardship with me and enduring much toil. Time has flown, and it is now forty-two years. For the last twenty years she has raised and taught the children and called on the name of Amitābha with the utmost sincerity and urgency. After taking refuge with the aged Master Yin she received the Dharma name Huiying, and recited the Buddha’s name and kept the fast with ever greater diligence. At any Dharma assembly in Suzhou or Shanghai she would gladly take part, and she often said: “Since we have obtained a human body, suffering is unavoidable; to end suffering one must call on Amitābha. But of what is called suffering, there are two kinds that should not really be counted as suffering: the hardship of diligence, and the hardship of frugality.” Some measure of her lifelong diligence and thrift may be seen in this.

Little did we expect to meet with the upheaval of war, wandering from place to place, until damp heat accumulated in her body; at first she gave it no thought, but in the end there was not a whole patch of skin left on her. When someone urged her to eat meat because of her poor nourishment, the lady firmly refused, saying: “I would rather die; and when I die, all these sufferings will be gone.” In the past two years she felt the hardship more and more. On the twelfth day of the seventh month her illness suddenly turned acute; her breathing was labored, the Western doctors were helpless and the Chinese doctors shook their heads. The lady alone said gravely: “No matter, no matter — the time has not yet come.” It happened that the aged layman Zhou Zanting comforted her by presenting a lotus flower; the lady received it with a smile and said: “When I see this flower, my heart opens. But frugal hardship and diligent hardship I shall hold to the very last instant, to finish out my life. You must not weep, and above all you must not spend much.” I and the family joined in assisting her recitation. When the lady could no longer make a sound, she signaled with her hand. I put my ear to her and comforted her, telling her that mental recitation was even better. It went on until twenty minutes to three in the afternoon, when amid the sound of recitation filling the room she passed away in peace. That night the whole family again recited around her through the night. The next day, at the encoffining, her face was as in life. Now, when someone foreknows the time and passes in peace, all who speak of it call it a sign of rebirth in the West. In truth, whether a person is reborn in the West must rest on that person’s own witness; no one else can presume to judge. For fear that it may be rumor and cannot escape being inaccurate, the ancients avoided writing what was unfounded — and this is also why I am unwilling to write accounts of rebirth in the West on others’ behalf. The title of this piece is A True Record of Leaving Suffering Through Buddha-Recitation.
Recorded by Zhang Yiliu,
(Original title: Laywoman Fang Huilang — “Amitābha Has Come,” Departing Peacefully for the West)

My younger sister née Du, whose Dharma name was Huilang, was sixty-three years old. Her husband Du Zifu still survives. They have one son, Weiping, and two daughters, one married into the He family and one into the Wang family. Two grandsons and three granddaughters. When my sister was eleven our father passed away, and she clung to our mother’s knee morning and night, knowing in every matter how to follow her mother’s heart. When grown she married into the Du family, serving her parents-in-law with filial piety and living with her sisters-in-law in harmony. Toward her husband she was respectful as toward a guest; in managing the household she was diligent and thrifty. In womanly work and womanly virtue she was truly without shortcoming. All her life she was honest, kind and gentle, just like our mother. She followed me on my official travels to various places and was never once proud or overbearing.

In her later years she lost the sight of both eyes, and I engaged physicians to treat her, but to no effect. I told my sister: “Your blindness has its own former cause. Apart from a lifelong vegetarian diet and reciting the Buddha’s name, to wear away your former karma, there is no other way.” My sister believed, vowed and practiced accordingly, brave and diligent. Though her sight did not fully return, she gradually came to distinguish the colors of people’s faces, and could move about without support — the benefit of reciting the Buddha’s name is inconceivable. Her constitution had always been frail, and in recent years she suffered slight illnesses from time to time. I often comforted her, saying: “For one who recites the Buddha’s name, distant retribution easily becomes near retribution, and heavy retribution is lightened. When your life ends, your karma will surely melt away, your wisdom shine clear, and you will have no other suffering.”

This year she had no particular illness anywhere in her body, only her food and drink dwindled day by day and she grew thinner and thinner. At the last she went without food for nearly twenty days, taking only a little boiled water now and then. Yet her body and mind were at ease and she recited the Buddha’s name as usual. It happened that Master Yuanqi, president of the Wuhan branch of the Permanent Memorial Society for Master Yinguang, came from Lingyan. She therefore asked to take refuge with Master Che, was granted the Dharma name Huilang, and received earnest instruction. One day my sister suddenly said to me: “If I am born in the West and the Buddha questions me, I shall not be able to answer — what then?” I said: “When the flower opens and you see the Buddha and awaken to the unborn, you will answer fluently of yourself; do not worry.” My sister was delighted. Her lodging was only a step from mine, and from then on I went in person every day to assist her recitation. On the first day of the intercalary fourth month, at eight in the morning, I went to assist, and had just reached her bedside when she said: “Amitābha Buddha has come.” I said: “To recite the Buddha’s name and see the Buddha means rebirth in the West beyond doubt. You go first, sister, and I will see you off; when my own time comes, will you come with the Buddha’s carriage to welcome me?” My sister said: “Yes.” Then twenty-four bhikṣuṇīs from the Qingji Monastery were invited, divided into three shifts to assist the recitation day and night without a break in the sound of the Buddha’s name. I too assisted from the side, and from time to time urged her to put down all ten thousand conditions and seek rebirth in the West with one mind. My sister’s consciousness was clear from first to last; she recited the Buddha’s name in a low voice, and sometimes silently. It went on until ten in the evening of the fourth day, when she passed peacefully to the West. Her whole body grew cold, yet the crown of her head was still warm, and her four limbs were soft. Her face in particular had an unusual luster, a smile brimming on it — her rebirth in the West is beyond doubt.
(Original title: The Mother of the Venerable Jingci Foreknows the Time, Her Face Wearing a Smile)

The mother of the Venerable Jingci, abbot of Fengguo Monastery in Yizhou, the Lady Chen, served her parents-in-law with filial piety and supported her husband and taught her children, each according to the proper way. She was virtuous, gentle and mild by nature, and all the neighborhood praised her. Yet at first she had not yet come to believe in the Buddhadharma. After the Venerable One had been shaved and dyed as a monk, he was diligent in Buddhist affairs and strove to spread the Pure Land school. Following the teaching that a son’s way is only accomplished when his parents are freed from defilement, he constantly kept his mother’s salvation in mind. So he would seize every opportunity to petition her, urging on her the benefit of reciting the Buddha’s name, or asking others to guide her from the side. He also silently dedicated the merit of his own daily practice, in repentance and dedication, to his mother. In the end she came to great faith through this, took refuge with her whole heart, and gained rebirth.

The Lady’s passing took place on the nineteenth day of the fourth month of the jiashen year. Several tens of days before, she had indeed contracted illness. Yet at the advanced age of seventy-nine her mind and spirits were still serene at the end. At noon that day, when the Venerable One told her to recite and think on the Buddha, she nodded and answered. Her grandson’s wife, at her side, asked whether there was anyone she remembered or anything she wished to entrust, and to each she answered no. When relatives and friends asked when she would go, she answered at once, “In a little while.” When asked again later she answered the same. When she had spoken she would call the Buddha’s name without cease; though her voice and breath were nearly gone, her lips and teeth still moved slightly. At five in the afternoon the members of the Buddha-recitation hall all dedicated the merit to the Lady. At nightfall they again assisted her recitation for rebirth. After about an hour of assisted recitation she passed away in peace. Three hours after death her whole body was already cold, yet the crown of her head alone was warm. Eight hours later, when she was bathed and changed, her four limbs were soft and her countenance exactly as in life; all who saw her exclaimed in wonder.

Though ordinary beings have no way to determine the grade of her rebirth in the West, all the auspicious signs — right mindfulness clearly manifest, foreknowledge of the time, a body free of pain, a smiling face, soft limbs, warmth at the crown — the Lady had them all. That she has taken a high place in the ocean-wide assembly is surely beyond doubt. All this was witnessed by the whole company, and I have therefore gathered it into a record, to submit it for the instruction of the good and superior.
Recorded by Xue Tongyue
(Original title: Laywoman Wang Cirui, Eyes Closed and Silent, Murmuring the Buddha’s Name)

The lady Wang, whose personal name was Cirui, received that Dharma name when she took refuge with the aged Master Jingbo of the Qingliang Monastery in our own district. She was kind by nature, silent and sparing of words, and disliked idle talk about others’ faults. From childhood she believed in the Buddha and knew that the karma of speech must not be lightly stirred. In the forty years since our marriage our bond as husband and wife has been deep. In managing the household and serving our elders I had much help from her as my inner support. In

she took refuge at the seat of the great Pure Land master the Venerable Yin of Mount Lingyan, receiving the Dharma name Kaiyue. From then on her faith and vows grew ever firmer, and she made vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation her daily practice. When this spring the Buddhist Academy invited the aged Master Xingci to Changshu to lecture on the Amitābha Sutra, my wife went every day to listen, and hearing the Master’s Dharma instruction in person she benefited greatly. Knowing the impermanence of worldly things, she constantly kept rebirth in the Pure Land in mind, and so she also took refuge with Master Xing. Every morning after washing she would recite the Amitābha Sutra and the holy names of Amitābha Buddha and Bodhisattva Guanyin as her daily practice. She bowed to the Buddha and applied herself with diligence.

This summer, because household affairs were many and tangled, she fell ill from accumulated toil: her abdomen swelled and the illness dragged on for three months, with a hundred medicines of no avail. In this illness she especially kept the holy name of Amitābha in mind, seeking to leave suffering and gain joy. It came to the night of the thirtieth day of the eighth month, when my wife saw three men in patched robes and vairocana hats standing together before her bed. Knowing that her worldly ties were finished, she at once charged the children concerning the arrangements after her death, earnestly warning them not to weep. From then on she closed her eyes and did not speak, murmuring the Buddha’s name. The next night, knowing that her illness could not be turned back, I invited Layman Lü Zuyang of the Buddhist Academy to our home to give instruction, setting forth the holy realm of the Pure Land, the majesty of its dependent and principal rewards, so that her right mindfulness might be clear and she might be reborn with one mind. While Layman Lü was instructing her, my wife thanked him from time to time, her mind clear and her right mindfulness distinct. It came to the small hours of the second day of the ninth month; my wife knew the hour of rebirth had come, and closed her eyes and fell silent, and amid the sound of the Buddha’s name proclaimed aloud she relinquished her karmic body and departed. After her rebirth in the West her whole body grew cold, but the crown of her head was still warm, her joints were soft, and her face was as in life; relatives and friends who saw her all exclaimed at the marvel. Judging by the sutras and the treatises, one may conclude that she went straight to Ultimate Bliss beyond doubt. Seeing this with my own eyes redoubled my faith and made me know that the Buddha’s words are not empty. I therefore write this record as encouragement to those who recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the West.
Recorded by Mao Xizhang
(Original title: Laywoman Li Miaoyan Sees the Buddha Emit Light and Is Sent to Rebirth by a Rare Fragrance)

My late wife, née Li, was kindness itself by nature and never wearied of doing good. She firmly believed in the Three Jewels, ate vegetarian food and recited sutras. At forty she took refuge with Master Qinghai of the Ruiming Monastery outside the south suburb of our district, and was given the name Ciguo. Later she and I together took refuge with Master Yingci, I receiving the name Miaohua and my late wife the name Miaoyan, and from then on she was known as Zhuang Li Miaoyan. She recited the Buddha’s name with me at the Wujin Buddhist Society for thirteen years. She was never ill, and though she was already seventy-three, her hair was not white and her teeth were not lacking; only her right ear was somewhat deaf. She never rode a carriage when coming or going near or far, and never used a staff going up or down; everyone said this was the blessing of the Buddha’s power.

This time, on the fourteenth day of the sixth month of the lunar calendar, she had fever and dizziness and could not relish food for three days. On the nineteenth, Guanyin’s birthday, she still forced herself up to keep the holy day. On the twenty-first the chills and fever came on violently. From then on Chinese and Western physicians consulted together and medicines of every kind were administered: the chills and fever stopped, dysentery began, her condition changed from hour to hour, and she could not take food. For more than ten days her illness increased rather than diminished. From this she knew she would not recover, and fixed her mind wholly on the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, seeking nothing else. After that neither Chinese nor Western medicine passed her lips; she only moistened her mouth and cleansed her intestines with Great Compassion water. Though her vital spirits declined, her mind remained very clear and she recited the Buddha’s name as before. On the afternoon of the twelfth she asked that those who assist the dying be invited to see her off to rebirth. From the morning of the thirteenth the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceased, and my late wife too leaned on her pillow and recited along, only in a somewhat lower voice. At about eleven in the afternoon she saw with her eyes the Three Holy Ones of the West sending forth a great radiance that illumined the world, brilliant and majestic. At the same moment a rare fragrance filled the room, wave upon wave assailing the nostrils. She said moreover that the next afternoon she would go to the West. At first we did not believe it; the next morning her spirits were especially good, and at the noon meal she still urged us to eat. When the meal was quite finished, and while we were singing the Buddha’s name aloud, my late wife joined her two palms, turned her head toward the west, and passed away in peace. Her illness had lasted a full month, and in all that time there was nothing unclean about her body, nor any moment when her speech was unclear. After her death the crown of her head was still warm at the eighth hour. My elegy for her reads: “She upheld her husband and raised the house, taught her sons to fame; consider her life — no evil done, all good practiced; in worldly and world-transcending practice, every task her spirit, every drop her blood. Deep in Pure Land work, her compassionate heart widely spread; see her end — the Three Holy Ones emit light, the ten directions receive and guide; the fruit of joy, the Land of Bliss prepared; all who hear marvel at wave upon wave of fragrance.” There is much in my late wife’s life and words fit to stir the world. Here I first record the course of her illness and the circumstances of her death, as a report to fellow students of the Buddha’s teaching.
Recorded by Zhuang Zhuqing
(Original title: Laywoman Zhang Huixian Knows Her Time Has Come and Passes Away in the Auspicious Posture)

Ms. Ye Zhang Huixian was a member of the Jinsha Buddhist Lay Grove in Nantong. She took refuge at the seat of the Venerable Yin of Lingyan, devoted herself to Pure Land practice, and set her whole mind on the West. Rising early and sleeping late, she was more diligent than ordinary. Last year (

) on the fourth day of the winter month, at the Grove she witnessed the auspicious signs of Layman Yi Huiming’s rebirth in the West and praised them without ceasing. Soon after, walking home with a staff, she was careless in her step and suddenly stumbled on one foot, and from then on lay in bed unable to rise. On the fifth her spirits were weary, and her fellow member of the Grove Zhang Huijie and others asked me to go to her house to assist her recitation and see the laywoman off to rebirth. I said: “I fear she will not be reborn in the West just yet.” Zhang said: “Last night while we were assisting her recitation, the laywoman knew her time had come and already gave instructions about family matters; so we know her escape from the sea of suffering is not far off.” So we went together to her house, and found the Buddha hall fully furnished with incense, flowers, lamps and candles. I and more than twenty fellow members of the Grove assisted her recitation in shifts, and for ten days and nights the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceased. By noon of the fifteenth the lady could no longer voice her recitation, only murmur. At the beginning of the hour of wei she passed away peacefully in the auspicious posture. The members of the Grove and her family continued to recite the Buddha’s name to speed her westward return. The next day the crown of her head was still warm and her face was moist and lustrous as in life. She was eighty-one. I would say that Amitābha’s great vow is true and not false, and that one who vows rebirth will certainly have that vow fulfilled. Looking at this lady — reaching the age of eighty, and at the hour of relinquishing her karmic body showing such manifest auspicious signs — I believe all the more that Amitābha has no empty vow and that Śākyamuni did not speak falsely; the truthful words of the golden mouth truly do not deceive me. I record this as encouragement to those who practice Pure Land. On an auspicious day in the third month of the guiwei year, respectfully set down.
Recorded by Hu Huiche,
(Original title: Layman Gu Shengxiang Sits Upright, Forms the Mudrā, and Knows His Time Has Come)

A fellow practitioner of the lotus, Genyuan, whose Dharma name was Shengxiang, was a daughter of the Gu family of Suzhou. Quiet and gentle by nature, from childhood she loved to read good books. At thirteen, when Master Dixian was lecturing on the sutras at the Jiezhang Monastery in the Western Garden, she reverently heard the wondrous Dharma and took refuge with the assembly. The aged Master turned to her and said: “You must apply yourself well and never be lax.” From then on she ate vegetables and recited the Buddha’s name, resolutely making her own decision. Some years later, when Master Yinguang was living at the Baoguo Monastery in Wu, she went often to pay her respects. Master Yin took honest recitation of the Buddha’s name as the primary practice, and reading the Mahāyāna scriptures as conditions allowed, together with doing no evil and practicing all good, as the auxiliary practice, and he earnestly encouraged her. From then on the laywoman’s pure faith increased; she practiced earnestly and did not fail her teacher’s instruction. When Master Yin passed away at Lingyan, she spurred herself on the more, devoting herself to Pure Land practice and becoming quite unlike the world. Her will was firm, and she always aspired to the highest grade of the lotus terrace.

But through the working of former karma, heavy offenses were lightly repaid: she contracted a lung disease and her vitality wasted away day by day. Famous physicians treated her, but to no effect. In the winter of the jiashen year she contracted pleurisy and lay tossing on her sickbed, her body growing weaker. By the middle of the twelfth month her illness grew more acute, and she knew she could not recover. So she said: “All dharmas come to an end, all things are as they should be; the body is the root of suffering, and one should seek deliverance. In this evil world of the five turbidities one cannot abide even a single morning. Moreover, with this great calamity now upon us, suffering grows the worse. At this final move I resolve to take the Pure Land as my home. Even if the Bodhisattva, following the cries of the suffering, should come in person to save me, I would still only beg the Bodhisattva to lead me to the Land of Bliss, there to be forever free of all suffering and to receive every joy — what is there in this bitter Sahā to cling to?” And she comforted her mother, saying: “Let not the six-character name be interrupted; held long, its benefit is inexhaustible, and we may look forward to meeting again.” She was serene in giving her instructions, wholly without distress. On the second day of the first month of this spring she suddenly asked for a small bottle of Master Yin’s Great Compassion Dharma water that she had kept for many years. When it was given her, she joined one palm and joyfully drank it to the last drop. Then she said: “I hope, by the compassionate Master’s vow, to follow the holy assembly of Amitābha when they come to receive and guide me to rebirth in the West. My spirit and consciousness will leave through the crown of my head.” Then she took a cupful of thin gruel. After a little, knowing her time had come, she told the assembly: “I wish to sit upright and straight, and I ask that good friends come to assist my recitation of the Buddha’s name.” It came to the hour of wei, and amid the sound of the great assembly’s recitation she formed the Amitābha mudrā with her hands and passed away in peace. For thirty-six hours, until the mourning rites, the crown of her head was still warm. Three days later, at the encoffining, her bearing was extraordinarily free and at ease, her four limbs soft, her color as in life; all who saw her exclaimed at the rarity. Truly, the Pure Land Dharma gate covers all three capacities and brings deliverance from birth and death, most simple and most swift. If one can believe, accept and practice it, one will naturally relinquish the karmic body with composure. Such a one as this laywoman may be called free of craving in mind, free of inversion in thought, right mindfulness clear and distinct, as if entered into samādhi; in a single instant her spirit came to rest in the Land of Peace and Nurture. The sutra says: the three realms are without peace, like a burning house. In these declining times the bitter sea of Sahā grows worse by the day. Apart from this wondrous method of honestly reciting the Buddha’s name and gaining rebirth with one’s karma, there is no other skill by which to escape. Now I wet my brush and respectfully record the laywoman’s practice of true faith and earnest vows in life, and the auspicious signs that prove her rebirth in the West at death. I exhort all who have the affinity to believe firmly and practice, for ten thousand practice means ten thousand go.
Recorded by Fan Zongjian,

blocks.text: 31. Rare Fragrance and a Rosy Face

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Bian Yiru — Music, Rare Fragrance, a Rosy Face, a Ringing Voice)

My mother was of the Bian family; her personal name was Yi and her courtesy name Yiru. She took refuge with the Great Master Miaozhen of Mount Lingyan and was granted the Dharma name Renmu. Her family was registered in Yangzhou and later moved to Rugao. She was bright and wise by nature, respectful, frugal, kind and loving, and was cherished by the elders of the clan. At twenty-one she came to my father, and for more than thirty years she managed the household and raised the children with toil. Ten years ago my mother, in a dream at night, passed a butcher’s door and saw a dead pig on the block with its eyes still opening and closing; waking, she was moved to pity and vowed to give up meat and fish. She asked the Dharma of the venerable layman Xiang Zhiyuan, a worthy of our district (whose personal name was Benyuan and courtesy name Ziqing, and who edited and published the collected writings of the Great Master Huiyuan and other books), and from this she took refuge in and revered the Three Jewels and set her heart on Pure Land practice. Amid her household work she recited the Amitābha Sutra and the Diamond Sutra daily as her regular practice. Though she had not read much, she understood quite clearly the meaning of “like a dream, like an illusion, like dew, like lightning.” She once said to others: “I do not presume to speak of my practice; I only seek to be free of birth and death.” The whole family was transformed by her and one after another took refuge in the Three Jewels. In
, fleeing the turmoil to Shanghai, my mother visited and paid homage at the great temples, and having come close to good teachers her faith and vows grew ever more earnest.

Three years later she returned. On the twenty-ninth day of the first month of the old calendar last year she was suddenly struck by a stroke: she could not speak, and her right limbs could not easily bend or stretch. We brothers Renseng knew it was the working of former karma, and so recited the Buddha’s name devoutly and repented on her behalf. From spring through winter not a day passed without it. Though my mother was ill, she too would at times murmur as if reciting the Buddha’s name. The family day and night sought ways to drive out the illness, but my mother had no thought of clinging to life at all. Even when medicine was brought, she took it only after being pressed. She only signaled to the family to offer incense and flowers to the Buddha from time to time. Hearing others recite the Buddha’s name, she could not contain her joy. We brothers Renseng would often sit by her bed and read Buddhist books to entertain her hearing, and the old lady would forget her illness in her contentment.

Our family had a Praise-the-Buddha Recitation Tower, which my mother had built with her own hands. When first ill she could still be helped up there with effort, and once there she would weep for joy, bow and praise, and could not bear to leave. Later, as her body declined, she wished to climb but could not. One day she had the family support her to the door, and gazing at the tower she cried without ceasing. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month she suddenly smiled and pointed at the ground before her bed, as if she saw something; when asked, she could not explain, and then pointed at the image of Amitābha on the wall. Asked whether she saw the Buddha, she nodded again and again in assent, smiling without cease. We brothers Renseng rejoiced inwardly and served the Buddha the more reverently. I reflect that my mother lay on her sickbed for a full year, and though she could not speak, her mind was clear and her right mindfulness had not faded. Her body had not the least pain or suffering — this cannot but be the blessing of the Buddha’s power.

On the twentieth day of the first month of the old calendar this year her illness came on again; she lay quietly as if in deep sleep, neither eating nor drinking, only her breathing to be heard. A physician was summoned, but she could not be treated, so more than ten bhikṣuṇīs and fellow practitioners of the lotus were invited to assist her recitation and see her off to rebirth. Through four days and nights her breathing was even, her condition unchanged, and the sound of the Buddha’s name unbroken. My father led the family in bowing and reciting with the assembly with redoubled effort. We brothers Renseng would each put our mouths to her ear at the bedside and call loudly, telling her to put everything down and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind. Though my mother’s eyes were closed as if in sleep, she would catch her breath and nod in answer, responding every time she was called, without the least discrepancy.

On the night of the twenty-fourth we again gathered the monks to bow to Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha and repent on our mother’s behalf for her former karma. Then we devoutly bowed to the Forty-Eight Vows and prepared a petition to Amitābha Tathāgata, vowing to dedicate to our mother’s rebirth in the Pure Land all the merit we brothers had gained in the past, present and future by bowing to the Buddha, printing images, spreading the teaching and releasing living creatures.
