And we begged that auspicious signs be shown, so that all who saw or heard might give rise to right faith and together ascend the shore of awakening. The bows were hardly finished when the assembly saw my mother’s countenance improve, her face rosy, her brow slightly moist, as if she had never been ill. They exclaimed: “We have assisted at many deathbeds, but never have we seen one at the point of death, face like dead ashes, take on a rosy color again.” At daybreak the next morning Renseng suddenly heard music in the air, exquisite and sweet, sounding and ceasing by turns, lingering long without dispersing. The Venerable Qincan, assisting the recitation at her bedside, heard it clearly as well. Asked what the sound was like, he described it the same; at first we thought nothing strange of it. Just then the two Venerables Defang and Zhenzong came in from outside and noticed a rare fragrance in the room. They asked what incense had been burned today, and why it differed from yesterday’s — and again we thought nothing strange. Presently her breathing grew hurried, the tone in her nose changed greatly, and the hollow sound rang like bronze. The Venerable Qincan said: “Listen closely, all of you — why does the sick woman’s throat sound ring like metal and stone? Truly a strange thing. Recite aloud and quickly to aid her birth in the West.” So a hundred voices joined as one, reciting and watching, earnest to the point of tears. And in that sea of solemn sound my mother slightly parted her lips and passed away in peace. It was

, the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the old calendar, at eight in the morning. Our family, following the Buddha’s regulations, did not wail or move the body, but continued to recite the Buddha’s name in reverent silence. Only after twenty-four hours did we bathe her and change her clothes: her four limbs were soft. The five fingers of her right hand, which had been drawn up by illness, now opened like anyone’s. Her face was rosy and wore a smile, just as on the evening before. The Venerable One said again: “I have seen many off to rebirth, but never have I seen a deathbed like this.” So he made a vow to lead the assembly in holding a Pure Land Buddha-recitation week, continuing to recite the ten-thousand-virtue name. More than ten people took turns day and night, brave and diligent, never retreating from their first resolve. From the twenty-fifth until the first seven-day period ended on the third day of the second month, the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceased day or night.

With such an excellent affinity, the family was filled with both grief and joy. Those who assisted the recitation also rejoiced and praised. All said that the Buddha’s grace is towering and cannot be fully told. So during the seven weeks of mourning the whole family ate vegetarian food and recited the Buddha’s name, adding the merit of releasing living creatures, lighting lamps, giving alms and gilding images, and dedicated it all to our mother’s rebirth, praying also for the universal benefit of sentient beings. The image of Amitābha Buddha in the Praise Tower has now been regilded. Layman Xie Dezun was asked to reverently paint the image of the Three Holy Ones of the West, to be carved in stone at the White Robe Nunnery so that rubbings may be made and circulated, enduring without end. Zhifang moreover wrote out by hand one copy each of Kṣitigarbha’s Original Vows Sutra and Samantabhadra’s Vows of Good Conduct, had them mounted into volumes, and sent them to the monastery as offerings. Such, in brief, was my mother’s turning to the Buddha and the course of her final rites.

There is one more thing that must not go unrecorded. Four days before my mother’s death, my father, since her illness was critical, made preparations for washing and dressing the body and sent someone to invite the laywoman Li Benyuan. The laywoman pondered a long while, then answered our messenger: “Your mistress will certainly be born in the West on the twenty-fifth; I shall come that afternoon.” When the messenger returned and reported this, all were astonished, judging by her condition that she could not possibly last so long. Yet it turned out exactly as she said, and the laywoman did indeed arrive at the appointed time. The others hurried to ask her about it. The laywoman said: “From the nineteenth I have been holding a Buddha-recitation week at my home, gathering the assembly to open the way. On the morning of the twenty-second, before rising

I dreamed that someone told me I was about to die, and waking I thought it strange. When day came and the messenger arrived, I was suddenly startled. I thought to myself that the recitation week must run to its completion on the twenty-fifth — how could I have time to come at once? But the Buddha’s power is inconceivable: I prayed devoutly to the Buddha, begging him to bless the sick woman to be born in the West on the twenty-fifth. So I added twenty-four recitations of the Heart Sutra each day, seeking the fulfillment of my wish — and now it has been verified.” Hearing this, the assembly marveled without end. The laywoman was a farmer’s wife living outside the eastern wall of the city, aged and laboring in the fields, a believer in the Buddha who practiced austerities.
Recorded by Yang Renseng and others

blocks.text: 32. Seeing the Buddha at the End

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Li Yingjin — “Amitābha Has Come, Go Quickly”)

My second wife, née Li, was named Yingjin. From the first she ate vegetarian food and loved goodness, and was known for her filial service to her parents. At twenty she came to me; she served my widowed mother as if she were her own, and raised my children by a former wife as her own. A year later she bore a son. Three years after that my mother died, and she assisted in the arrangements for the funeral, sparing nothing of propriety. But her constitution had always been weak, and the sudden great bereavement and excessive toil brought on illness year after year. At first, on the advice of the Xihua Hall, she enshrined an image of Bodhisattva Guanyin and held the White Robe Spirit Spell, seeking blessing and benefit. When the Tongshan Society was established in our county, she and I joined one after the other, and though several years passed we gained no Dharma benefit from it.

From the autumn of the jimao year, laymen Wang Zhuxuan and Zhang Peiqiu urged her forward in the Pure Land Dharma gate. At the first hearing of its excellence she felt as if she had found a priceless treasure, and so cast aside all her former studies, recited the Buddha’s name with one mind, and sought rebirth in the West — and it is now seven years since. I recall that three years ago Yingjin suffered from a severe headache; because she took too much medicine, cold sweat broke from every pore of her body, and she came near to death. In that crisis she suddenly saw the whole room full of Buddhas, and pointed out one like the image of the God of Longevity, wearing a yellow Daoist robe and leaning on a staff, who came swaying toward her; after a while the Buddhas gradually disappeared. From then on her illness gradually improved (she recovered). Last autumn Master Xiusheng was spreading the Dharma in our city, and she again received instruction, which led her to recite the Buddha’s name and make vows with even greater diligence, so that walking, standing, sitting or lying she never forgot it. She often prayed for recovery and peace of body, for release from family ties and for the wide encouragement of all — only then would her wish be fulfilled. Little did we expect that this first month she would suddenly contract a liver-attacking-spleen illness, taking little food and drink and growing thinner, with no medicine proving efficacious. Suddenly, before dawn on the sixteenth, she sat up and said: “Quickly call the children here; I should wait a little.” Then she said urgently: “Do not delay — Amitābha Buddha has come, let us go quickly.” When the children were called and came, she only asked whether they had all arrived. Then I propped her up to sit at ease, and heard a faint sound of phlegm in her throat; and she closed her eyes and passed away seated. Her mind and consciousness were clear, and she had no suffering. Moreover she saw the Buddha at the end and passed away seated in an instant. At the encoffining, when my eldest son lifted his mother’s head, he felt warmth, for the crown of her head was still warm. Judging by the sutras and treatises, this must be solid evidence of rebirth in the Pure Land. Gongchen is no man of letters, but writes plainly according to the facts, and still begs the monks and laity to confirm it.
Recorded by Cheng Gongchen
(Original title: Laywoman Yang Mingjia — True Faith and Earnest Vows, Skilled in Buddha-Recitation)

The laywoman Guo Yangfang, whose Dharma name was Mingjia, was the second daughter of Mr. Yang Yuchen of Linghu in Wuxing, Zhejiang. In childhood she received her family’s teaching; she was filial, friendly, kind and loving, skilled in poetry and calligraphy, and delighted in goodness and generosity. At twenty she married Layman Guo Tingjing of Shanghai. Layman Guo, whose courtesy name was Jilan, was accomplished in painting, and his landscapes and figures all reached the highest rank. The laywoman would inscribe poems and prose at the head of his paintings to bring out their meaning, signing herself Shaolan, and so their dwelling was called the Twin Orchid Studio. Mr. Guo had a sister, the laywoman Peijing, who was also skilled in painting. Brother and sister often reverently painted many images of Bodhisattva Guanyin, all of which the laywoman respectfully inscribed; these they gave to relatives and friends as offerings, broadly forming Dharma affinities — so it is clear that her virtuous roots were planted in former lives.

At thirty, because she taxed her mind to excess, the laywoman contracted a lung disease; feeling the suffering of human life, she took up a partial vegetarian diet in order to repent. In the bingzi year, the Shanghai Buddhist Pure Karma Society held a Dharma assembly for the protection of the nation and the averting of calamity, and respectfully invited the aged Master Yin to preside and give instruction for seven days, proclaiming the Pure Land Dharma gate. Mr. and Mrs. Guo heard the Dharma and awakened to faith, and at that time took refuge at the compassionate seat, receiving the Dharma names Mingchan and Mingjia — this was the beginning of the laywoman’s practice of pure karma. Yet because her karmic obstacles from former lives were deep, her lung disease came and went. Again and again the three Masters Miao, De and Xing gave her instruction one after another, telling her that with faith and vows and Buddha-recitation she would certainly be reborn with her karma, and so the laywoman’s faith grew firmer and her recitation more diligent. Afterwards, because the dust and clamor of Shanghai were so heavy, Laywoman Mingchan asked Master Miao to buy several rooms on South Street in the town of Mudu in Suzhou as a place for the laywoman and Ms. Peijing to practice pure karma together, for the site was near Lingyan and its surroundings secluded and lovely. Because she herself suffered from lung disease, with heavy obstacles and deep karma, and had read Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Original Vows Sutra and knew it came from the karma of killing over many lives, in recent years the laywoman practiced abstention from killing and the release of living creatures with all her strength, kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, brave and diligent without interruption. When she was ill, Western physicians often urged her to eat meat, and the laywoman would simply smile and pay it no heed. This year the laywoman was approaching fifty. On the eighth day of the first month her old illness grew worse, and she knew she would not recover; so on the twenty-third she invited six nuns, including Masters Yunhai and Kuanhou, to assist her recitation in turns, day and night without cease. Though because of her heavy karma there were many obstacles, happily the laywoman’s faith and vows had always been true and earnest and her recitation skillful, so that she could avoid turning with the demons and not lose right mindfulness. Even at three in the afternoon of the twenty-seventh, when the demonic obstacles grew fiercer, yet by the power of the assembly’s devout recitation, and further favored by the aged Master Miao of Lingyan and Layman Hu Songnian, who came together to instruct her to put everything down, rouse right mindfulness and seek rebirth in the West, the laywoman’s mind gradually cleared and she passed peacefully to the West; the next day the crown of her head was still warm. On the twenty-ninth she was encoffined according to the Buddha’s regulations, and after the seven weeks her coffin is to be carried to the Lingyan Mountain Monastery for cremation. The laywoman practiced diligently all her life, and at the end her conditions were excellent: she left suffering and gained joy, her wish fulfilled. The merit of Buddha-recitation is truly inconceivable. Alas! The three realms are without peace, like a burning house; filled with every suffering, most dreadful. I exhort all who have the affinity to practice pure karma together, forever escaping the suffering of rebirth and sharing the joy of purity — the benefit is indeed great. I therefore record the truth to report to my fellows.
Recorded by Yang Xinlian
(Original title: Laywoman Jiang Changjing — Amitabha Came Early to Help Me Recite the Buddha's Name)

My adoptive mother, of the Yuan family, née Jiang, whose Dharma name was Changjing, lived in Hankou, Hubei. She sought refuge under Master Qingde and received the five precepts at Yuanzhao Monastery in Hankou. She kept a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha's name for thirty-three years, and at the age of sixty-nine she was born in the West. In her daily practice she was ever diligent, never slackening through cold or heat. Every morning she rose at exactly four o'clock to recite the Buddha's name, and by day she devoted herself to bowing to the Buddha. Even in the hottest days of the third summer month, when her robes were soaked with sweat, she would simply change into several fresh sets of haiqing robes. Such was my mother's ordinary diligence in practice. If she saw a suffering person with no clothes to wear who came begging at her door, she would rather take off the clothes she herself was wearing and give them away. Or if she met a poor man who had no way to get through the New Year and so came to steal from her house, she would tell the thief to take what he wanted while she went to the kitchen to fill a bowl with rice, and let the thief eat his fill before he left. At Guiyuan Monastery she provided a feast for a thousand monks, and those who came to receive the offering numbered more than a thousand. Such was my mother's ordinary practice of offering to monks and giving to the poor.
In

, in the first month of the lunar year, my mother showed signs of slight illness. Once she suddenly wept and said: “Hankou will meet with a great calamity.” Her family asked whether it would affect them, and she replied: “We shall not be much affected, but the people's suffering will be unbearable!” After the tenth day of the fourth month, as she was about to return to the West, she saw with her own eyes the Three Sages of the West come to welcome her, and she knew that the hour of her return had come. She instructed them: “Go quickly to the shrine hall and burn incense; the Buddha has come to welcome me, and I am going.” Her family said, “Old Mother, since you are going to the West, you should ask Amitabha Buddha to choose an auspicious day. Today is an ordinary day; there is no need to go.” Mother said: “I know.” Several days later she said: “You have done me harm — these past days Amitabha Buddha has not come.” Her family said, “Old Mother, do not be anxious; when the hour of your return arrives, the Buddha will surely come again to welcome you.” The next day she said: “I wish to be seated in a jar, and within the jar must be placed rush pith and rosin; hurry and prepare everything for me.” Just then the Japanese soldiers were causing turmoil and all trades were on strike; in the whole market there was only one jar, of poor quality. Though it had been bought, it had not yet been carried home. Mother said, “Hurry and bring the jar.” Her family said, “The jar has not arrived.” Mother said: “Why did you buy me such a poor jar?” After a little while the various items all arrived, and when the family looked at it, it was indeed of poor quality. Such was my mother's clear awareness of things as she approached her end. On the morning of the seventeenth she said: “I wish to have my head shaved. Go quickly to Guiyuan Monastery and ask the chief seat monk to come and give me the precepts.” She added: “Quickly burn sandalwood water and bathe me.” When the bathing and change of clothes were done, the chief seat monk arrived, shaved her head, and conferred the novice precepts. Having received the precepts, she lay down on her right side. Such was my mother's adherence to the precepts as she approached her end. On the morning of the twentieth she said: “Today I shall return to the West. Go quickly to Guiyuan Monastery and invite the masters to come and help me return to the West.” By eight o'clock the masters had arrived. Mother had them raise her up and seat her upright in a chair, her feet crossed in the lotus position, the precept certificate hung on her breast, a rosary in her hand. Mother said: “Bring a cloth pillow and place it behind my back.” Suddenly she said with joy: “Amitabha Buddha, together with all the sages, has come! Do not weep, but recite the Buddha's name with me.” Having said this, she herself recited the Buddha's name several times, and the assembly joined in reciting the Buddha's name. At ten o'clock my mother peacefully passed into stillness, as if entering meditative concentration. Such was my mother's serene return to the West at the very end.

The next day at ten o'clock, when she was placed in the jar, she sat upright exactly as before. On the day of cremation, those who came to see her off and recite the Buddha's name numbered more than a thousand, and all marveled at it as something rare. When the relics were gathered, the bones had a golden-yellow hue, and pale white śarīra were obtained, seven in all, large and small. Most rare of all: when my mother was placed in the jar she was wearing a grey haiqing robe, and after the cremation
four corners of the haiqing were picked out
turned blue
and along the edges the threaded beads were clustered in rows, snowy white and distinct; when two people pulled with both hands, they still would not break. In

, in the winter, Hankou was bombed everywhere, and the people's houses were all but destroyed, yet my mother's house alone was safe and unharmed. Looking back on my mother's predictions, not the slightest detail was off.
Recorded by her adoptive daughter Chen Lüyuan
(Original title: Laywoman Shao Xiangdao, Foreknowing the Time, Passes Away Seated Without Illness)

Lady Shao Xiangdao was a native of Pingchao in Nantong. In her youth she received her family's instruction and became well versed in propriety; in due course she married into a family of virtue and kept herself frugal and restrained. In middle age she suffered the loss of her husband and grew all the more straitened. At that time, among the people of Pingchao who had taken refuge with Master Yinguang, the teaching of the Pure Land was widely spread through the town. When the lady heard the Master's teaching, it was as if she awoke to something from a former life; she threw herself wholly into upholding it, shut herself away in the upper room of her house, and day and night recited the Buddha's name without cease. At first, when she practiced sitting cross-legged, she suffered greatly from pain in her feet, and weeping, she knelt before the image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and earnestly besought his blessing, and so she gradually became perfectly at ease in it.

Later, when the town suffered the violence of bandits and her house was utterly destroyed, she went out to live at the Tangzha Lay Buddhist Grove. Once, in a dream, she bowed to the Buddha, and the Buddha, commending her faith and practice, promised that in the dinghai year (

) on the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, at the hour of si, she would be reborn. She occasionally told others of this, and some did not believe her; in time it proved exactly as she had said: without illness, she passed away seated cross-legged, at the age of seventy-one. At the moment of death her face wore a smile, radiant as in life. On the eighth day of the first month of the wuzi year she was cremated; Master Huifen preached the Dharma and applied the torch, and white smoke rose into the sky and drifted west. More than ten solid relics were found, two of them shaped like flowers as large as a bowl, white in color, here and there showing red-brown.

Alas! The kalpa of slaughter in this age is cruel indeed. If a person can truly gather in his mind and take refuge in the Buddha, he will preserve his own life; how could weapons and soldiers harm him? Read the Universal Gateway chapter of the Lotus Sutra: all who call upon the power of Guanyin, even in the most perilous and evil circumstances, can be freed — the Buddha's word is surely not false. The lady dwelt day after day amid terror, yet devoutly upheld the Buddha's name and was utterly without fear, and in the end she went west in auspiciousness. Is she not a great mirror of compassion for a troubled age? I would that all who wish to escape this kalpa of slaughter might know together where to turn.
Hui Ru
(Original title: Laywoman Jiang Zhida Recites Aloud Three Times and Passes Away in Peace)

The laywoman's name was Huaiying. In her youth she received the instruction of the inner chambers and had not the least trace of cosmetic vanity. At twelve she suffered the loss of her father, and soon after the death of a younger brother. Her mother, née Chen, loved her all the more and kept her at her side morning and evening, never permitting her to be apart for a moment, and for this reason her studies were broken off. At sixteen she was betrothed to Huijia, and at twenty-three she came to his home as his wife. She managed the household wholly on the principle of diligence and thrift, and to the end of her life never employed a servant or maidservant. When Huijia took refuge under Master Yinguang of Lingyan, the laywoman had long been quietly practicing and silently transformed; she too asked to receive the same acceptance, and was given the Dharma name Zhida. To the end she regretted that she had never been able to follow Huijia and meet the old Master in person. Afterwards, whenever she heard that eminent monks and great virtuous ones at the Lay Buddhist Grove were expounding the three refuges, she would join in repentance and listen to the Dharma. She especially loved to read the vernacular exhortations to the world published by the Honghua Society, and never let them out of her hands. Her constitution was always weak, and with
, when the times grew troubled, anxiety and toil brought on illness; it would be treated and then recur, and she grew ever thinner and more frail.

Last year in the first month, the laywoman suddenly said to Huijia: “Birth and death are a grave matter, and impermanence is swift. Our daily practice is, to be sure, provision for rebirth, but the arrangements at the end are precisely the essentials for the journey west. I hope that from now on you will tell me more about this final matter.” Huijia then took up the Guidebook for the Final Rites, together with what concerns the end of life and what should be noted in assisting recitation, and explained it to her. Hearing it, the laywoman was filled with both sorrow and joy. In the end, because the chronic illness was deeply rooted, on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month, at the hour of xu, amid the sound of Buddha-recitation, she passed away in peace. Before her death the laywoman suddenly called Huijia and said: “Tomorrow morning you may invite the good and superior people to assist my recitation. And please set before my bed an image of the Buddha Who Receives and Guides, and the holy countenance of Guanyin.” After that, apart from murmuring the Buddha's name, she said nothing more. The next morning the good men and women of the Lay Buddhist Grove all came to assist the recitation. The laywoman was overjoyed, and from time to time joined her palms in reverence to the Buddha. As the sun was setting, her spirits were as usual, with no change at all; those assisting the recitation all said that her time of rebirth was still far off. But at the hour of xu, the laywoman suddenly recited aloud three times, following the assembly, “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” and passed away in peace. At that time her son Xinming and daughter Jieming were kneeling reverently at the bedside reciting the Buddha's name, and still did not know their mother had passed, but thought she was asleep. Only on the morning of the twenty-seventh did they bathe and change her, and she lay face upward, perfectly straight, her hands and feet level and straight, in no way crooked or bent. Until she was placed in the coffin, her whole body remained soft and her face as in life; those who saw it marveled as at something rare.
Mid-Autumn day of the guiwei year (
), Sun Huijia
(Original title: Laywoman Zeng Jingshi, Her Faith Sincere and Earnest, Chooses the Day of Her Rebirth)

The laywoman's original surname was Zeng; she married into the Zhu family and was given the Dharma name Jingshi. She was from Chahe in Huai'an. In her later years she took up the Buddhist faith, and for more than ten years ate vegetarian food on certain days only; three years before her death she began a full vegetarian diet. She was gentle by nature and skilled at needlework. She was a friend of my mother. My mother once said to Jingxin: “Old Mrs. Zhu recites the Buddha's name differently from ordinary people: every word and every phrase is clear and distinct, neither hurried nor slow, never slackening in cold or heat; in the future she will surely be born in the Land of Lotuses.”

, in the sixth month she contracted malaria, which in the seventh month turned to dysentery. In the last third of that month she said of herself that she was going to leave. My mother urgently tried to stop her, saying: “Tomorrow you cannot go. Among cultivators there is no such taboo, but by worldly custom the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month is a red-sand day, and for a dead person it is inauspicious for the household.” The laywoman answered: “Then I shall wait and go on the first day of the eighth month.” At that time her daughter and her grandson's wife were at her side and heard it all, and my mother answered, “Good.” The next day she was indeed without trouble, and that night there was heavy rain. On the morning of the day after, the first of the month, her grandson's wife came to our house to ask my mother to come and dress her. My mother went with her, and found the laywoman lying on her side on the sickbed, a palm-leaf fan in her hand, peaceful as if asleep. On drawing near to feel her breath, she had already long since passed away. She was seventy-four years old. Although her full vegetarian diet had been brief, her faith was sincere and earnest and her practice of Buddha-recitation deep, and so she attained such auspicious signs — ample proof of her rebirth.
, in the summer, Jiang Jingxin supplemented this account at the Bamboo Grove Buddha-recitation Hall.
Jiang Jingxin
(Original title: Laywoman Shi Jingyuan, Foreknowing the Time of Rebirth, Returns West Seated Upright)

The laywoman was a native of Dashi Village in Licheng Township, west of Lake Baoying in Jiangsu. She was forty-three when she parted forever from her husband. He left two sons and two daughters, all still young. The inheritance was not much; she tilled and weeded diligently herself, hiring no laborers, thus both saving expense and avoiding suspicion. She kept the household and raised the children with unsparing diligence and thrift. In her early years she followed outside teachings, and her original aspiration was not fulfilled. After her husband's death she at once took up a full vegetarian diet, and those she drew close to were all good people.

She had a second daughter who was endowed with good roots from former lives and unstained by worldly ties; she left home and became a nun with the Dharma name Nengcan. The laywoman had at first followed outside paths, and so had little understanding of the Buddhadharma. After Nengcan left home, she often went to the Haiyan Chan Grove to draw near to good teachers, and only then did she realize the errors of her earlier blind practice. She reproached herself for her poor conditions and for having let the days slip by. From this she took refuge in the Pure Land Dharma gate and received the name Jingyuan. Last year, when Layman Jiang Jingxin came to Li for the memorial gathering for Master Yinguang, Jingyuan joined the association with sincere faith. When she obtained the certificate of introduction from Master De, her joy was beyond words. Afterwards, reading the Honghua Monthly, the various records of rebirth, and the auspicious signs at the death of the local Wang Li Jingxiu, she praised them all the more frequently. Only then did her faith and vows become true and earnest, and her practice gain strength.

Last autumn her past karma came to fruition: the four elements fell out of harmony, and the illness dragged on for more than a hundred days. On the fourth day of the winter month, the auspicious day of Master Yinguang's second anniversary, monks and laypeople gathered in clouds at Haiyan Monastery, and just as the Buddhist service was brought to its perfect close, her second son, Shi Jiye, arrived and respectfully asked that recitation be assisted for the laywoman. The fourfold assembly, having chosen and agreed, at once brought the image of the Buddha Who Receives and Guides and went to her house, where they assisted the recitation according to the Dharma, hoping that if her lifespan were not yet exhausted she might quickly recover, and if it were exhausted she might at once be born in the West. Truly the Buddha's power is inconceivable: after three days of devout assistance by the great assembly, the laywoman's illness and pain vanished as if lost, her mind and spirits were clear and refreshed, altogether like a well person. She said: “For now I dare not put you all to further trouble; please come again to assist the recitation on the evening of the seventeenth.” Hearing this, the assembly followed her wish. When the Buddhist service for Amitabha's birthday was finished, the Great Master Longxiang, together with his disciple Nengcan and two or three fellow lotus friends, went at the appointed time to see her off. Master Long gave a detailed exposition, and the laywoman listened with palms joined; though her mouth did not speak, her mind was at peace, lucid and clear. The recitation continued until the early morning of the eighteenth, when amid the sound of Buddha-recitation she passed away seated upright, as if entering meditative concentration. She sat erect for three days, neither leaning nor tilting. Only after three days was she placed in a jar for burial, in preparation for future cremation, all in accordance with the Buddha's regulations, to help raise the grade of her lotus. Thus foreknowing the time and returning west seated upright, she was certainly reborn beyond doubt. For such an ordinary woman, had she not relied wholly on the Buddha's power for rebirth with her karma carried along, then even to make her understand any other Dharma gate would have been hard, much less to hope for such real benefit. Many in the world still harbor doubt and slander toward this Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; truly they are driven by karmic obstruction, and there is nothing I can do about it. I hope that those of discernment and good fellowship will awaken, have faith, and not let this supreme benefit be obtained by the foolish and ignorant alone.
Guang Yuan

blocks.text: 39. At Ease in Birth and Death

inline.s: (Original title: The Centenarian Mother of Ying Daosheng, At Ease in Birth and Death)

The mother of Ying Daosheng was a native of Xiying Village near Yaying Town in the eastern district of Yin County. She ate vegetarian food and recited the Buddha's name for nearly eighty years. At ninety-nine she could still sweep the ground and draw water outside the door, and at the age of one hundred and two she passed away without illness. At the end she sat upright facing west and instructed her children and grandchildren to recite the Buddha's name diligently. A rare fragrance filled the room and did not fade for three days.
Da Mu
(Original title: Laywoman Zheng Xina, Palms Joined and Smiling, Passes Away Seated in Peace)

Zheng Xina was a native of Quantu Town in Fuding County, Fujian. She took up the Buddhist faith in middle age, and her Dharma name was Bucai. Though little educated, she could remember most of the sutra meanings she heard. Straightforward by nature, whenever she saw a fault in others she would frankly admonish them, and so many were transformed by her; and she never slackened in doing good. After fifty she grew silent and spoke little, gave up meat and took a vegetarian diet, and devoted herself wholly to Buddha-recitation. In her later years she suffered from a swelling of the breast; though the pain was severe, she did not count it as suffering, and recited the Buddha's name all the more earnestly.
In the spring of the guihai year (

), she suddenly fell into a coma. On waking she told her family: “I traveled to a place like the Iron Enclosure described in the Kṣitigarbha Sutra. The sky was dim with no light, and the walls of the city were so high they could not be measured. Within the city were screams and shouts, and the clatter of iron chains was like tangled hemp; those who heard it were terrified and their hair stood on end. I feared I had fallen into hell. Then I asked myself: I recite the Buddha's name, so why have I fallen here? At once I roused the right mindfulness and single-mindedly called on the holy name of Amitabha; in a little while the city vanished and I gradually revived.” She also told her daughter: “Someone showed me that half a month from now, on a certain day at eight o'clock, I shall part from you all; at that time you must invite laymen and laywomen to come to the house and recite the Buddha's name.” On the day, the guests finished their recitation and said: “Her complexion and spirits are like those of an ordinary person; she may not necessarily depart tonight.” So they dispersed. At seven in the evening she went to the latrine; her daughter wanted to help her, but she said there was no need. When she had finished, she washed her hands herself, straightened her clothes, and climbed onto the bed, sitting upright and reciting the Buddha's name without cease. At half past seven she told her daughter to light the incense and candles, and a moment later, with palms joined and smiling, she sang out: “It has come!” After that there was no sound, and when her daughter looked closely she had already passed away seated in peace. Checking the time, it was exactly eight o'clock. She was eighty-two years old. A month after her burial, a certain Dharma master was invited to speak the Dharma for the cremation; as the fire was lit, three jeweled lotuses soared into the air and departed, as many people saw. In the third month of the wuxu year I was visiting a friend by night and happened to meet the laywoman's granddaughter, who told me of these events. Moved, I recorded them. A factual account by Hong Lingyuan of Wanchuan.
(Layman Hong Lingyuan was a native of Jiaxing and worked in Hangzhou. He was head of the Hangzhou poetry circle.)
(Original title: A Record of My Late Mother's Return to the West)

My mother was from Daishan. At nineteen she married my father and managed the household with diligence and thrift, toiling the year round. Only in the last three years did she follow my cousin's advice, take up a full vegetarian diet, revere the Buddha, and practice diligently; even in illness she never once slackened. In the beginning of the seventh month of 1947 the old lady fell ill, and when I came home to visit her, my cousin told me that she had already seen Amitabha Buddha and had also seen before the Buddha a heap of something bloody and mangled. My cousin said to her: “These are the creatures you killed in the past; you should repent and make vows to save them.” After my mother repented and made her vows, the sight vanished. On the morning of the third day my mother said again: “I see before the Buddha a lotus flower, very small in shape and green in color, with a dry texture; I have asked the Buddha to change it for another.” That evening my mother joined her palms at her breast and held them there for half an hour before lowering them, and said that she had seen the Buddha again, that the lotus had changed to yellow and was as large as a cartwheel. On the fourth day my mother again saw the Buddha and heard heavenly music, but because she heard the plaintive voices of her children, which stirred her affections, the Buddha suddenly vanished. Around three o'clock the next day my mother again saw pure light shining, but her body suddenly became gripped by unbearable pain. My cousin comforted her, saying: “This is the Buddha erasing your karmic obstacles; you must persevere in reciting the Buddha's name.” My mother nodded and agreed. At two o'clock the next day, with palms joined at her breast and amid the assisted recitation of the assembly, she passed west in peace. At eight the next morning, when she was bathed and changed, her whole body was soft and the crown of her head still warm; at nine, when she was placed in the coffin, her face suddenly took on a golden-yellow hue, solemn and kindly, and the crowd marveled. With such auspicious signs, her rebirth is assured.
Recorded by Fei Juanruo, 1947 (Note: idle passages were removed in the second edition)
(Original title: Laywoman Zheng Guoli Bows and Recites Day and Night to Attain Rebirth at an Appointed Time)

From childhood Laywoman Zheng Guoli followed her parents in the Buddhist faith. After marriage she took refuge under Master Miaoru of Baoqing and, according to her teacher's instructions, cultivated the Pure Land Dharma gate, single-mindedly upholding the six-character sacred name and seeking birth in the Western Pure Land.

The laywoman bore four sons and one daughter. Her husband did not believe in the Buddha, nor did her daughters-in-law support her faith, yet her own faith was firm and earnest, and she persisted in her vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation without ever slackening. When she was in her forties her husband died, and as none of her daughters-in-law was willing to support her, she set up her own household and devoted herself single-mindedly to quiet practice. Her daughter worked in Shenyang and built a room especially for her, inviting her there to live out her years. Three years later, learning that Master Miaoru had come to reside permanently in Baoqing, she moved back to Baoqing to draw near the Master and hear the Dharma, and following the Master's instruction she practiced with diligence. She revered the Buddha as though the Buddha were present: at every meal she first made an offering to the Buddha, and if she herself had leftovers she would cook fresh rice for the offering; for decades it was as one day, never once remiss.

The old laywoman lived alone, and there were many inconveniences in daily life. Sometimes when there was no one to carry water, she would catch rainwater to drink, and in winter she would melt snow. One day Laywoman Yue Guoli came to see her; seeing her in such hardship, she said to her: “You live alone in such a cold room, with frost on all four walls, and there is no end of difficulty in getting water or lighting a fire — have you not had enough of this wretched place?” The old laywoman said: “I pray every day, but the Buddha will not come to fetch me!” Yue Guoli said: “It is not that the Buddha will not come, but as I see it, you have not asked with a sincere heart!” These words struck her deeply. She thereupon repented with all her heart, resolved firmly to seek birth in the West, and kneeling before the images of the Three Sages made a great vow, saying: “Amitabha Buddha, Bodhisattva Guanyin, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta! Your disciple Guoli earnestly seeks birth in the West. I am seventy-five this year; even if I were due to live to eighty, I do not want it. I beg the Buddha to look down in compassion and bless me, to pity me above all and take me at once!” And so she bowed and recited day and night. Truly, sincerity works wonders and devotion brings response: on the fourth day she put her clothes in order and bathed, and early on the sixth day she locked the door and went to her son's house half a li away; entering, she sat down on the kang, took off her hat and face mask, and was reborn. The Amitabha Sutra says: “If for one day, or even up to seven days, one recites the Buddha's name single-mindedly without distraction, one will be received and guided by Amitabha Buddha and reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.” This is true and not false.

Why did she go to her son's house to be reborn? It turned out that the old laywoman had long before said to her fellow practitioner Laywoman Guozhen: “At the end I shall go to my son's house. If I died in my own home, with only myself there and no one to see it, people would say I died of coal-gas poisoning or of illness.” From the old laywoman's calm arrangements it is clear that her pure karma had long since ripened and that she foreknew her rebirth; her detachment at the end was a teaching given through her own body, an example set for those who practice Buddha-recitation. Everyone in the county who follows the path praised this affair with one voice, and I record it especially to strengthen the faith of those who recite the Buddha's name and seek birth in the West.
, Baoqing County, Heilongjiang — Yue Anxing
(Original title: The Mother of Layman Miaoyuan, Her Pure Karma Ripe, Is Reborn with Composure)

My mother was originally from Zhaoxing Shanjiang. Her family was poor from the start, and after she married she went with my father to Ningbo and lived in a small lane west of the lake. My mother was a devout Buddhist, kind by nature and full of sympathy for the poor; whenever she met someone in difficulty she would always help as best she could, and to beggars in particular she often gave rice and vegetables.

My mother bore five sons and two daughters. In the year she turned forty-five my father died. There was much to manage at home, and in order to recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly and cut off afflictions, she handed over the household finances and all such matters to my eldest brother and his wife. In

, my mother came to live in Hangzhou, reciting the Buddha's name as devoutly as ever. She still did what she could in the way of giving and merit. Though already advanced in years, she often helped the neighbors look after their children.
, when my mother was seventy-eight, she suddenly said to us: “I would best like to be reborn on the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha's birthday.” We paid it no attention. In

, my mother was eighty years old. On the eighth day of the fourth month of that year she changed into a new set of clothes; after lunch she rinsed with boiling water the rice bowl she used especially for her vegetarian meals, handed it to my eldest brother, and said half in jest: “Today is the eighth of the fourth month; I am returning this rice bowl to you, so that you cannot say I am unhygienic.” We still did not take it seriously, for at that time my mother was in good health and we had noticed nothing unusual about her. Around two in the afternoon, as always, she went to the neighbors' to look after their children. After she came back, before dusk, she sat herself in a rattan chair, joined her palms, and recited the Buddha's name. And in the very midst of that recitation she passed away seated in peace and was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. My wife and I had long ago, moved by my mother's faith and recitation, also taken refuge in the Buddhist gate. In the past we had heard many accounts of people reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss through single-minded Buddha-recitation, but this time we saw with our own eyes that our mother, free of all illness and pain, seated in a rattan chair reciting the Buddha's name, was peacefully reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Even more unforeseen was this: two years earlier my mother had merely wished to 'be reborn' on the eighth of the fourth month, the Buddha's birthday, and yet she was able to move the Buddha's grace to bless her and receive and guide her to rebirth. As the vow text says: “If at the end of life one knows in advance the time, is free of physical suffering

and the Buddha with all the sages, holding a golden platform in their hands, come to welcome me.” My mother truly had her wish fulfilled. Therefore I believe that if one only recites the Buddha's name sincerely, and as the Diamond Sutra teaches us, cultivates the practices of patience and giving with a mind that does not dwell on the five desires of the world, then at the end of life one will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
st month — recorded by Miaoyuan
(Original title: Strange Signs at My Maternal Grandmother's Rebirth)

My maternal grandmother, Old Mrs. Li, lost her father in childhood and lived in poverty. After she married, her husband took a concubine elsewhere. The old lady served her mother-in-law with great filial devotion, and bore with patience the arrogance of her sisters-in-law who relied on their wealth and power. Through her life she raised three orphaned children of close kin, treating them all as her own. Kind, gentle, and virtuous, her conduct surpassed that of ordinary people. Whenever things went against her, she would always yield and blame herself, saying: “My own virtue is not sufficient.”

When she was in her forties her husband fell into trouble and was imprisoned, and she then resolved to have faith in the Buddha. She and her daughter took up a vegetarian diet and recited the holy name, praying for the Buddha's blessing and asking that her husband be freed from his suffering soon. When he was released from prison, she at once set up a shrine hall and offered fresh flowers every morning; later, when circumstances changed, she fixed only half an hour of reciting the Buddha's name with her rosary at morning, noon, and evening. At sixty she lost her husband, and at seventy she lost a son, and her resolve to seek birth in the West grew ever more urgent. In her later years my mother brought her to our home to care for her, and though her body was weak she still recited the Buddha's name with her rosary at the three times of day without cease.

, my grandmother was already ninety-three. At the end of the fifth month she stopped eating and took only ice cream and fruit juice. Chinese and Western doctors were asked to examine her, and all said there was no illness, only the weakness of age that kept her from rising from bed. My mother and I and the others recited the Buddha's name every night, praying for blessing, and though her throat hurt she never ceased silently reciting the Buddha's name. On the night of the fourth day of the sixth month a rare fragrance suddenly filled the room, cool and richly fragrant, penetrating to the depths of one's being. Both I and my little daughter smelled it, and thinking the old lady was about to be born in the West, we woke the whole family; three minutes later the fragrance vanished. On the afternoon of the third day she had difficulty breathing and told us to recite the Buddha's name. Her children and grandchildren gathered around to assist, and two hours later she suddenly pointed her finger out the window (toward the west), raised her head half a foot from the pillow, and looked all around at everyone once (for seven or eight days she had been unable to turn over, and could not raise her head at all), as if bidding farewell; and when her head fell back on the pillow she had already passed away. When she pointed toward the west we saw the whole sky full of colored clouds, and though the sky was clear a fine drizzle fell for several minutes; we went on reciting the Buddha's name. At this point my father, afraid that the neighbors would hear and be affected, and that if too much time passed it would be hard to dress her, came in and told us to stop reciting. We had recited for more than two hours before changing her clothes; at that time her body was soft as in life, and as we lifted her to dress her, two strands of clear mucus as long as two feet and as thick as chopsticks flowed out (these are the jade chopsticks, the sign of one who passes away seated and attains the Way).

It was the height of summer, and the body lay in state for twenty hours without the slightest odor. Strangest of all, our home was on the outskirts of the city, where the neighbors kept pigs and chickens, so that ordinarily there were a great many flies; yet during the three days after my grandmother's rebirth, neither in our house nor in the neighbors' houses on either side was there a single fly. Everyone was amazed, and I have recorded it faithfully as above.
Recorded by Guoxu and Guoxin of Jiamusi

blocks.text: 45. A Rare Fragrance Fills the Room

inline.s: (Original title: A Record of My Kind Mother, of the Yue Family, née Wang, Who Recited the Buddha's Name and Was Reborn)

My mother was gentle by nature, diligent and thrifty, humble and respectful, and self-denying in her dealings with others. Though the family was poor she served her parents-in-law with filial devotion and raised her children well; her reputation for virtue and honesty was praised by the whole neighborhood.

My mother bore five sons and two daughters; I am the youngest. My second brother left home and became a monk, and my remaining three brothers and two sisters all died before my mother. My mother's lot may truly be called grievous.

After my second brother left home, my mother took refuge in the Three Jewels and came to believe deeply in the Pure Land. She kept a full vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha's name; though she could not read a single character, she could recite all the sutras and mantras from memory. At every meal she first made an offering to the Buddha, and if new vegetables or fruits came on the market she would not dare taste them before offering them to the Buddha. Even in illness she never slackened in bowing and reciting; for decades it was as one day. Because her circumstances were often adverse, every night she would bow in shame and repentance for her past karma and dedicate the merit to the Pure Land. She often blamed herself for being unable to save others, and so resolved to have a Western Ship made to deliver the kin and neighbors of her village.

In her youth and middle age my mother was often ill, but after she took refuge in the Buddha she practiced with diligence, and in old age her health became robust instead. In the autumn of her eighty-fifth year she showed slight illness, but her spirits were pure and clear, her body free of suffering, and she recited the Buddha's name as usual. I invited the laypeople of the shrine hall and our family members to assist the recitation together, when suddenly we heard my mother say: “A great lotus, a great lotus!” Old Layman Liu, who was assisting the recitation, sat cross-legged on the kang reciting the Buddha's name, and looking up he saw the Three Sages of the West appear in the sky, with Amitabha holding a lotus in his hand; he at once came down from the kang and prostrated in reverence. At that moment a rare fragrance filled the room, and all present smelled it; my mother became still and motionless, and followed the Buddha to rebirth. It was eight o'clock in the evening of the fifth day of the ninth month. The next morning her face was as in life and her limbs were soft, and the crown of her head was still warm when touched. Laymen Cao and Han, who took part in the encoffining, also smelled the rare fragrance. Such were the manifest auspicious signs of her rebirth.
Respectfully recorded by her youngest son, Yue Wenshan, who attended her to the end
(Original title: My Grandmother Shen Minghui, Blind in Eye but Clear in Mind, Foresees Her Own Funeral)
My grandmother, of the Wang family, whose Dharma name was Minghui,
, on the seventh day of the tenth month, at Badaogou in Dandong, Liaoning, knew in advance that the time had come and was reborn in the West, at the age of eighty-two.

My grandmother was meek and sparing of words, both wise and filial. She had three sons and two daughters, and the household prospered. At forty-five she lost her husband, and her eldest son and eldest daughter died one after another; the old lady, overcome with grief and bitterness, went blind in both eyes. At sixty-two her youngest son married, and her daughter-in-law was most filial, often supporting the old lady to the temple to bow to the Buddha and hear the Dharma. From that time the old lady suddenly felt that life had hope, and she took refuge in the Three Jewels, received the five precepts, kept a full vegetarian diet, and recited the Buddha's name.

Because her eyes could no longer see, my grandmother could not burn incense or bow in worship, and so she single-mindedly upheld the ten-thousand-virtue sacred name of Amitabha Buddha. Having passed through all the vicissitudes of life, she knew well that the joys and sorrows of the world are passing clouds, and that only seeking birth in the West and escaping birth and death is the great matter. Therefore her faith was firm and her vow earnest, her reverence and sincerity supreme; she laid down all conditions and single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name. Whether the fires of war were at her eyebrows or she was cut off from grain and drink, she paid no heed at all to favorable or adverse circumstances, asked nothing of family affairs and nothing of her children and grandchildren, and was unmoved by joy or anger in her heart — only single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name, twenty years as one day.

In 1952, one day she said to her daughter-in-law: “I can still live five years; now I must take my Buddha-recitation in hand.” After that she recited not only by day but every night until past midnight. On the morning of the first day of the fifth month in 1956 she said to her daughter-in-law: “I shall die this year on the seventh day of the tenth month. Eight monastics will recite sutras for me. Our family will give the masters forty yuan. Thirty people will wear mourning at the funeral. Our family will have both white rice and white flour, and food left over for relatives and friends. Everything except the coffin I have already seen.” Two days later she said the same thing again to her second daughter, and her grandchildren also heard it. Yet not one person believed it. For by 1956 in Dandong no one wore mourning garments at funerals any longer, much less invited monks to recite sutras; and besides, at that time one laborer in the family had to support a household of seven, and they could not even eat their fill of cornmeal — how could they dare imagine having white rice and white flour to entertain relatives and friends?

Half a year passed. In the beginning of the tenth month the old lady fell ill, and the doctor diagnosed heart and kidney failure, beyond treatment. In the last few days, as she lay dying, her mind was clear, she had no suffering, and she showed no sorrow at parting. On the sixth she told her daughter-in-law to send a telegram calling her son home, and asked that the masters from the temple be invited to recite Guanyin for her. At three in the afternoon she wanted to change into her final grave clothes, but her children and grandchildren, seeing her spirits clear and her breath easy, refused to dress her in them. So she sat up herself and put on the clothes. When they wanted to carry her, she insisted on walking herself, and supported by my second uncle and my younger brother Jin she walked to the funeral bed set up in the outer room and sat down on it sideways; they helped her lie down comfortably, and she asked the masters to recite the Rebirth Mantra for her, and said to brother Jin, “Tell me when your father comes back.” A little later my elder sister Zhihua arrived and burst into tears as soon as she entered the room. Grandmother said, “Do not cry; this is a good thing; hurry and recite the Buddha's name!” She herself closed her eyes and recited. By nine in the evening her pulse gradually weakened, and my second uncle gave her a cardiac stimulant injection, hoping to wait for my father's return. Near ten, grandmother said: “The heavenly gate has opened, and I hear the sound of drums and music.” At half past ten my father arrived and knelt at once before the funeral bed; grandmother's lips moved but she could not speak, her head turned a few times to left and right, and then she quietly passed away.

At this point the old master of his own accord told his disciples to return to the temple, and invited six bhikshunis to come and assist the recitation together. Afterwards my second uncle prepared eight red envelopes (five yuan each, forty yuan in all) as offerings to the masters. (My second uncle had not come home for years and knew nothing at all of what my grandmother had said.) Just then it happened that a distant relative had moved from Shandong to Dandong to open a shop for renting out goods; it had not yet opened for business when this funeral came along, and he of his own accord brought a coffin canopy and mourning shirts. When everyone put them on and counted, there were exactly thirty. The children and grandchildren living apart sent rice, flour, and vegetables to entertain the relatives and friends. All of this matched the old lady's predictions exactly.

The old lady laid down all conditions, practiced with diligence, and single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name seeking birth in the Pure Land. Not only did she foreknow the time five months in advance and foretell her funeral arrangements without the slightest error; not only was she free of physical suffering and free of greed and delusion in her mind, but she could even direct her own assisted rebirth in person (ordinarily she had no idea at all what assisted rebirth was, nor had she ever seen or heard of it). The children, grandchildren, relatives, and friends who heard her predictions with their own ears and saw the facts with their own eyes were all amazed and deeply moved. This is enough to prove that the Pure Land Dharma gate is the most direct of the direct: one need only believe deeply, vow earnestly, and practice vigorously. Ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go — not one is left behind. Truly it is a Dharma gate of special distinction. I hope that all fellow lotus friends will firmly believe in the Pure Land, single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, and together be born in the Land of Lotuses.
Recorded by Guoxu of Jiamusi, Heilongjiang —
nd month
(Original title: Laywoman Yang Qinfang, with Rich Rare Fragrance, Is Welcomed by Amitabha)
Laywoman Yang Qinfang was a native of Shenjiamen Town in Putuo County, Zhejiang, and lived in the Xida neighborhood committee. She was born in
and passed away in
, in the
th month, on the

th day, at the age of seventy-seven. The laywoman at first did not believe in the Buddha. At seventy-five her son died of a sudden illness, and moved by the impermanence of human life she resolved to eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha's name. Whenever she recited, her voice was earnest and urgent, and the neighbors all heard it. From her first resolve to her rebirth, less than two full years had passed.
, at the end of the

th month, she caught a cold, and on the fourth day of the tenth month took to her bed. She saw a white lotus bud fall upon her breast, and at that time her family all smelled a rich rare fragrance in the room, which dispersed only after half a day. In her illness the laywoman had no suffering at all. On the
th month, on the

th day (the twenty-fourth of the ninth lunar month), toward evening she suddenly instructed her family: “Hurry and assist my recitation; I am going with Amitabha Buddha.” Her family asked, “Do you see the Buddha?” She answered, “I see him.” Then she joined both palms in the gesture of reverencing the Buddha. Her family wanted to invite pure companions to assist the recitation, but the laywoman stopped them, saying: “Do not go calling people at night.” Then she said loudly: “Move aside a little; the Buddha has come.” Next she traced her son's name with her finger. Her younger sister had believed in the Buddha for many years, and seeing this, at once spoke to her solemnly: “Now that the hour of your death has come, you should set your mind wholly on the West and thereby escape birth and death. You must lay down all conditions and give no thought to either friend or foe; only recite Amitabha Buddha and follow Amitabha Buddha. Above all, do not think of your son.” The laywoman nodded in assent. At that time many people in the room recited in unison: “Namo Amitabha Buddha!” The laywoman silently recited along. Before long she passed away smiling. It was twenty minutes past seven in the evening. Twenty-four hours after her death her whole body was soft and the crown of her head still warm, proving beyond doubt that she had been reborn.
Zhou Jiajun
(Original title: Following in My Mother-in-Law's Footsteps)

My mother-in-law always lived in a small room in the old family house at Bajiu Camp in the county town of Linhai. She was amiable and kindly, good and benevolent, and on excellent terms with the neighbors. I have been married to her only son, old Zhang, for thirty years. We both work in Hangzhou, and sometimes during the Spring Festival and other holidays I go home with my husband to visit my mother-in-law. We would buy chicken, fish, and other meat dishes for her to eat, but she always gave them to us and ate only vegetables such as pickles and bean curd herself; at that time I thought my mother-in-law was simply too frugal. She usually spoke very little, and did not chat with us much about worldly matters; toward her two little grandsons she was also quite detached, only quietly moving her lips a little to herself (at that time I did not know she was reciting the Buddha's name).

was also the last time I saw my mother-in-law. I noticed that in her basket were incense, candles, a rosary, and the like, and only then did I learn that she was an old woman who recited the Buddha's name single-mindedly. From this I realized that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down she was constantly reciting the holy name “Amitabha Buddha.”
In '87

, my mother-in-law was eighty-two. In the middle of the twelfth month a long-distance call suddenly came from Linhai: “Your mother is gravely ill; tell old Zhang to come back at once.” My husband went back to the old home and found his mother in fine spirits, with no sign of illness at all; yet she said to her son in earnest: “My time in this world is nearly up.” And she laid out her funeral arrangements in good order. Her son, seeing that his mother's health was indeed as good as ever, thought it was the groundless fretting of old age and talking nonsense, and merely said a few words of comfort. Because he had come in haste and had made no arrangements for work at his office, he planned to take the first bus back to Hangzhou the next day; his mother nodded in agreement and told him to go to bed early.

The next morning the neighbor Sister Hua hurried to the guesthouse and said to old Zhang: “I saw that your mother's door was not closed, so I took a bowl of porridge into the room to offer her, but to my surprise your mother was sitting on the bed and had already passed away.” My husband rushed home and saw his mother sitting on the bed, her clothes neatly arranged, her complexion ruddy, her expression serene — a very picture of 'the auspicious signs of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.'
In '88

I too began to believe in the Buddha, knowing perfectly well that single-minded Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth in the West and escape from birth and death. At that time I always thought that Buddha-recitation was the path of illiterate vegetarian laymen and laywomen, that I, having attended university and being educated, could not be like the old women who burn incense and recite the Buddha's name, but should strive for something higher. So I planned to practice the superior Dharma gate of Chan, and I read books on Chan and studied the recorded sayings of the ancient virtuous ones. But having no clear teacher and not applying myself in real practice, I only let the days slip idly by. Seeing before my eyes my mother-in-law's freedom from physical suffering, her mind free of greed, her foreknowledge of the time, and the true-to-life auspicious signs of her rebirth, sounded a warning bell for me again and again; and the Essential Selections from the Collected Writings urged, encouraged, and guided me to practice the Pure Land Dharma gate. Master Yinguang's instructions pointing to the Pure Land — such as “For ordinary beings in the Dharma-ending age who wish to realize the fruit of sagehood, all who do not rely on the Pure Land are wholly deluded” — were truly like a bright lamp dispersing my ignorance. Now I deeply believe that Buddha-recitation by holding the name embraces all three capacities, and I am resolved to follow in my mother-in-law's footsteps: without pride or impatience, with a sincere heart and perseverance, advancing toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Chen Peiyou
(Original title: Laywoman Xiang Huanqing — The Inconceivable Merit of Assisting Recitation)

My mother's surname was Xiang and her given name Huanqing; she was the eldest daughter of Mr. Xiang Shiyuan, a senior figure in the historical and journalistic circles of Zhejiang. She was gentle and generous by nature, but influenced by the new learning she held no religious belief, and often argued with my father over questions of faith.

, in the summer, because of the war the whole family moved back to their native place. In autumn my father came down with acute enteritis. In the countryside doctors and medicine were scarce, and my father's abdominal pain was unbearable; he told my mother to beseech the blessing of Guanyin. My mother had never believed in the Buddha, yet now, quite unlike her usual self, she washed her hands, burned incense, and devoutly prayed to the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion. Truly, a sincere heart works wonders: all at once a rare fragrance filled the room, and my father's pain was cured without any medicine. Having personally received this response, my mother turned from opposing the Buddha to believing in him.

, in the third month, my mother, already seventy-six, suffered from blood in the stool and abdominal pain. Long treatment brought no cure, and she was transferred to the provincial hospital, where the diagnosis was advanced intestinal cancer, beyond treatment; she was told to go home and rest quietly. We children nursed her with great care, and at the same time urged her, saying: “Human life is impermanent, and where there is birth there must be death; hurry and recite the Buddha's name and seek birth in the West.” When in pain my mother could recite with all her heart, but when the pain eased she would again think of worldly trifles. So I urged her on the one hand, and on the other recited sutras before the Buddha, beseeching the Buddha's blessing.

So it went for many days. Seeing that my mother's illness had lasted long, that her body grew weaker day by day, and that she had lately stopped taking food or drink, we began on the twenty-third day of the ninth month to assist her recitation at her bedside. By noon of the twenty-fifth she said: “I am going. Take down the mosquito netting; I want to be clean. Let me relieve myself, so that I may go to see the Buddha fresh and clean.” We did everything as she asked, and continued assisting without cease; we saw my mother's lips move slightly as she recited along with us. At midnight she said: “You are all working too hard (at that time more than ten family members, lotus friends, and my mother's students were assisting the recitation) — go and rest a while.” Seeing that her mind was perfectly clear, we left two people behind and played an audiotape to assist the recitation.
The next day (

th), at four in the morning, seeing my mother's breathing grow faint, we called everyone up to assist the recitation, and I said to her in a loud voice: “Mother, hurry and recite along with us; beseech the Buddha to receive and guide you, and be reborn in the West.” She nodded once and her lips moved slightly, and at four-thirty she passed away in peace. We assisted the recitation until ten-thirty, when my wife felt her; the whole body had gone cold, but the crown of her head was still warm. This was unquestionably birth in the West.

We went on reciting the Buddha's name until five o'clock on the twenty-seventh, a full twenty-four hours, and only then bathed and changed her. By then her whole body was cold, all her joints were soft, and her face was as in life. On the twenty-ninth we bade farewell to the body at the crematorium, and her face was still as in life. The people at the crematorium said: “We did not apply any makeup to her; people like this are very rarely seen.” After the cremation there were many hard, snow-white crystals like coral in her ashes.

Looking back over my mother's final days and the period of assisted recitation, there are several points worth recording: 1. The physicians said the cancer cells had spread throughout her body and predicted that she would suffer greatly at the end; yet during the assisted recitation my mother had only slight pain that she could endure, and in the last ten hours before her death there was no pain at all. 2. Several hours before her death, many family members dreamed that my mother was about to be reborn and that they must hurry to see her off. 3. Many of the family members who took part in the assisted recitation found that after leaving the scene, whether on the road or at their workplaces, the sound of the Buddha's name filled everywhere; even at the funeral the sound of wind in the mountain trees became the sound of the Buddha's name. This proves that the merit of assisting recitation benefits both self and others and is inconceivable. Had my mother not had the assembly to assist her recitation, she would not have been so peaceful at the end; this too must be the good roots, blessings, and conditions she planted in past lives.
Respectfully recorded by Lin Kezhi of Linhai
(Original title: Old Mrs. Pan, Doing Good and Reciting the Buddha's Name, Gives Off Fragrance at the End)

Old Mrs. Pan was already ninety-eight years old, and lived in Jibao Village, Liangshui Township, Baoqing County, Heilongjiang. At fifty she took refuge in the Three Jewels, kept a full vegetarian diet, revered the Buddha, and quietly cultivated the Pure Land. In the last few days before her death, fragrance emanated from her whole body, and she was reborn in auspiciousness…

All her life the old lady was good and compassionate, sacrificing herself for others and reckoning neither gain nor loss; toward orphans and poor families in particular she showed redoubled care. She was always strict with herself and never spoke of others' faults, and she also urged others not to discuss people's failings; but the good deeds of others she praised everywhere. The neighbors all called her “a great good woman such as cannot be found.”

The old lady could not only do what others could not do, but also endure what others could not endure. In the year she turned eighty, one of her sons and one of her daughters died one after another within forty days. Such unimaginable grief — how could an ordinary person bear it? Yet the old lady's practice of Buddha-recitation was deep, and her mind and body were settled; she showed no great grief, but even urged her relatives to restrain their sorrow, while she herself practiced all the more diligently, reciting the Buddha's name without cease whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Not only did she practice diligently herself, she also led others in reciting the Buddha's name and cultivating, broadly forming good connections, single-mindedly protecting the Dharma, and seeking birth in the Pure Land.

On the morning of the eighth day of the eleventh month in 1991, wafts of fragrance drifted through the old lady's room, to everyone's amazement. At that time there were seven outsiders in the house — colleagues of her grandson and a doctor — and with the family members more than ten people in all. Apart from her grandson's wife, whose sense of smell was impaired by rhinitis, all the rest smelled the fragrance, which was rich and delightful. Everyone at once went from room to room searching for the source of the fragrance. In the old lady's room they found that something about her was slightly amiss, and they hurried to change her clothes; before the buttons were done up, the old lady had peacefully returned to the West. Because the old lady's good deeds had moved people over the years, five generations of her family had all taken refuge in the Three Jewels, believed in the Buddha and recited his name, and at the end the whole family assisted her recitation and chanted sutras for her rebirth in the West. Even by the next day the old lady's joints were still soft, her face as in life, and a rare fragrance filled the hall, drifting in waves, so that even the neighbors smelled it.

In her life the old lady did good and accumulated virtue, and practiced with diligence. Not only did she live to the great age of ninety-eight, free of illness and suffering, but she needed no one to attend her in daily life. At seventy she once saw the Buddha's light, and people many times smelled fragrance about her. A few years ago she told her daughter: “My Buddha-recitation no longer wanders off the thought.” Her peaceful passing and the fragrance that filled her body and other auspicious signs show that Old Mrs. Pan's pure karma had long since been accomplished. The children, grandchildren, relatives, and friends who witnessed these facts were all amazed and deeply moved. The merit of Buddha-recitation benefits both self and others and is inconceivable; the Pure Land Dharma gate is truly the most direct of the direct, and the old lady's attainment of joyful great liberation is proof of it.
Recorded by Guoxu of Jiamusi
(Original title: Laywoman Cai Chixi, Diligent in Buddha-Recitation, Foreknows the Time)
At Tianwang Monastery in Jiaocheng, Ningde, Fujian,
-year-old laywoman Cai Chixi foreknew the time and passed away in peace on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month.

The laywoman had good roots from former lives. At ten she began to keep a morning vegetarian diet, and at fifty she took up a full vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation, practicing with diligence: day and night her hand never left her rosary and her mouth never left the Buddha. To all good works — printing and distributing sutras, building temples, releasing living creatures, and delivering the dead — she gave her utmost and delighted in helping, giving as conditions allowed.

On the eighteenth day of the seventh lunar month she showed slight illness and stopped eating and drinking. Her grandson's wife Saibi, fearing that at her age something might happen, asked at her bedside whether there was still time to summon her daughter Guanghui from elsewhere to see her. The old lady answered: “Rest easy, there is time; I leave on the twenty-fourth of this month.” When her daughter Guanghui returned on the twentieth, she and fellow practitioners and relatives assisted the recitation day and night, and the old lady recited along with the assembly, her spirits clear and bright. On the twenty-fourth she lay in the auspicious posture, and within the last half hour she joined her palms three times; the last time she clearly recited “Amitabha Buddha” in a loud voice, and was reborn. The time was twenty minutes past seven in the evening of the twenty-fourth. After twenty-four hours of recitation her countenance was as in life, and when her clothes were changed her body was soft as cotton. Truly she foreknew the time, and her rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is beyond doubt.

At six o'clock on the second day of the eighth month she was cremated. It had rained heavily for days on end, day and night without stopping; but during the cremation and the gathering of the ashes, a brilliant sun suddenly broke through the black clouds and shone upon the cremation kiln. After the ashes were gathered the heavy rain resumed without cease. From the ashes were picked out many śarīra of pale red, green, white, purple, and black, of various sizes, as well as pieces like white coral and pale yellow ones. The more than one hundred members of the fourfold assembly who took part in the cremation, seeing these auspicious signs, were all deeply moved to admiration. It was the first miracle of birth in the West seen in Ningde since Liberation.
Recorded by Lin Jiayuan of Nanda Road,
, eighth month, fourth day
(Original title: Laywoman Xi Rongzhen, Six Years of Buddha-Recitation, Fulfills Her Vow of Rebirth)
My mother, Xi Rongzhen, lived in Minsheng Village, Xigemu Township, Jiamusi. In
she took refuge in the Three Jewels in the autumn and devoted herself to the Pure Land. On the third day of the third month of
she was reborn as she had wished, at the age of sixty-nine.

Her maternal family was poor and bitter. My mother married into the Ma family at twenty. Her mother-in-law and her sister-in-law died early, leaving a young brother-in-law, a young nephew, and the six children of our own family; my mother raised them all with equal care. My grandfather was old and paralyzed in bed, and my mother tended him in eating, drinking, and relieving himself without any look of distress. The household was large and life was hard; my father often lost his temper, but my mother never quarreled with him, and toward relatives and neighbors she was always ready to take the worst of it and endure insult. Relatives and friends all praised her as both virtuous and filial.

My mother had deep good roots from former lives and revered the Buddha from childhood; twenty years before, she had taken up a full vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation, and in the autumn of '85 she received the three refuges and five precepts, and following her teacher's instruction recited the Buddha's name with utmost sincerity, seeking birth in the West. Her daily task was ten thousand recitations of the Buddha's name; in the morning she bowed to Guanyin and then upheld the Great Compassion Mantra, and in the evening she bowed to Amitabha, never breaking the practice whether busy or at leisure. Her faith in seeking birth in the West was true and her vow earnest, all the more so in her last two years.
