Many times she made the vow: “I cannot speak well or preach, and I cannot save others; I only beg the Buddha's compassionate blessing to let me be reborn in accordance with the Dharma, so that when people see it they will have faith and recite the Buddha's name, and a whole group of them will be saved.” She told her children: “When I die, do not weep; recite the Buddha's name well for me. To see me off to rebirth is true filial devotion.” To her eldest daughter she said: “You have stability of mind; you must take the lead well and guide everyone in seeing me off.”

On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month in 1991 my mother suddenly had a heart attack and showed signs of danger. Her daughter-in-law was frightened, but she said: “Do not be afraid; I shall not die this year. I cannot go until I have been to the temple next year on the nineteenth day of the second month to take leave of my master and fellow practitioners.” A few days later she indeed recovered. On the twelfth day of the second month this year she said to her granddaughter: “I want to go and stay a few days at each of your aunts' homes; this trip of mine will be my last.” She stayed two days at each of her daughters' homes, and on the eighteenth day of the second month she went to the temple and said to her master and fellow practitioners: “I have come to take leave of my master and friends.” Everyone thought she was joking and paid no attention. In the city she attended a Dharma assembly for four days in a row, walking a great deal every day, and her health was excellent.

At six in the evening on the third day of the third month her younger cousin came to visit. In the middle of their conversation she slowly collapsed on the kang and could not speak. While everyone bathed and changed her, they recited the Buddha's name aloud to assist her; her children all hurried there to see her off, and each with utmost sincerity besought the Buddha to receive and guide her. Her third daughter said to her again and again: “Mother, you must lay down all conditions, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and beseech the Buddha to receive and guide you.” She beckoned with her hand for something; my father thought she wanted to speak and took her hand, but she drew it back and pointed again toward where the rosary was. When the rosary was given to her, she counted the beads with one hand and beckoned farewell with the other. The family turned on the tape recorder, and she gently patted her chest in time with the rhythm of the recitation for more than ten minutes, showing no sign of pain. By half past four the next morning there was a little white froth at her mouth and her breathing was rapid. At this point her fifth daughter, Xiuxia, saw a wisp of white smoke rise slowly from the top of her cap, as thick as a little finger and nearly half a foot high. When she looked again, her mother's breathing had stopped. Everyone continued assisting the recitation for eight hours, and when they touched the crown of her head it was still warm. Three days later her body was still very soft, the muscles of her face could still be moved up and down, and her complexion was as in life. After the cremation, one third of her ashes showed three colors: white as pure snow; blue as indigo; green as emerald — bright and gorgeous, truly rarely seen. On the night of the first seventh day, her third son-in-law Runfan dreamed that my mother came drifting in dressed in black; when she reached him the garment turned to white gauze, her face was that of a child, her hair black, and she stood barefoot on a lotus. Runfan said: “So you too keep up with the fashions, old lady?” She said: “In my place there is whatever one wants; if you cultivate well you can come too.” When he woke, her third son-in-law was deeply moved; he resolved to believe in the Buddha, gave up alcohol, and kept a vegetarian diet for forty-nine days for my mother's sake.

Edified by these auspicious signs — our mother’s foreknowledge of the hour of her passing, her peaceful end, the warmth at the crown of her head, her body staying soft as in life, and the rest — several dozen relatives and friends who had not believed in the Buddha all knelt down and joined in the recitation of the Buddha’s name; many have already of their own accord made offerings to the Buddha and come to believe!
Truly, by the extraordinary grace of the Three Jewels, our mother’s great vow — to manifest auspicious signs throughout her life and thereby save others — has been brought to fulfillment!
Respectfully recounted by Ma Xiuxian, Xiukun, Xiuxia (holder of the five precepts), Xiufen, Xiufang, and Shichao (holder of the three refuges), and others.
(Original title: The Xu Family’s Grand-Aunt Goes to the Pure Land Carrying an Umbrella)

My family lives in Shangyang Village, Dongtianmu Township, Lin’an County, Zhejiang Province. Our neighbor Auntie Xu had a grand-aunt in her household who was devout in her faith in the Buddha. Whenever she went to a monastery to worship the Buddha, whether the weather was clear or rainy, she would always carry an umbrella and place it beneath the Buddha’s seat; after worshipping and burning incense, she would carry the umbrella home with her and keep it in a clean place in the house. When her time came, she was free of illness and pain, reciting the Buddha’s name single-mindedly without pause. Suddenly thunder rolled and rain poured down in torrents, yet within the house the light was golden and radiant, and the grand-aunt passed away peacefully amid the sound of the Buddha’s name. But the thunder would not abate, nor would the rain cease. Then the family remembered the umbrella the grand-aunt had carried on her pilgrimages to the mountains, and in haste they placed it before the old woman’s spirit tablet and burned it. A wonder occurred: the umbrella was burned entirely to ash, yet its whole form remained unbroken; suddenly there came a report, a gust of wind blew the umbrella upright, and slowly at first, then swiftly, it drifted westward with the whirlwind. Everyone said that the old lady had gone to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss carrying her umbrella.
Recorded by Nian Dao,
in the year
, the 11th
month.

blocks.text: A Report Sent Back After Rebirth in the West

inline.s: Translation:

Layman Zhu Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also known by the courtesy name Xingwu, was a man of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine, and in his leisure often cultivated the method of quiet sitting.

, on the advice of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he changed to the practice of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate and was quite diligent. The following summer he happened to catch a cold and lay weary in bed. Wang went to visit him and urged him to go to the outskirts of the city, the renowned Yunqi Monastery, to rest and recover while listening to the lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and accompanied him there. Returning after ten days, Wang visited again and found him suffering from diarrhea as well. He urged him, saying: You are a physician and can diagnose and treat yourself, but now that the illness has come to this, I fear your understanding and judgment may be wanting in accuracy; why not summon another physician for a consultation, so that you may recover sooner? The layman said: No, no. After you went to hear the sutra, there was one night when I saw Amitabha Buddha in a dream, and I joyfully made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating with the five limbs to the ground, I saw the Great One in White, his body likewise tall, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing his robe might brush against me, he lifted the hem with his hand and floated gently past my side, his smile brimming with warmth. Observing his manner, he seemed about to receive me and lead me to the West; what need is there to summon another physician for a further diagnosis? Before long the illness grew worse; knowing his time had come, he entrusted Wang with inviting a bhikshu to his home to assist in recitation, and thus on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month, he passed away seated in lotus, reciting the Buddha’s name.

When Wang, on his behalf, invited the bhikshu to come and recite the Buddha’s name, the layman said of himself: I will surely depart tonight. Wang, half-doubting and half-believing, made an agreement with him, saying: At present, rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation is attested only by the auspicious signs at death; after rebirth in the West there is no other conclusive proof. If you attain rebirth in the West this time, you must come in person to report and prove the truth of it; remember this most earnestly. The layman said: How shall I report? Wang said: Have you not seen the record in the books of Que Gongze’s reporting after rebirth in the West? The layman said: That manner of reporting requires nothing less than the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I do it? I can only report through a dream. Wang said: That is fine too, so long as it proves it.

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Laymen records: “Que Gongze was a man of Hebei. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty he lived in Luoyang, his life leisured and joyful, free and unconstrained, and he regularly recited the Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma. After Que Gongze passed away, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery in Luoyang. When evening came and the sutra was being recited, a voice was suddenly heard in the air. The assembly looked up and saw a person whose form and countenance were bright and beautiful, who said: ‘I am Que Gongze. I have already been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and now, together with all the superior ones, I have come here to hear the sutra.’ Everyone in the hall saw this sight. There was a man named Wei Shidu who lived in Ji Commandery and was a disciple of Que Gongze; his mother often offered vegetarian meals to the monks. That same day, toward noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed right before Wei’s mother. Examining it closely, they saw that it was the very bowl Que Gongze had always used, and it was filled with rice whose fragrance filled the whole hall. Everyone who ate the rice from the bowl went seven days without hunger. The eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Daolin praised this event without end.”
[Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma] Translated by Dharmarakṣa in the Western Jin, it is the earliest translation of the Lotus Sutra.

After he passed away seated, in accordance with the Buddha’s rule he was placed in the coffin and then cremated, and his ashes were placed in a stupa. When all was done, it was already mid-June. Time flew like a galloping colt; in the blink of an eye July, August, and September had all passed, and there was no news at all. I secretly thought that the layman had not attained rebirth in the West, or that, having attained it, he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement to report back had not been fulfilled. But unexpectedly, on the last day of the eleventh month (the end of the eleventh lunar month), Wang, suffering from a toothache, lay resting in bed in broad daylight. In a daze, he saw the layman ascend the stairs and sit on a stool. (Original note: Because Wang recited the Buddha’s name, his bed was placed beside the Buddha hall upstairs.) His build was as before; he wore a half-new flat cap and clothes that seemed recently washed, all clean, with a radiance shining in. His expression was bright and lively, his face like a full moon, and his skin delicate and tender like a handsome boy of eight. Compared with the face full of whiskers, the fallen teeth and wrinkled face of his lifetime, he seemed another person entirely. Had Wang not been his most intimate friend, knowing him to the utmost, and moreover a childhood companion, he would almost have failed to recognize him. For such beauty of bearing was something the layman had never possessed in all his life.

At the sight, Wang was overjoyed and astonished beyond measure; in his incoherence he asked abruptly: “Ah! So you have truly been reborn in the West! Otherwise, how could you have such a bearing? You yourself do not know that your face is now completely that of a tender, handsome boy. In life you lost more than half your teeth, and I once invited you to Songzhu Ju to have them set — do you still remember?” The layman said: “Yes, yes. I have come specially to tell you and report.” Wang said: “The West is a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, no easy place to reach, yet you have actually arrived.” He answered: “My having attained it is entirely through the power of faith and vows.” Wang said: “How could you get here?” He answered: “Very easily — with a single thought one is there; in time you will know it yourself. When one wishes to come, one looks toward the darkness; when one wishes to go, one looks toward the brightness; that is all.” Wang asked again: “Have you seen the Buddha?” He answered: “Not yet.” “Why could you not see him?” “My meritorious practice is too shallow; I have not been born into the pond of seven jewels.” “If not born into the pond of seven jewels, where were you born?” The layman sighed deeply: “Alas, the place where I was born is merely the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderland.”

Before the conversation was finished, Wang Jueru suddenly woke up. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that Layman Zhu's speech and bearing, radiant and full of auspicious marks, stood vividly before his eyes — utterly unlike any inverted dream. He rose and looked at the clock; it was just past five in the afternoon. A month later, with winter ended and spring returned, Wang Jueru chanced to meet Wang Nengzhi, a relative by marriage of Layman Zhu. The moment they met, Wang Nengzhi said to Wang Jueru in haste: “How strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came to talk with me several times, saying that he had already been reborn in the borderland of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and had come specially to report. I have long wished to visit you and tell you all this.” Wang Jueru eagerly asked what Layman Zhu had said. Wang Nengzhi related: “The moment I saw him, I asked, ‘Where have you been these past few months, and why did you not come back sooner to report?’ Layman Zhu replied, ‘I was detained for a long while in the underworld on a certain matter. It was only by the grace of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who sent someone to escort me, that I could steal the time to come.’ He went on, ‘When I was alive, I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — have you practiced in accordance with them? In the past you ran a restaurant and slaughtered many creatures; your offenses are extremely heavy. From now on, besides striving in Buddha-recitation, you must all the more repent, and you must take up a vegetarian diet and strictly abstain from killing. Rebirth in the West is a share for every person, and it is very easy — by no means give up on yourself. I very much regret that I took up Buddha-recitation too late and that my practice was too poor; you ought to enter into practice as early as possible, as the essential thing.’ And so on.” After Layman Zhu had reported back, Wang Jueru's friends, hearing of this, all urged him to write it out and publish it, to awaken people's faith. Wang Jueru therefore wrote it plainly according to the facts, and appended to the manuscript a note: “I solemnly make this vow by the precepts: there is not a single false word, nor have I added or subtracted so much as one word of Layman Zhu's replies in the dream.” Yesterday he sent it by special letter to this journal, requesting its publication. We now publish his account to inform the monastic and lay community of the whole land.

blocks.text: The Effortless Rebirth of Layman Wei Guoxing

inline.s: Feeling the fleeting shadow of each inch of declining time, / dreading that the store of future merit is not yet amassed; / purifying the heart in the Dharma Hall, / adjusting the robe and facing the pure, / forgetful of sleep past midnight, / diligent from dawn till dusk.” This Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu pronounced; and such did Layman Guoxing of western Shu put into practice.
On March 7, 2003
the fifth day
of the second month
of the lunar calendar),

around Focheng Temple in Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, Sichuan Province, auspicious clouds gathered into a canopy, a gentle breeze wafted peacefully, sacred birds sang, and rare incense scented the air. At exactly noon, faint heavenly music was heard as the clouds parted like scattered blossoms. Within the temple, monks and laity gathered in a crowd and recited the Buddha's name in unison. Amitabha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and the pure and oceanlike assembly of Bodhisattvas, treading upon a thousand-petaled lotus, assembled in the sky above the Buddha Hall. More than three hundred people witnessed the Buddha with their own eyes; their emotion was uncontrollable, and weeping rose and fell in waves. Layman Wei Guoxing ascended the golden lotus platform and, amid the company of the Buddha and the host of Bodhisattvas, passed blissfully onward to the West, exactly as he had wished.
Layman Wei Guoxing was born on May 4, 1927
the fourth day
of the fourth month
of the lunar calendar),
in Xinglong Village, Third Cooperative, Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, Sichuan Province. Honest and sincere by nature, he made his living as a carpenter, and

he took refuge and received the precepts at Shengshui Temple. Deeply devoted to the Pure Land, he gave himself heart and soul to mindfulness of the Buddha, resolved with one mind to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Toward the Buddha's teachings he was reverent and respectful to the utmost; he never declined to do a good deed because it was small, nor engage in an evil one because it was small. Every wholesome undertaking — releasing living beings, printing sutras, giving charity, assisting at deathbed recitation, and supporting temples — he always strove to perform to the measure of his ability.

In 2002 he fell ill with esophageal cancer, and all the more diligently did he recite the Buddha's name. He said that for one who recites the Buddha's name, the appearance of karmic hindrances is a case of a heavy offense being repaid lightly, and a test from the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, so that one's rebirth at the end of life might be unobstructed. His family wished to send him to hospital for treatment, but he firmly declined, saying, “If I am to be hospitalized, let it be in the great hospital of Amitabha Buddha.” On this matter he asked the counsel of his master. Master Dexin instructed him: “At such a time you should redouble your efforts beyond ordinary measure. All the more concentrate your single mind and vigorously recite the Buddha's name; let go entirely of body and mind, and with utmost sincerity and earnestness seek rebirth as the essential matter. If your allotted years remain, the illness will heal of itself and create a wonder; if your allotted years are exhausted, then it is the time of your rebirth. At the very least you should strive to know the hour of your coming and, welcoming the Buddha's guidance, set an example for practitioners of recitation in later generations, and create a still greater wonder, benefiting countless sentient beings.” Hearing the master's instruction, his mind indeed opened and his understanding was freed, and he smiled radiantly. Before the Buddha he vowed to make the suffering of his illness a strengthening condition for his recitation and aspiration for rebirth, to let go utterly of his whole body and mind and the world, and to recite the Buddha's name with a wholly reverent heart, single-mindedly seeking rebirth in the Lotus Land.
One day he finally found Master Dexin and said, “Master, I have a joyful matter to tell you.”
What joyful matter?” asked Master Dexin.
He said, “While I was reciting the Buddha's name, the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas told me that in a few days they would come to take me to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

This was truly astonishing! How extraordinary! Hearing him say this, Master Dexin was filled with joy and exultation, and said to him with great earnestness, “Since you have attained such depth of practice and have received the Buddha's own prophecy, we should hold a seven-day recitation dharma assembly for your rebirth, to serve as a farewell with supportive chanting. On the day of the assembly you may follow Amitabha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva and be reborn in perfect freedom. You set the time.”
Then let it be the twenty-ninth.”
Good, then it is agreed!”
The assembly began on the twenty-ninth day of the first lunar month and concluded on the fifth day of the second lunar month, lasting exactly seven days.

On the day the assembly was fulfilled, he said to everyone, “I must bring this assembly to a perfect completion. Why? Because many suffering beings say: ‘You always say that studying the Buddha's Way is good — but where is the good

The good lies in freedom over birth and death. And where does that freedom lie? Let us look! I will do it right before your eyes. If I fall short in it, then those who study the Buddha's Way would be speaking falsely. Therefore, in completing this great undertaking of my practice of the Dharma, I am giving you a model to behold. These suffering beings are deluded and upside down — but reflect: the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics…”

On the day before his passing, he himself led the assembly to the edge of a stream to release living creatures, and together with them walked around the Buddha reciting and chanting. On the night before his passing, he spoke to the assembly, saying: “There are still eleven hours,” and after lowering his head to glance a while at the watch on his wrist, he went on: “I am a man who loves to renounce above all. Even when I went everywhere to spread the word, I too was renouncing; yet everyone was filled with doubt, doubting this very fact — just think of it, what on earth is this? If you do not believe me, then on the fifth day of this lunar month please come and see for yourselves. Some people say that this old man has lost his mind. I tell you, this is the truth. Let me report to you: why do I do this? People in this world, all of you must renounce (he uttered the word ‘renounce’ with a very heavy and earnest tone) before you can put on clothes, before you can take a bath, before you can even cut your toenails and leave (making a gesture of helplessly letting go of the world). I deliberately want to do something that has a bit of form to it. Why? I deliberately want, while still alive, to stay here at Focheng, Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, for seven days. These seven days I am holding my seven-day recitation retreat here. Each day I join in reciting sutras, bowing in repentance, circumambulating the Buddha, and walking while reciting — but those who were told to come in are all coming on the twenty-ninth to bow to the Buddha, chant the sutras, and bow in repentance, because there are many who came merely out of curiosity and doubted the twenty-ninth I spoke of. As for this rebirth dharma assembly of my practice ground, at the opening ceremony on the first day — the afternoon of the twenty-eighth — the president of the Sichuan Buddhist Association gave the opening address (he lowered his head and looked at his watch), and tomorrow, the fifth, in the afternoon the closing ceremony of the rebirth dharma assembly will be held to conclude it. I hope you all will not regard this practice ground as superstition, or as some sort of scheme, or as ghosts and spirits, or as some Falun Gong organization stirring up trouble at this place. You who recklessly talk nonsense and take Buddhism for superstition — Buddhism is education; it educates people to walk the right path, the road of prosperity. These people teach you to do no evil and to practice all good, to be filial to your parents, and to take filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness as the foundation. Of all virtues, filial piety is first; of all evils, lust is foremost. And now in this society everything has been turned into places of entertainment…”

At ten o'clock on the morning of the fifth day of the second lunar month, with two hours still to go before Layman Wei's passing, he held a farewell ceremony together with the more than fifteen hundred lay practitioners present and those who had come to watch the spectacle. The venerable elder bowed and offered incense before the Buddha in the great hall with calm composure, and finally gave an instruction to the assembly: “Venerable ones, good and wise friends, fellow practitioners, honored guests, and good people all — today is the day of my passing, and the seven-day recitation dharma assembly for rebirth has come to a perfect and successful conclusion. On this last day of parting, I thank you all for your care!” At that moment everyone was deeply stirred, overcome with a mingled grief and joy.

Thereupon Master Dexin, together with Layman Wei's family and the monastic and lay assembly, escorted him slowly into the Rebirth Hall of the lay practitioners' building. Before the Buddha, with utmost reverence, he prostrated and offered incense, then sat upright on a wooden chair, his hands forming the Amitabha mudra, and chanted the Buddha's name aloud with the assembly. Suddenly auspicious light entered the room, and a rare fragrance and sublime music arose — all who saw and heard it felt at once a peace of body and mind. When they looked again, Layman Wei Guoxing had already passed calmly away in the Buddha's presence. Freedom over birth and death — a song sung for a thousand ages; the art of reciting the Buddha's name at its utmost peak. From ancient times, masters of the Chan school and the teaching schools have stood dense as a forest in their great attainments; those who have transcended birth and death, left the dust, and been freed from the wheel of suffering, and who have done so as they willed, have never gone beyond this summit.

In lay life, Layman Wei Guoxing was but a carpenter, no man of high intellect or uncommon gifts; in a mere three or five years he recited the Buddha's name and was reborn in the Buddha-land — an attainment without precedent and beyond compare, enough to move heaven and earth and make spirits weep. From this it is fully proven that the words of the Buddha and the patriarchs are not false: whether the simple man or the simple woman, the wise or the virtuous, if one but gives rise to heartfelt faith and vows, and with all one's heart recites the Buddha's name seeking rebirth, all attain it equally — of a myriad who practice, a myriad go. Master Yinguang said: “One should give rise to a resolute, earnest vow: may I be freed from the suffering of the Saha world, may I obtain the bliss of the Pure Land. The urgency of this vow should be like one who has fallen into a latrine pit desperately seeking to get out, or like one bound in prison longing for home; since one's own strength cannot free one, one must beg someone of great power to pull one out.” He also said: “A single ‘Namo Amitabha Buddha’ — once you have recited it to the point of familiarity, there is still abundant power left over to become a Buddha! What regret is there in not studying other methods?” May all beings know that the light of life is as fleeting as lightning, and be wary of the dangers of the wheel of transmigration; uphold the Name and recite the Buddha, and attain success in this very life. Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha! “Unify the six faculties, and let the pure thought continue without break — this is foremost” indeed!
Recorded by Dharma Master Zhixing

blocks.text: On the Practice of Assisting the Dying toward Rebirth

inline.s: In this life, the suffering of illness is the hardest of all to bear. When illness leads to death, the pain is all the more bitter. At such a moment, if the assisting recitation is done effectively, one can turn thoughts of suffering into right mindfulness and, by virtue of the power of that vow, attain rebirth. Yet there are many different ways of assisting recitation, and unless they come from tested experience, some may even disturb the dying so that they cannot attain rebirth — this must be regarded with deep care. I recently met Dharma Master Tonghui and spoke with him about the method of assisting recitation. According to his practical experience, two points are most essential, and I record them as follows.

1. Whenever one accompanies a dying patient toward rebirth, there should be at least three people to a group. The voice should be clear and distinct, not too loud, so as not to disturb the patient. At first recite the six-syllable name (Namo Amituofo); when the patient is at the point of crisis, one should change to the four-syllable name (Amituofo), so that although the patient's strength is slight he can still follow — with six syllables his breath would fail. If the patient has already ceased breathing, change back to the six-syllable Buddha-name and continue until the recitation is brought to a complete conclusion.

2. If the patient senses that he is being harassed by demons, and suffers so that he can hardly bear it, continuing for days without relief, one should then invite three people who can recite the Śūraṅgama Mantra to recite it together, at least three times. By virtue of that mantra's power the evil demons will depart far away, the patient will be free of suffering, and he can then lift up right mindfulness and be reborn in the West.

May this merit adorn the Buddha's Pure Land; / Above, may it repay the fourfold graciousness; / Below, may it relieve the three paths of suffering. / May all who see and hear this / Awaken the bodhi mind; / When this body of retribution is ended, / May we together be reborn in the Land of Bliss!
Namo Amitabha Buddha
Namo Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva
Namo Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva
